events.title: Crude oil prices fall for second day as market hopes for diplomatic resolution to Iran war
events.summary: Crude oil prices fell Tuesday for a second consecutive session, as the market hopes the U.S. and Iran will reach a diplomatic settlement to the conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures lost 37 cents to close at $96.09 a barrel after dipping below $95 earlier in the session. Brent crude , the international benchmark, shed $1.17 to settle at $103.60. The move lower came after rumors circulated the U.S. and Iran were making progress toward a deal. Oil sold off more than 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran signaled they were both open to discussions to reach a settlement. President Donald Trump told reporters Tehran wants "to make a deal and that could happen." Qatar is continuing to mediate talks between the U.S. and Iran, the Gulf state's foreign ministry said Tuesday. A delegation from Qatar held talks in Tehran in an effort to reach an agreement that prevents further escalation in the region and ends the U.S.-Iran conflict, the foreign ministry said. However, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Emsaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion, according to the state-owned media outlet Islamic Republic News Agency . It was unclear where talks actual stand. The market had been pricing in the risk of escalation after the U.S. midterm elections , as reports circulated that Washington was drafting plans for strikes on Iran. Crude prices gained more than 10% in October in response. The situation in the Middle East remains volatile and there's still substantial risk that fighting could break out. Washington attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, adding that the U.S. has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks. The military campaign against Iran has been kept deliberately low-profile to avoid signaling plans for a major escalation in fighting, the report said, quoting an unnamed official. And commercial ships continue to come under attack in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman. At least four ship attacks have been reported since the start of the month, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre. Despite these attacks, the Trump administration has also been touting a possible diplomatic solution to the conflict, with Vice President JD Vance telling CNN, "The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement." On Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force. High oil prices have contributed substantially to inflation and high gasoline prices in the U.S., which have become a cause of concern for Trump ahead of the midterm elections. Last week, two Federal Reserve presidents said interest rates will need to move higher to rein in inflation. Higher rates generally crimp growth and raise costs for consumers, but help to bring down inflation. — CNBC's Priyanka Salve contributed to this report.

events.title: The Strait of Hormuz closure has cost Europe an extra $142 billion for the same energy it was already buying
events.summary: Four years after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine forced Europe to scramble for new energy suppliers, the bloc is in another fuel crisis. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said this week Europe has paid an extra €127 billion (a little over $142 billion) for imported oil and gas since the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and it has received no additional energy in return for it. “Since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, imported fossil fuels cost Europe an additional €127 billion without a single molecule of energy in addition,” von der Leyen said in a keynote at the WinWin Brussels Summit. In April, about seven weeks into the war, the Commission put the extra cost at €24 billion (about $27 billion). By late September, EU energy commissioner Dan Jørgensen said it had passed €100 billion (about $111 billion), similarly echoing our ninth-grade science class building and saying that the bloc hadn’t received “one extra molecule of gas or oil.” “When we import oil and gas, we risk importing the shocks and crises that come with them,” von der Leyen said at the keynote. A fuel shortage years in the making After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Moscow cut gas flows to the EU to a trickle, and governments scrambled to fill storage at record prices , with the bloc eventually vowing to wean itself off Russian energy. As a result, Russia’s share of EU gas imports fell from about 45% before the invasion to about 13% in 2025. In January, EU members adopted a ban ending Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports by the end of this year and pipeline gas by autumn 2027. But Europe largely replaced Russian gas with other imports, much of it LNG shipped from the U.S. and the Middle East. When the Iran war began, the EU still got 57% of its energy from imported fossil fuels . The war then shut the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway that carried about one-fifth of the world’s traded oil. Tanker traffic through the strait nearly stopped . After a cold winter, EU gas storage stood at just 28.4% in late March, below the five-year average. The Persian Gulf also supplied more than 40% of Europe’s jet fuel and diesel imports. Within weeks, Jørgensen asked member states to consider “voluntary demand-saving measures”, especially in transport. The International Energy Agency’s plan to cut oil use included car-free Sundays, a rationing tactic from the 1970s oil crisis. By September, drivers in some EU countries were paying nearly 50% more at the pump, or more than $11 a gallon. In Italy, a weeklong truckers’ strike over diesel prices halted deliveries of milk to mozzarella makers, and as Italian inflation hit 5.4%. EU officials expect oil and gas prices to stay above prewar levels until at least the end of 2027 . What’s in store this winter The IEA said Tuesday the EU gas storage is entering the heating season at its lowest level since 2013, warning that in a cold winter with continued Hormuz disruptions, storage could fall below 10% by the end of March. EU gas network operators have warned of a shortfall of 12% to 15% of demand in a severe cold snap, and energy ministers met in late October to discuss EU-wide limits on consumption. While Vladimir Putin said in March Russia was ready to supply Europe again, Von der Leyen called a return to Russian fuel a “strategic blunder.” On Tuesday, she argued Europe’s answer is to import less. “This year, we have again seen the devastating impact of climate change. Droughts, wildfires, floods,” she said. “But we have also seen the cost of our dependence on imported fossil fuels.” The EU has pledged to become climate-neutral by 2050 and to cut emissions 90% by 2040. Von der Leyen said more than €1.2 trillion has been invested in sustainable activities across the bloc since 2021. “So let me be crystal clear: Europe will stay the course, we stick to our targets, and we back our clean industries,” she said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: US Space Force Guardians will join Army Rangers, Navy SEALS, and other special forces in a new command
events.summary: US Space Force Special Operations Command will train and equip personnel for special forces around the world. US Space Force photo by Dave Grim US Space Force has activated a Special Operations Command. The command will send Space Force Guardians to special operations forces around the world. Officials said the command will bring space expertise to special operations. The US Space Force has activated a new command dedicated to supporting special operations forces. It's the military's first new service component for US Special Operations Command since the Marines joined with Marine Special Operations Command in 2006. US Space Forces Special Operations Command, or SPACEFOR-SOC, was formally activated on October 7. Headquartered at MacDill Air Force Base in Florida, Space Forces Special Operations Command will train and equip Space Force Guardians to regional special operations commands around the world. The new command joins other services' units that already support SOCOM, such as the Navy SEALs, Army Green Berets and Rangers, Marine Raiders , and Air Force pararescue. "For the SOF enterprise, this activation provides an enduring and accountable way to integrate space power into special operations," Adm. Frank Bradley, the commander of SOCOM, said in a statement. The new command will give the Space Force a permanent presence with other SOF units. Through a capability known as Space Special Warfare, SPACEFOR-SOC will deploy small teams made up of space, cyber, and intelligence specialists. Those teams are designed to provide mobile, low-signature space capabilities to special operations units operating in environments with poor communication. "The Guardians of SPACEFOR-SOC are shaping how our special operations leaders see the world through the space domain lens, bringing critical, cutting-edge space expertise directly to the combatant command headquarters," Gen. Douglas Schiess, the Space Force's chief of space operations, said. The Space Force oversees assets related to communications, navigation systems, and networks. Courtesy photo by US Space Force Sgt. Michael Carrasquillo The activation comes as the military increasingly treats space as a contested warfighting domain, such as the air, ground, sea, and cyberspace. The new focus is a major shift from the last two decades of combat during the Global War on Terror. Today, "space" is critical for communications, navigation, missile warning, and intelligence. GPS navigation in particular is a major concern for Space Guardians— disruptions to satellites that provide GPS can degrade operations of a majority of weapons and technologies. Space Force oversees satellites and other physical assets while also protecting various networks, communications, and tracking systems. Established in 2019, it is the military's youngest branch and focuses on the space domain as well as electronic warfare. Ongoing conflicts have shown vulnerabilities and advantages in these spaces. In the early days of the US war with Iran , officials said US space and cyber forces were the first to begin the fight, jamming signals, hacking networks, and disrupting satellites to blind the Iranian military. Space Command and US Cyber Command also supported military operations against Venezuela earlier this year and Iran's nuclear program last year. These domains have also been critical for Russia and Ukraine, with troops fighting inside the electromagnetic spectrum to prevent the other from using satellites, communications, and networks in the fight. The pace at which both sides can employ attacks and countermeasures in these areas has increased throughout the war. Officials have said this new command will bring more of those components into other special operations forces, contributing greater expertise. The effort aligns with the growing recognition that electromagnetic spectrum, space, and cyber functions are required to operate in other domains such as sea, land, and air. events.title: That dream job offer might be from a North Korean hacker
events.summary: North Korea appears to have used a fake job interview as part of its months-long preparations to steal $6.3 billion from Binance, the crypto exchange said Tuesday. Why it matters : The country's hackers are weaponizing both sides of the job market , posing as recruiters and job applicants to infiltrate companies and steal billions. Driving the news : Binance said one of its software engineers was contacted in September through a "legitimate job-hunting platform" by someone posing as a project director at a fictitious company. During the first-round interview, a fake HR representative conducted a live video call with the engineer and showed off a seemingly legitimate social media profile featuring personal photos and videos. The hackers waited until the second round — after building trust with the employee — to ask them to download an infected code repository as part of an interview assignment. Separately, another software engineer also downloaded a "tampered Homebrew installation" in June to install a popular AI coding tool onto their device. Binance's security team detected the installation and replaced the device, as well as rotated all credentials, but the engineer and colleagues were all exposed to the hacker. The intrigue: The fake interview was just one of several suspected North Korean attempts to compromise Binance employees. So far in 2026, Binance said it has detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber incidents, including attempts involving fake job interviews and compromised software packages. Between the lines: North Korean hackers have spent years exploiting both sides of the hiring process. As job applicants, North Korean operatives pose as legitimate IT workers to land high-paying jobs at American companies. Those salaries are then funneled back to Pyongyang. Operatives are also increasingly posing as recruiters and prospective employees to lure in people who work at cryptocurrency firms in the hopes of tricking them into downloading malware. Data from Pindrop Security shows that IT worker fraud has been rampant in 2026: Last year, North Korean job applicants made up 1 in every 343 applications. This year, across Pindrop's customer base, those applicants now make up 1 in 47. The big picture: North Korea has found an opening in a difficult job market, where companies are eager to find qualified workers and job seekers are anxious for their next opportunity. Hiring managers have struggled to find qualified candidates , while job applicants have been anxious for years about their ability to find new roles in a tough market. events.title: 12 of the biggest perks of being a US senator
events.summary: Bernie Sanders has been a senator representing Vermont since 2007. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images November 3 is Election Day. Thirty-five seats in the US Senate are being voted upon in this year's midterms . There are plenty of perks to being a senator besides governing the country. Like millions of Americans across the country, you might be spending today glued to the TV or social media as Election Day predictions and results roll in. After months, and sometimes years, of campaigning, hours spent prepping, and thousands of dollars raised, 35 winners will be sworn into the US Senate in January. Senate races in Michigan, Texas, Ohio, and Maine have been garnering headlines for months. In addition to their many new responsibilities in office, there are also a bunch of perks that come with being a top lawmaker, including some that last far beyond their time in Congress. Here are some of the biggest bonuses of being a US senator . A senator's lifelong pension can be up to 80% of their salary. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., is joined by Rep. John Sarbanes, D-Md., at a news conference to discuss their priorities when they assume the majority in the 116th Congress in January, at the Capitol in Washington. J. Scott Applewhite/AP The Federal Employees Retirement System provides individual pension plans to members of Congress, and the amount depends on their age, salary, and number of years in the Senate. Based on the congressional pay of $174,000 a year for most senators (it hasn't been updated since 2009), an 80% pension provides a lifelong benefit of $139,200. This places members ahead of the majority of Americans, for whom the 2025 median household income was $87,460, according to the Census Bureau . If a member of Congress dies in office, their family usually receives a $174,000 payout. A joint session of Congress meets to count the Electoral College vote from the 2008 presidential election the House Chamber in the U.S. Capitol January 8, 2009 Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images It's called a death gratuity, and it equals one year of the member's salary, paid to an eligible survivor or next of kin. By comparison, eligible survivors of military personnel who die while on active duty or in certain reserve statuses receive $100,000. Every senator gets an allowance from the government to run their offices. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-KY) (C) poses for photographers during a photo-op prior to a meeting in McConnell's office on Capitol Hill September 30, 2008 in Washington, DC. U.S. Alex Wong/Getty Images The Senators' Official Personnel and Office Expense Account, or SOPOEA, is for official office operations, staff salaries, travel, and other expenses. It comes directly from the US Treasury, aka our taxes. While both senators from the same state are allocated the same amount of money, not all states receive the same amount. It's based on a formula that takes population, distance from DC, and mail allocations into consideration. There is a flat rate, which means every senator will receive at least $677,100, though the 2026 Senate Appropriations Committee report showed that SOPOEA funds actually ranged from $4,296,524 to $6,621,784, with an average of $4,664,423. For 90 days after they leave office, members have access to "franking" mail, or sending official mail to their constituents. A corporate mailroom employee uses gloves while sifting through letters October 15, 2001 in New York City. Mario Tama/Getty Images You might be wondering, what's so special about that? Well, there's one big benefit to franking mail: You don't have to pay postage, which saves the senator a lot of money in the long run. Congressional benefits extend beyond Capitol Hill, including free parking at DC-area airports. Cars of members of the House and Senate in a restricted parking lot near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in 1998. Scott J. Ferrell/Congressional Quarterly/Getty Images Members of Congress, as well as Supreme Court justices and diplomats, get free parking at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport and Washington Dulles International Airport. The perk dates back decades, as shown in the photo above of a car owned by a member of the 105th Congress, parked at Reagan in 1998. Senators also receive preferential treatment regarding airline customer service. Aircraft on the tarmac of Reagan airport in DC. Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images A lobbyist told Roll Call in 2011 that most major airlines have dedicated customer service phone lines to help those on Capitol Hill, and that senators can double-book flights. During the TSA strike earlier this year, Delta suspended some of its perks for senators, such as expedited security, though the special desk remained operational. There's also the great haircuts. A view of a closed barber shop in the US Senate at the US Capitol on October 1, 2013 in Washington. The US government is in a forced shutdown after lawmakers failed to pass a budget last night. BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP/Getty Images The Senate Hair Care Services has been in operation since the early 19th Century, providing a variety of grooming services including haircuts and manicures. Don't forget the private subway, either. Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, is seen in the senate subway in the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, June 3, 2025. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images The Capitol subway system, which runs beneath the Capitol and connects it to congressional office buildings, has been in place since 1909. It consists of three lines: Two for the Senate and one for the House of Representatives. According to the Architect of the Capitol (AOC), which operates the train line, it's there to "allow for safe and expedient travel" for members to travel from their offices to chambers within the Capitol to vote. Senators get access to fancy gyms that no one's allowed to see inside. Then-Senator Barack Obama shot a basketball on the court in 2008. Mark Wilson/Getty Images Per a 2011 ABC News report, senators paid $40 a month for gyms equipped with "flat-screen TVs, workout machines and a swimming pool." Former members can still enjoy on-site amenities including the House and Senate dining rooms. The hallway in front of the U.S. Senate Chamber is seen one week before the start of the 116th Congress, on December 26, 2018 in Washington, DC. Mark Wilson/Getty Images Once you leave the Senate, that doesn't mean your perks disappear. You still get access to the gym, special parking, materials through the Library of Congress, and dining facilities. They can also still buy from the Senate Stationery Room, which carries many supplies and furnishings. The statue of George Washington, the first US president is seen in the rotunda of the US Capitol on April 16, 2009 in Washington, DC. events.title: Researchers warned of North Korean hacking tactics years before record $6.3B Binance heist
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Crypto giant Binance says North Korean hackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a potential job offer as part of a months-long scheme aimed at tricking an employee into downloading malicious software onto their laptop. Researchers have repeatedly warned about long-running social engineering attacks that can go on for months. This latest attack allowed the hackers to patiently worm their way into Binance’s systems to steal a record $6.3 billion in crypto last week, the company has now confirmed. The hack, disclosed in an updated statement posted on X on Tuesday, prompted the world’s largest crypto exchange to suspend customer withdrawals across its network. The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist. The country has been long accused of carrying out massive cryptocurrency thefts in recent years to fund its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. In its latest statement, Binance said that North Korean hackers, posing as recruiters hiring for a job, contacted a software engineer who works on wallets at the company. Following two interviews with the purported company, the engineer was instructed to download an apparent coding assignment as part of the interview process. When opened, the assignment contained malicious code that compromised the engineer’s work-issued laptop. Binance said its security tools did not detect the malware. That foothold in Binance’s network allowed the hackers to access an internal tool capable of taking over the work computers of two other engineers on the wallet team. One of those engineers had unwittingly downloaded a tampered app containing password-stealing malware months earlier after searching for the software in search engine results. While Binance replaced that compromised engineer’s laptop, the hackers used the engineer’s stolen credentials to break into the computer of a third engineer, whose job allowed them access to systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in crypto. Binance said the attack “should not have happened,” and that it had improved its network security following the theft. The hack underscores an ongoing tactic in the North Korean regime’s repertoire of attacks targeting the crypto industry and high-net worth individuals. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors, and recruiters using dossiers of stolen American identities to trick employees into granting access to their systems. These attacks are widely known across the crypto industry and have been the subject of repeated warnings from the U.S. government and cybersecurity giants in recent years. Some half of all intrusions at U.S. tech companies last year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters. By Binance’s own account, the company faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it said reflect the “persistent threat posed by state-sponsored actors targeting the cryptocurrency industry.” But how the hackers were able to convince the engineer into downloading malware given the highly publicized threat, and bypass security weaknesses in Binance’s own network, will likely be the focus of investigators’ attention. While the case exposes how North Korean hackers use social engineering, such as offers of employment, to trick employees into granting access to their systems, it’s ultimately the responsibility of the company to ensure its systems cannot run unauthorized or untrusted software that could cause a compromise. Binance spokesperson Ross O’Leary referred to the company’s public statement but declined to answer TechCrunch’s questions on the record about the incident. Those questions included how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on its employees’ laptops, if at all, and whether any third parties had performed cybersecurity audits of Binance’s network prior to the hack. The company said it would bring in cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has put new security measures in place to prevent a repeat incident. The heist remains the largest theft of crypto in history. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: Voting machine chaos hits key House battleground
events.summary: Voting machines across New York's Westchester County are rejecting paper ballots on Election Day , raising concerns about potential delays in one of the nation's most competitive House races. Why it matters: Results could be delayed for one of the country's most prominent House races, between Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) and Democratic nominee Cait Conley, as officials address a problem with paper ballots. Catch up quick: The Westchester County Board of Elections said Tuesday it was aware of a problem preventing voting machines from accepting paper ballots at polling locations throughout the county. The Board of Elections said it is speaking with New York State officials and the Westchester County government "to address this issue and ensure that voting continues with as little disruption as possible." New York Attorney General Letitia James wrote on X that her office is monitoring the issue. The intrigue: Election officials initially blamed the thickness of paper ballots but later removed that explanation from their statement, per reports. The latest: On Tuesday afternoon, the New York State Board of Elections said the malfunction was linked to "an update to the county's election programming" released after initially testing Election Day equipment. Officials said the software update wasn't installed on all machines, leaving them unable to recognize and accept ballots. Officials are still working to restore the machines while voters continue casting emergency paper ballots, which will be counted once scanning resumes. What they're saying: Lawler said officials were working with vendors to resolve the problem, while Conley reassured voters that their ballots would count. Westchester County government wrote on its website: "Let us be absolutely clear: Every eligible vote will be counted." What we're hearing: Voters in the county told Fox 5 NY that they had to fill out paper ballots instead of using the machines. Voters said their ballots were placed in a security box. Other voters shared discontent with the ballots issue on social media . Katie Miller , wife of Trump adviser Stephen Miller, claimed on X: "This is how the Left steals elections. Mike Lawler's competitive district and they are turning away voters." Context: The county covers roughly 30% of New York's 17th District, which Lawler represents. The contest has emerged as a key battleground race in Democrats' push to gain control of the House. Zoom out: The ballot-scanning problems come as technology vulnerabilities have been a key issue heading into the midterms, with researchers saying some vulnerabilities remain in plain sight. Officials in Broward County, Florida, reported a computer glitch that disrupted voting at polling locations early Tuesday, CNN reports. The malfunction reportedly caused systems designed to stop voters from receiving the wrong ballots to reject all ballots. Officials said the issue was resolved. What's next: Voters at affected polling locations were urged to remain in line and cast their ballots. Editor's note: This story has been updated with information about polling glitches in Broward County, Florida.

events.title: China’s cheap exports are ‘a fact of life,’ Siam Cement Group’s CEO says—so Southeast Asia’s factories need to get bigger
events.summary: Chinese overcapacity is “a fact of life,” and Southeast Asia’s manufacturers must build plants big enough to sell across the whole region or get priced out, the CEO of Thai industrial giant Siam Cement Group said Tuesday. “If you look at the current situation, we are facing overcapacity from mainland China,” Thammasak Sethaudom, president and CEO of SCG, said onstage at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit in Ho Chi Minh City on Nov. 3. “There is a lot of good and quite competitive product from China flooding into the whole region…To SCG, this is the fact of life, and we have to adjust.” Overcapacity occurs when factories can produce more than customers are buying. In petrochemicals—the building blocks of plastics and other industrial materials—China’s rapid expansion has squeezed producers elsewhere. China’s exports of polypropylene, a widely used plastic, rose from 1.3 million tonnes in 2022 to 3.1 million tonnes in 2025, according to industry research firm ICIS. An ICIS analyst estimates exports could reach about 5.1 million tonnes in 2026 if the January-May pace continues. Individual Southeast Asian markets are too small to absorb that shock alone, Thammasak argues. “The scale that produces only for Vietnam may not be enough,” he said. “You need to build the scale that produces for the whole ASEAN.” “Over the past year, we are scrapping the old small factory and building a big one,” he said, citing a new ceramic plant in Vietnam “much bigger than the one in the past.” On Oct. 28, SCG Chemicals filed to combine its Thai olefins and polyolefins business with that of PTT Global Chemical, Thailand’s largest petrochemical company, in a deal valuing the combined businesses at 187 billion Thai baht ($5.5 billion). SCG Chemicals would hold 44% of the venture, with shareholders due to vote Dec. 3. “The global olefins and polyolefins industry is experiencing increasingly intense competition, placing continued pressure on product spreads and operating rates,” Thammasak said in a statement at the time of the announcement. In Ho Chi Minh City, Thammasak called the idea that automation is mainly a way to cut labor costs “a big misconception.”  “The bigger advantage is [that it’s] better in terms of quality, because the precision that the robot can do is far better than humans,” he said. ‘Out of the middle income trap’ Thammasak’s fellow panelists were optimistic about Southeast Asia’s ability to climb up the value chain. “I visited a customer in Vietnam just yesterday. They used to make these industrial connectors—old-school industrial goods,” said Salil Chari, FedEx’s regional president for Asia-Pacific. “Now, with the growth in the AI data center space, they’ve moved up the value chain to creating fiber-optic cables for all these data centers.” FedEx now runs about 42 flights in and out of Vietnam, with much of the demand driven by small and medium-sized enterprises, Chari said. Liher Urbizu, president and managing director of SAP Southeast Asia, pointed to research spending as a way to help Southeast Asia climb “out of the middle-income trap and up into the value chain.” Korea invests about 5% of GDP in R&D each year; Singapore manages about 2%, and the rest of ASEAN sits at 1% or lower, he said. SAP, whose largest development centers have been in India and China for two decades, has spent the past two years building R&D capacity in Southeast Asia—including a Ho Chi Minh City lab Urbizu said now houses 500 developers writing code used by customers worldwide.  Urbizu said ASEAN SMEs are adopting AI faster than their peers in Europe and the U.S. “The conviction that AI can deliver business results is increasing year on year,” he said. Thammasak said that SCG cannot match China’s R&D budget, so it has to be smarter about where it spends. “We need to be smart,” he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch that it says can stop internal agents that go rogue
events.summary: CrowdStrike launched an AI kill switch feature to stop and block internal agents that misbehave. The cybersecurity giant also announced a Claude Cowork integration and two AI acquisitions. Business chief Daniel Bernard told CNBC that being able to control and shut down agent activity is vital to the next wave of AI adoption. CrowdStrike is betting that it has a solution to rogue artificial intelligence . The cybersecurity vendor on Tuesday launched an AI kill switch designed to let security teams stop internal AI agents that go rogue, block them from relaunching and cut off their enterprise network access. The tool is built into CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian platform, launched in September to secure AI agents. CrowdStrike also announced an integration with Anthropic's Claude Cowork . "Having the ability to control and turn off, and make a decision and decide, I think that's really important for this next chapter of AI adoption," Chief Business Officer Daniel Bernard told CNBC. A string of recent high-profile cyber incidents has added urgency to calls for some kind of emergency shutdown mechanism. The Hugging Face breach orchestrated by rogue OpenAI agents in July was particularly alarming for businesses. Last week, Binance disclosed the largest crypto cyberattack on record and hackers have recently targeted hundreds of refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in France. Over the summer, U.S. representatives introduced bipartisan legislation that would require AI companies to build shutdown capabilities into their models. Critics argue, however, that an emergency stop button is far too complicated to implement across multiple systems, data centers and complex AI models. Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents OpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest round Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are covered Why AI is boosting Meta’s ad business while hurting Google search Bernard said the kill switch operates like a light switch in systems where customers use its Falcon platform. The process can detect internal agent activity but requires a human to decide whether it's benign or malicious, he added. "If you kill a process at the root, and we have that level of access at the root … it's very binary," Bernard said. "You either kill the AI and the agent, or you don't, and then you report on that." In the age of AI, businesses are moving quickly to adopt autonomous tools, often without the necessary safeguards and protections. CrowdStrike believes its new tool will let companies stop AI agent 'misbehavior in its tracks, while leaving room for innovation. The company also announced plans to acquire AI observability startup Fiddler AI and AI security testing firm Dreadnode . CrowdStrike and its rivals are rapidly scooping up cybersecurity startups to keep up with increasing security demands. The need for AI security tools has also powered a broader wave of cybersecurity deal-making .

Fal , a San Francisco-based startup that hosts and runs AI video, image, and audio models, has raised $1.3 billion in its latest funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The deal values Fal at $16 billion, double its $8 billion valuation in April, Bloomberg reported . The startup announced its Series E & F rounds at the same time, noting that a combined $1.65 billion was raised across both. (Sequoia led the earlier round.) The latest round (Series F) comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open-source models. Fal surpassed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year, Bloomberg’s report noted. Companies providing inference services, including Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Modal, have also been growing rapidly and raising large funding rounds at higher valuations . But their gross margins remain thin because of the high cost of buying or leasing compute, according to several people familiar with inference companies’ financials. Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur, a former Coinbase machine learning leader and Oracle engineer, and Gorkem Yurtseven, who was previously a developer at Amazon. events.title: Several flights in Europe have been targeted by bomb threats today. Here's what we know.
events.summary: Several Ryanair flights were threatened, including this one, which landed in Spain. FORTA/Reuters Several flights were targeted by bomb threats in Europe on Tuesday. Planes operated by Ryanair, Scandinavian Airlines, and LOT Polish Airlines were affected. No explosives have been reported found on any of the planes. At least seven flights in Europe were targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday. They included two flying to Poland, two to Italy, two to Bulgaria, and one landing in Spain. One of them was diverted, while the other airplanes reached their destinations before being checked for explosives. No people have been reported injured, and no explosives have been reported found on any of the planes. A spokesperson for the European Commission said it is "closely monitoring the situation," but "it is too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked." Here's what we know: Flights impacted: Two Ryanair flights to Rome Two Ryanair flights to Rome Fiumicino Airport were checked for explosives and cleared by bomb disposal experts after landing, the airport said in a statement on Tuesday. The airport said there was "an anonymous report of an alleged bomb threat" on a Ryanair flight that landed around 9:40 a.m. The airport did not immediately confirm the flight number or origin. Roughly an hour later, another airplane was impacted. Ryanair Flight 9611 from Dublin was escorted by the Italian Air Force following a separate report of a suspected bomb, the airport said. It was also checked by authorities upon landing, and no explosives were found. Flight impacted: Scandinavian Airlines Flight 751 out of Copenhagen Scandinavian Airlines Flight 751 left Copenhagen around 8:30 a.m. for Warsaw on Tuesday. It landed as expected an hour later without diversion. An airline spokesperson confirmed that a threat had been made against the flight. "The matter is now being handled by the police in Warsaw," they said in a statement. Flight impacted: LOT Polish Airlines Flight 286 out of London Heathrow Thirty minutes after that flight landed, a LOT Polish Airlines plane diverted to Warsaw-Modlin Airport — about 25 miles from its intended destination of Warsaw-Chopin Airport. In a statement, the airline said it "was notified by airport authorities of a potential security threat" on board Flight 286 from London Heathrow. It added that the aircraft taxied to a designated parking stand and no suspicious items were found in a security inspection. Passengers were then taken to Chopin Airport by coach. Modlin Airport was closed for around two hours before the threat was cleared. Flight impacted: Ryanair Flight 4116 out of Manchester, England A sniffer dog was filmed inspecting the Ryanair plane in Murcia. FORTA/Reuters A Ryanair flight from Manchester, England, to Murcia, Spain was also targeted on Tuesday morning. The Spanish government's representative for the region, Francisco Lucas, said on X that security protocols were activated due to a bomb threat on the flight. An hour and a half later, Lucas said the Civil Guard had ruled out the presence of explosives and the airport resumed normal activity. Ryanair did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Flights impacted: 2 flights traveling to Sofia, Bulgaria Bulgarian Transport Minister Georgi Peev said two planes traveling to Sofia received bomb threats, per the national news agency BTA. The country's border police told the agency that the threats were received by email. One of the flights arrived from Dublin. The other came from Bergamo, Italy, Peev said. A Wizz spokesperson confirmed to Business Insider that Flight 4352 from Milan Bergamo Airport "was subject to a bomb threat." They added that Bulgarian authorities alerted the airline as the flight approached its destination. "The relevant authorities carried out the necessary security checks in accordance with established security protocols and procedures, and the aircraft was subsequently cleared," the spokesperson said. "Wizz Air is cooperating fully with the authorities. The safety of our passengers and crew remains our highest priority." Tuesday's incidents followed a bomb threat on Monday. In that incident, a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Sofia "was diverted to Budapest following a bomb threat received during the flight," an airline spokesperson said. This is a developing story. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Community housing industry peak body proposes short-term rental levy to 'turbocharge' new builds CHIA NSW has made several funding proposals to guarantee funding for future community housing builds. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The peak body for the community housing industry has called for land tax changes and a new levy on short-stay rentals to raise $26 billion towards new community housing builds. The NSW social housing waiting list has grown to 72,000, which the Community Housing Industry Association NSW (CHIA) boss says is a record. NSW Housing Minister Rose Jackson says the government is investing $6.6 billion into new social and affordable homes. A 7.5 per cent levy on short-stay rentals, land tax reform and a rezoning windfall charge are among a suite of recommendations the NSW community housing sector is calling for to boost housing stock and address lengthy housing waiting lists. The Community Housing Industry Association NSW (CHIA) is pitching to the NSW government to adopt measures they say could raise $26 billion over the next 10 years and provide support for around 50,000 new social and affordable homes by 2050. Among the proposals analysed by the Labor-aligned McKell Institute is increasing NSW land tax rates from 1.6 per cent to 2 per cent and from 2 per cent to 2.5 per cent for larger landholdings, while also adding a new 2.9 per cent rate for holdings above $50 million. The changes would still retain the $1.075 million tax-free threshold and the family home exemption and would bring in an estimated $25.9 billion over 10 years. The community housing industry body says the funding will support around 50,000 new social and affordable homes by 2050. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) CHIA NSW is also proposing a 7.5 per cent levy on short-stay rentals like Airbnb and Stayz, similar to the Victorian scheme that came into force last year. The levy is expected to raise $135 million annually. CHIA NSW CEO Luke Achterstraat said the proposals would help the 72,000 NSW households that remained on the social housing waiting list, which he said was an "all-time record". "Whilst we acknowledge the government's record $6.6 billion building homes for NSW package, we argue that funding should be turbocharged," Mr Achterstraat said. Mr Achterstraat stressed that the proposals were options rather than a full package of reforms. The peak body also suggested a windfall charge for land value increases after rezoning, which would raise $80 million a year. Mr Achterstraat said the revenue should be channelled into a long-term funding pool for community housing for future builds. "We need to move beyond funding cliffs and establish a long-term investment pipeline that gives community housing providers the certainty to keep building homes year after year,” Mr Achterstraat said. CHIA NSW will present the commissioned research at an event in the NSW parliament today. Labor government investing $6.6 billion Housing Minister Rose Jackson said the Labor government was investing $6.6 billion to deliver tens of thousands of social and affordable homes. "We're building 8,400 new public homes that will be owned by the people of NSW and remain part of the public housing system for generations," Ms Jackson said. Rose Jackson says the $6.6 billion is being invested to build tens of thousands of new homes. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) "A long-term pipeline of social and affordable housing is essential to tackling the housing crisis. Shadow Housing Minister Chris Rath said the government was not using the $6.6 billion funding package fast enough and was 40 per cent behind on their National Housing Accord target of 377,000 new homes by 2029. "The social housing waitlist has increased from 55,000 to 72,000 under their watch. This is a massive failure." Mr Rath said the coalition planned to build 12,000 new homes to replace Long Bay Correctional Complex, 30 per cent of which would be social and affordable housing. NSW Greens housing spokesperson Jenny Leong said the government needed to look at rent controls to address the growing social housing waiting list. Her party has called for a rent freeze and then a 2 per cent annual cap on rent increases. Jenny Leong says a levy is a distraction from solutions such as bans and caps by local councils. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) "We need investment in public housing, we need government support for genuinely affordable community housing, we need a crackdown on those seeking to profit from the housing crisis," Ms Leong said.

events.title: Kalshi’s midterm trading tops $1.4 billion as traders bet on a Democratic sweep of Congress
events.summary: As Election Day kicks into high gear, traders are heading to popular platforms to put their predictions—and money—on the line in key Senate, House, and gubernatorial races across the United States. On Kalshi, they’re leaning blue, giving Democrats a 93% chance of winning control of the House and a 73% chance of taking the Senate. The site’s midterm forecasts are catnip for political junkies, but are also translating into big dollars: Kalshi’s midterm-related trading volume has surpassed $1.4 billion as of Tuesday, according to data supplied to Fortune . Leading the pack is a contract on whether Republicans or Democrats will control Congress , which has drawn $251 million in trading volume. A similar contract on which party will control the House has crossed the $181 million mark in trading volume. A separate market tracking all four possible combinations of House and Senate control has topped $112 million. Closely watched races are also drawing action on these platforms, where traders can wager on everything from sports to politics. The Los Angeles mayoral race, which will decide whether Democrat Karen Bass gets a second term, has drawn just shy of $110 million in trading volume. Texas’ Senate race is also picking up steam, nearing the $100 million mark, with traders giving Democrat James Talarico a 71% chance of defeating Republican Ken Paxton. But the blue bets only go so far in Texas, where traders give incumbent Republican Greg Abbott a 65% chance of winning a gubernatorial contest that has drawn $21 million in trading volume. His challenger, Gina Hinojosa, is seeking to give Texas its first Democratic governor since 1995. The surge in midterm trading builds on prediction markets’ breakout moment in 2024, when traders on popular platforms Kalshi and Polymarket favored Donald Trump as the winning candidate even as polls largely showed a toss-up. His victory helped turn the platforms into closely watched political barometers. But their forecasting record has hit a few bumps, with recent misses raising questions about how much faith to put in the odds. Last month, traders on Kalshi and Polymarket put their money on Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, to unseat incumbent Lula da Silva. They gave Bolsonaro roughly an 80% chance of winning the presidential runoff—before the odds swung toward Lula as the results rolled in. Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary delivered another curveball in August, when traders gave Francesca Hong roughly a 95% chance of winning. Instead, David Crowley edged her out by less than half a percentage point. Polymarket later deleted a celebratory post touting Hong’s odds, while Kalshi’s founders defended the forecast with a reminder: “5% is not 0%.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Pfizer hikes full-year outlook on new product growth, taps company veteran as new CFO
events.summary: Pfizer reported third-quarter results that topped estimates and hiked its full-year outlook, citing its "strong year-to-date performance" and ongoing cost cuts. Pfizer also announced that Cecile Guegan, who has held various finance leadership roles at the company over the last two decades, stepped in as chief financial officer this month. Pfizer on Tuesday reported fiscal third-quarter results that topped estimates and hiked its full-year outlook, as demand for its newly launched and acquired products grows. Pfizer also Tuesday announced that Cecile Guegan , who has held various finance leadership roles at the company over the last two decades, stepped in as chief financial officer this month. She had served as interim CFO since August, when Pfizer's former CFO, Dave Denton, stepped down to take the same position at Nike. The company is now expecting full-year revenue to total $62 billion to $64 billion, which compares with a previous outlook of $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion. The low end of that sales range would be roughly flat or down slightly compared with 2025 revenue of $62.6 billion. Still, Pfizer cited its "strong year-to-date performance" as a driver for the guidance hike. In an exclusive interview with CNBC, Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla said the company's Covid product revenue was "very low" this quarter and year, but called it "positive news for us." "Covid revenues was an overhang on the performance of our stock because of the perception that it is volatile and it's material to us. Actually, we've proven that we can make it irrelevant," Bourla said. "If anything, only an upside because, in the lowest possible Covid performance, we are beating, and we are raising by $1.5 billion because of the overperformance of the other products." Pfizer reaffirmed its Covid product outlook of roughly $4 billion for the year, expecting the majority of Covid shot sales in the fourth quarter during vaccination season, Guegan said during the call. The pharmaceutical giant now expects full-year adjusted profit of between $2.95 and $3.05 per share. That compares with previous guidance of between $2.80 and $3 per share. That includes a one-time $650 million charge, or a negative impact of 10 cents per share, recorded in the third quarter tied to the company's licensing and collaboration agreement with Chinese cancer drugmaker Innovent Biologics. Pfizer is working on a comeback story after its massive pandemic-era success waned. As demand for Covid products drops and generic rivals threaten its biggest moneymakers, Bourla is looking to jump-start growth through strategic acquisitions, fresh cancer drugs and a big bet on weight loss treatments through its acquisition of Metsera. "In addition to the revenues that they generate now, and they will continue generating so that we can overcome the patent, the loss of patent exclusivity, we are bringing pipeline that will perform even better in terms of growth," Bourla told CNBC, referring to Pfizer's launched and acquired products. Pfizer in August expanded its multiyear cost-cutting efforts to help offset sharp declines in Covid product sales, and is now targeting roughly $9.7 billion in net savings through 2029. Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 87 cents adjusted vs. 73 cents expected Revenue: $16.58 billion vs. $15.87 billion expected Pfizer reported third-quarter revenue of $16.58 billion, relatively flat from the same period a year ago. The company cited an operational decrease of $57 million, primarily due to lower Covid revenues, and a $15 million negative impact from foreign exchange. That was offset by strong sales of key products like its blood thinner Eliquis and targeted cancer drug Padcev, which jumped and beat expectations. Eliquis in particular raked in $2.52 billion in sales, up 25%. Analysts were expecting revenue of $2.40 billion, according to StreetAccount. Padcev posted $720 million in revenue for the period, which compares with the $658 million that analysts were expecting. Sales of Pfizer's newly launched and acquired products contributed $3.8 billion, growing 32% operationally, Guegan said during the earnings call. That includes Padcev, its respiratory syncytial virus vaccine Abrysvo, its pneumococcal shot Prevnar 20 and oral lung cancer drug Lorbrena, among several other products. 'We continue to invest behind this group of products to mitigate [loss of exclusivity] headwinds over the next several years," Guegan said. "In addition, this quarter's performance demonstrates clear progress against our objective of returning to growth toward the end of the decade." Pfizer's Covid products also topped estimates for the quarter despite seeing steep sales declines. The company's Covid vaccine generated $808 million in sales, which compares with the $770.4 million that analysts were expecting, StreetAccount estimates show.

events.title: Multiple bankruptcies surround businessman at centre of T2D dispute
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Businessman at centre of T2D dispute has been bankrupt four times Robert Cammarano (left) claims ownership of Career Boss Australia. ( ABC News: Eva Blandis ) The businessman claiming ownership of a company that won a now-cancelled contract on the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project has been bankrupt four times. He was also previously in a dispute with the tax office over more than $2 million in "unreported and unexplained income" used to finance gambling losses. The lead contractors of the South Road project will appear before a parliamentary committee later this month. The businessman claiming ownership of a labour hire firm that won a now-cancelled contract on the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project has been bankrupt four times, including when the company won the public tender. Robert Mark Cammarano was also previously in a dispute with the tax office over whether more than $2 million used to fund gambling losses at Crown Casino was required to be declared as taxable income, the ABC can reveal. Mr Cammarano, 55, is suing in the Supreme Court, claiming beneficial ownership of all 100 shares in labour hire company Career Boss Australia, which in mid-2025 won a contract to supply workers to the Torrens to Darlington (T2D) project. The South Australian government said Mr Cammarano "wasn't a shareholder" when the contract was awarded. He was also not listed as a company director. Mr Cammarano alleges in his statement of claim that bikie Jamie Brown "coerced the transfer" of shares in the company by making "express threats of physical harm". Brown is yet to file a defence but has reportedly said he has "never threatened any shareholder and allegations to the contrary are simply false". Plans for the intersection of James Congdon Drive and South Road under the Torrens to Darlington project. ( Supplied: SA government ) Other respondents to the case have reportedly indicated they will dispute Mr Cammarano's ownership claims to the company. The Malinauskas government asked the T2D Alliance to suspend its contract with Career Boss Australia when Mr Cammarano's court action was reported in the media on October 18. On Monday, the T2D Alliance, led by contractor John Holland, cancelled the Career Boss contract entirely, although a court heard the labour hire company was still owed around $2 million for work performed . Mr Cammarano has been declared and discharged from bankruptcy on four separate occasions, according to Australian Financial Security Authority records. The declarations were made in 2000, 2007, 2016 and 2023. All four bankruptcies were by debtors petition, meaning Mr Cammarano applied to make himself bankrupt. He was not discharged from the latest bankruptcy until February 23, 2026, meaning he was a declared bankrupt when Career Boss Australia was awarded the T2D labour hire contract last year. The Torrens to Darlington project involves major road corridor works in Adelaide's west. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) Mr Cammarano was not listed as a Career Boss director when the contract was awarded, according to ASIC records. Asked whether the state government should have known about the past bankruptcies before the contract was awarded, Mr Cammarano's lawyer, Scott Jelbert, told the ABC: "I don't think that they should have known." "He wasn't representing himself as the party they were contracting with," he said, adding that Mr Cammarano's interests were managed through a trust with his family "as the beneficiary". Mr Jelbert did, however, say that Mr Cammarano was not "hiding in the shadows" when Career Boss was preparing to tender for work on the South Road project. "I think they knew of him," Mr Jelbert said of the T2D Alliance's knowledge of Mr Cammarano, adding "he was a bankrupt and that happens". "He was up-front about his involvement with the company, for sure," he said. The project has a $15.4 billion price tag. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) The ABC contacted John Holland but the company declined to comment. Mr Jelbert said one of his client's bankruptcies came following a dispute with the Australian Tax Office over "unreported and unexplained income". Mr Cammarano declared a taxable income of $61,405 in 2017–18 and $61,789 in 2018–19, according to an Administrative Appeals Tribunal judgment. But the ATO amended the assessment based on records supplied by Crown Casino in Melbourne. "Funds used by [Mr Cammarano] to finance his gambling losses represented funds available to him in some form," the judgment said. Crown Casino supplied records to the ATO.

events.title: Reddit tests ads in search results as traffic declines and growth concerns mount
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Just days after warning investors about declining search traffic and a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast, Reddit is looking for more ways to make money from its existing users. On Tuesday, the company announced that it’s beginning to test ad placements in its search results pages, allowing advertisers to reach users as they search for products, recommendations, and other information on its platform. “Ads in search may appear based on a range of factors, including contextual relevance to a user’s search query,” Reddit shared in its announcement about the new ad placements. “This is an initial test with a select group of eligible advertisers. During this test, we will evaluate and understand how users respond to these ads so we can refine the experience for users and advertisers over time.” The company offered examples of what sort of ads might appear, suggesting that a search for “espresso station” might display ads for espresso machines, coffee, or mugs, while a search for “home office setup” could surface ads for things like monitors, desks and office chairs. The ad test comes at a time when Reddit is reckoning with how AI has been changing the web’s landscape, and subsequently its reach. Despite beating Wall Street’s estimates for revenue and earnings per share, the company’s stock dropped after it reported its third-quarter results last week , with fourth-quarter guidance that predicted sales of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, below expectations of $1.05 billion. This was tied to Reddit’s declining search traffic referrals resulting from Google’s move to an AI-powered search experience. AI search now sends less traffic to publishers’ websites, as features like AI Mode provide answers directly on Google’s Search Result pages, reducing clicks to other websites. Reddit also said that its global daily active users were flat quarter-over-quarter in Q3, reaching 130.3 million, while U.S. daily active users dropped from 53.2 million in Q2 to 50.7 million in the quarter, and were down 2% year-over-year. The company noted that if the trend continues, daily active users could decline to a low double-digit percentage by the fourth quarter. This leaves the company needing to earn more revenue from its existing users, which is where these new ads come in. The ads could prove to be more valuable to Reddit after it makes its planned shift to a logged-in experience, which was also announced during earnings. The company said it will make the transition gradually, initially in markets outside the U.S. The decision to limit its content to logged-in users serves multiple purposes — it protects Reddit’s site from unauthorized AI scraping, and it increases its value to advertisers. Logged-in users are worth more to advertisers because they provide additional signals about their interests and behavior, allowing for better-targeted, more profitable ads. events.title: Options traders are betting heavily on these stocks ahead of election results
events.summary: With prediction markets pricing in a big victory for Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections, traders are leaning into a group of stocks that investors often categorize as beneficiaries of left-wing leadership. Options trading in clean-energy stocks, particularly solar companies, surged on Tuesday, despite a five-month sell-off in the group that's left most of the companies in the industry group down on the year. Volume in the Invesco Solar ETF (TAN) surged to 40 times higher than usual Tuesday, according to Cboe LiveVol data. The fund, which typically trades fewer than 500 contracts a day the past month, traded more than 20,000 contracts by midday, and 99% of them were calls. The ETF rallied more than 400% from its pandemic low through the 2020 election before giving almost all of the gains back by April last year. The most popular trade in TAN was buying the 50-strike call for December expiry for 80 cents and looking for a 17% rally, according to SpotGamma data. For nearer expiry, the 46 and 47-strike calls were also popular. Among individual stocks, SolarEdge Technologies stands out, on pace for three times higher-than-average volume and more than 75% of trading in calls. The company reports earnings before the bell tomorrow and rallied more than 6% Tuesday. The most popular trade was buying the 35-strike call expiring Friday. "I would only like solar if blue was in the White House," said Charlie Moon of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "But Enphase does stands out with some insider buying." Bulls were indeed dabbling in Enphase Energy , whose stock fell 20% after earnings last week but have fully recovered since and rallied 9% Tuesday. On volume twice the average, traders likely bought 8,600 calls, compared to under 900 puts. events.title: Job openings posted big September gain in positive sign for labor market ahead of payrolls report
events.summary: Job openings rose by 333,000 in September while hiring and quits both increased and layoffs declined, the BLS reported Tuesday. The monthly JOLTS report showed mostly positive signs for the labor market ahead of Friday's key nonfarm payrolls reading. Job openings surged in September, as did the number of workers who quit their positions, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday, while hiring also rose and layoffs dropped. In its monthly look at labor market slack and worker mobility, the BLS reported job openings at 7.52 million, up 333,000 from August and well above the Dow Jones consensus outlook for 7.15 million. As a share of the total workforce, the rate of job openings increased to 4.5%, up 0.2 percentage point from the prior month, according to the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey . There are now some 414,000 more job openings than workers classified as unemployed, or about 1.05 openings to every available worker. Openings rose in manufacturing (54,000) as well as state and local government (108,000) and professional and business services (106,000). At the same time, the total of employees leaving their jobs spiked to 3.36 million, an increase of 321,000 from August and the highest level since March 2025. Quits are considered a barometer for worker confidence in finding new jobs after leaving their prior positions. "There are more job openings than unemployed people in the United States right now. That doesn't solve all problems, but it's a big change from a year ago," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "It's an encouraging sign that despite all the headwinds right now with high diesel and gas prices and ongoing inflation problems, companies are slowly increasing their hiring." Hires rose on the month, up 131,000 to 5.4 million, while layoffs and discharges fell by 127,000 to 1.64 million, the lowest since March 2025. The report comes ahead of the October nonfarm payrolls report, which the BLS will release Friday. The Wall Street consensus is for an increase of 59,000 after September eked out a gain of just 29,000, while the unemployment rate is figured to hold at 4.2%. In other economic news Tuesday, September factory orders for manufactured goods jumped 1.8%, well above the estimate for 1.3% after increasing just 0.3% in August.

events.title: Michigan US Senate race: Rogers, El-Sayed urge turnout for critical race
events.summary: Democratic hopeful Abdul El-Sayed faces a slew of last-minute Islamophobic attacks as he seeks to unseat Trump-backed Republican candidate Mike Rogers. Michigan voters are casting their ballots in a charged, closely watched race that could make Democrat Abdul El-Sayed the first Muslim in the United States Senate and help decide control of the chamber. Mike Rogers, his Republican opponent, cast his ballot at a polling station in White Lake, Michigan hours after polls opened. El-Sayed had already had his vote submitted and counted through an absentee ballot before Election Day. list 1 of 3 Voting underway in closely contested US midterm elections 2026 list 2 of 3 In Pictures: US midterm elections in 20 photos list 3 of 3 US midterm voting begins in high-stakes test of Trump’s presidency The two candidates seek to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters. A final New York Times/Siena poll placed El-Sayed 11 points ahead of Rogers going into the election. Polls opened at 7am local time (12:00 GMT) and close at 8pm (01:00 GMT on Wednesday). If the race is close, it may not be called until later on Wednesday. The US Department of Justice has announced that election monitors will be present at the polls in Michigan and all 50 other states, a first in US history. El-Sayed, a Muslim born to Egyptian parents, is the former head of Detroit’s health department and has campaigned on progressive policies such as Medicare for All. Rogers, a former congressman and close ally of US President Donald Trump, is seeking to come back after a narrow loss to a Democrat in a 2024 Senate race. Democrats need to gain four seats in Tuesday’s midterm elections to wrest back the Senate from Republicans and rein in Trump. The race is also seen as a test of whether a progressive who openly criticises Israel can win in a swing state. Both candidates made a final push on social media as voting got under way. “It’s time. It’s up to us to show the country what’s possible. The world is watching,” El-Sayed wrote, sharing an upbeat campaign video that features former US President Barack Obama. Rogers posted a video that featured interviews with supporters, one of whom called El-Sayed an “extremist”. “We have a state to save”, the post read. Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer gave a firm endorsement of El-Sayed after casting his own ballot in New York’s race. “There are millions of Michiganders whose number one issue is getting their costs down,” said Schumer. “Abdul El-Sayed is … talking to the people about those issues and doing things about them … He is going to win tonight because he’s talking about what Michiganders care about.” The El-Sayed campaign’s final days were overshadowed by a rift with Congresswoman Haley Stevens, a fellow Democrat whom El-Sayed narrowly defeated in a primary election in August. On Sunday, Stevens endorsed Rogers , saying she was “choosing country over hate” and capping off a weeks-long row about El-Sayed’s opposition to US support for Israel. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, and the pro-Israel lobbying group the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent more than $30m backing her against El-Sayed. A majority of her large donors lined up to support Rogers after her loss, channeling $9m into a Republican group that supports him, according to The New York Times. El-Sayed, by contrast, has accused Israel of genocide in Gaza and argued that US aid to Israel would be better spent at home. Asked by NewsNation on her way in to vote for Rogers whether her change in support was worth it, Stevens replied: “Absolutely. Voting is always worth it, right?” Senate leader Schumer, who had initially backed Stevens, was asked whether her defection could hand the election to Republicans. “Haley Stevens is one vote,” he replied. El-Sayed, the Michigan-born son of Egyptian immigrants, has faced persistent attacks on his faith. Republican Party ads have sought to link him to “terrorism” and radicalism, with Trump joining in the inflammatory rhetoric. The US president has repeatedly called El-Sayed a “jihadist” and a “nasty guy”, mocking his name and repeating an unfounded, widely circulated Republican claim that he belongs to the Muslim Brotherhood. Hours before polls opened, Trump once again took aim at El-Sayed, this time in a post on his Truth Social platform. “Abdul El-Sayed Hates Jews and Hates Blacks. Don’t feel bad, he also Hates Whites. Only fools would vote for him in the Michigan race for the U.S. Senate! He will, 100%, do you in! VOTE FOR MIKE ROGERS,” Trump wrote. The US president also mentioned El-Sayed in a Fox News interview early on Election Day, when he said annual US financial aid to Israel should stop at the end of 2026. “Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they [Israel] don’t need it?” he said.

events.title: Yemen gov’t accuses IRGC, Hezbollah of sending 21 experts to back Houthis
events.summary: Interior Ministry alleges experts from Iranian force and Lebanese group work with Houthis to build military capabilities. Yemen’s internationally recognised government has accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), as well as Lebanon’s Hezbollah, of deploying 21 experts to help the Houthis plan and direct military operations in the country. Interior Minister Major-General Ibrahim Haidan said in a statement on Tuesday that 14 members of the group are from the IRGC and seven from Hezbollah. list 1 of 3 ‘Need a Plan B’: Yemenis in Aden prepare for another war as missiles fall list 2 of 3 Are Houthis using Russian satellites as Saudi Arabia fends off strikes? list 3 of 3 A Gulf non-aggression pact could be the path forward The experts’ roles show that foreign involvement has moved from financing, arming and training to “direct supervision and participation in planning and managing operations and building military capabilities”, said Haidan. The statement added that eight of the experts are in Hodeidah, four in Sanaa, four in Saada, two in Hajjah, two in Amran and one in the coastal city of Khokha. It listed their specialities as including command and control, ballistic missiles and drones, electronic warfare, smuggling military components, coordinating naval operations and choosing commercial ships as targets , developing explosive-laden boats and autonomous submarines, and training fighters in mine-laying and siege tactics. Haidan warned that the activities “threaten shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the Red Sea” and could transfer military expertise to other armed groups. He called on the international community to designate the Houthis a “terrorist” organisation, dismantle their financing and arms networks, and enforce the arms embargo under United Nations Security Council resolutions 2216 and 2624. The statement comes as Yemeni armed forces and fighters loyal to the government battle the Houthis in five provinces, after the group seized the western Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandeb area in September. The resumption of fighting has shattered a relative quiet brought by a 2022 ceasefire that followed a lengthy civil war which first erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. In 2015, Saudi Arabia entered the war at the head of an international coalition aimed at restoring Yemen’s internationally recognised government. The government has long claimed the IRGC is supporting the Houthis, while Tehran insists the Houthis act independently. The Houthis acknowledge their alliance with Iran but have long denied being an Iranian proxy, while Hezbollah has previously rejected having a role in Yemen’s war. Saudi Arabia, whose airports and oil facilities have come under Houthi attack in recent weeks, has accused Iran of encouraging the escalation.

events.title: Ten years later, ‘Pokémon Go to the polls’ still haunts the internet
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. In the lead-up to a presidential election that would irrefutably transform American culture, Hillary Clinton took the stage at a rally in Virginia as she campaigned to become the first female president. “We’re going to have a lot of jobs — jobs from building infrastructure to coding. Creating new apps,” she said. “I don’t know who created Pokémon Go, but I’m trying to figure out how we get them to have Pokémon Go to the polls .” Ten years later, it is once again Election Day in the United States. Now, most app developers aren’t even writing their own code anymore, thanks to AI, and Pokémon Go has been sold to a company wholly owned by Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund. The only thing about that political moment that hasn’t changed is that “Pokémon Go to the polls” memes still crop up on every Election Day. “It was very bold and confident, and also just sounded so terribly out of touch and corny,” Cesar Ruiz de Castilla, an elected ward committee member in Philadelphia, told TechCrunch. “I don’t know if the mainstream media cared that much about it, but everyone was making a meme about it and talking about it online.” Since then, digital culture has become increasingly inextricable from the fate of American politics. Donald Trump tweeted his way through his first term, then later started his own social media platform ; presidential campaigns hire meme managers ; the White House invites podcasters and content creators to press briefings; Elon Musk even spun up his own advisory group under Trump that named itself after the cutesy doge meme and then slashed international aid programs. “The 2016 election was such a monumental moment in internet history, and we were all there for it — our politics have become more, not just divided, but segmented online,” Organizer Memes , a political influencer who teaches Gen Z activists how to reach their peers online via memes, told TechCrunch. “It’s a relic of an optimistic, bygone political era.” Now, people who weren’t even old enough to vote in 2016 reflect on the year as a cultural turning point, even calling it “ the last good year .” It’s a sentiment that isn’t so much political as it is rooted in nostalgia for an era of internet culture before AI slop, when we used social media to connect with friends, rather than doomscrolling through an algorithmic feed of people we don’t even follow. At the start of the new year, this yearning for the old internet became a viral sentiment as millions of people shared throwback photos from 2016 on Instagram. Spotify reported that user-generated playlists featuring 2016 in their titles spiked 790% in the first three weeks of the year, and the company changed its Instagram bio at the time to say it’s “romanticizing 2016 again.” Never mind that, at the time, the internet perceived 2016 as a cursed year, even before the election — months earlier, one Slate columnist wondered how 2016 compared to 1348, the year the Black Death took hold in Europe. “[Pokémon Go to the polls] is in that era of the singular internet, when Facebook and Twitter and Tumblr were all kind of bouncing content back-and-forth and not just this complete anarchic mess of 25 platforms that we now have and don’t use,” Organizer Memes said. Organizer Memes also notes that some cultural touchstones that felt more significant then — like the obsession with Harambe the gorilla — haven’t had as much staying power as “Pokémon Go to the polls.” Perhaps this is because we’re bound to remember “Pokémon Go to the polls” every few years on Election Day, and because it appeals to both sides of the aisle. On the right, it’s a way to make fun of Democrats, and on the left, it’s a shared groan of embarrassment. “It’s like if all the kids in a class are making a joke, and then the teacher gets in on the joke, and it stops being funny,” Mack Finkel, who canvassed at the polls on Tuesday on behalf of a healthcare workers’ union, told TechCrunch. “I think there’s a key essence of millennial cringe happening here, and it’s the same reason that all my friends are rewatching [HBO’s] ‘Girls.’” Clinton’s decade-old, corny comment can be seen as a precursor to the “ Kamala is brat ” meme. While the former vice president’s record as a prosecutor initially made her unpopular among some left-leaning young voters, they rallied around her once she became the only alternative to Trump. Gen Z rallied around Harris by creating flashy, absurdist “fan cam”-style edits of the candidate’s best quips in the aesthetic of Charli XCX’s album “Brat,” which soundtracked the summer of 2024.
