events.title: Grok Bot is growing fast—but Elon Musk says its costs are ‘unsustainably high’ compared to revenue
events.summary: Grok is on a streak. On SpaceX’s Q3 earnings call on Oct. 20, CEO Elon Musk told analysts the company’s AI bot is “seeing the fastest growth of a product that I’ve ever seen in my life.” But that growth comes with a cost. On Sunday, Musk responded to an X user who asked him to reset their Grok Bot usage allowance after it ran out four days early.  “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue,” Musk wrote on X .  Musk’s reply highlights a problem facing AI companies that even users who pay for AI can cost more to serve because they use AI agents that perform more compute-intensive tasks.  Grok Bot, an AI agent developed by SpaceX that launched in August , can carry out multi-step tasks on users’ behalf such as browsing websites, drafting emails, and processing invoices, and it can work across apps and websites as well.  SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell told analysts on the recent earnings call that Grok Bot reached 800,000 paid weekly users earlier that month, double the number of users in September. She said businesses are “the fastest-growing category,” using Grok for IT, sales, marketing, and engineering. Musk added that customers are using Grok more as its capabilities improve. “We’re seeing users use it more per week, not use it less,” he said on the call. But people using Grok Bot more could cost SpaceX. Unlike chatbots that respond to individual prompts, AI agents work through several steps to complete more complicated tasks, which use up more computing power. More frequent users, therefore, drive up SpaceX’s costs without necessarily paying more.  Meta is facing a similar problem with Muse. CEO Mark Zuckerberg told analysts in Meta’s October earnings call that Muse, which attracted 10 million users since it launched on Sept. 8, is costly to run, and so the tech giant expects to improve its compute efficiency tenfold in the next year.  This cost dilemma comes as SpaceX pours billions into its AI business. Its “Super Intelligence” division made $7.56 billion in Q3 revenue, up from $813 million a year prior. It also reported $431 million in operating profit, compared with a $1.7 billion loss a year earlier.  But it’s spending more on AI infrastructure than that division is bringing in revenue. SpaceX spent $16.4 billion on AI capex, more than twice the Super Intelligence division’s quarterly revenue and accounting for 84% of its total $19.6 billion in Q3 capex, according to its SEC filing . Much of its Super Intelligence revenue growth came from leasing out data center capacity to Anthropic and Google . This means SpaceX now must decide how much computing power to devote to its own AI products and how much to rent to other companies. Musk told analysts SpaceX aims to “split it 50-50” between the two, but also said demand for Grok could change that calculation. “I think Grok Bot may end up being what uses most of our Super Intelligence compute,” he said.  Compute demand has been strong. Musk said SpaceX is “hounded relentlessly” by hyperscalers and smaller companies searching for compute, and those contracts are being renewed at higher dollars per watt.  “It’s not impossible that we will have a six-month payback period for compute next year,” he told analysts.  SpaceX did not respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. events.title: Sullivan: What the 2026 midterms could mean for energy investors
events.summary: A Democratic Congress could be good for offshore wind and solar energy. If the Republicans maintain control over one or both houses, we could see the administration more urgently expand domestic energy production. Texas will matter most for utility stocks and data center plays. Why you should be watching one ship carrying Russian diesel fuel bound for America on the maritime radar. GET THIS IN YOUR INBOX FIRST: Subscribe to CNBC's "Power Insider" newsletter. Don't expect huge near-term moves in energy stocks off the results of the midterms. But there are some investing implications over the longer-term. Let me break it down. Yes, it's entirely possible that one or both houses of Congress will shift to Democratic control. That's not my opinion. It's what many of the research reports, polls, and prediction markets are suggesting as of this writing. For argument's sake, let's say that this time the polls are correct. The election ends with a "blue trickle," and Democrats win out with a slight edge in the House, Senate, or both. It won't be enough to meaningfully change, well, anything. If the election ends with just a slight lean to the Democratic side, it won't be enough for a veto-proof majority. Candidates can specify policies — like halting the growth of data centers — all they want, but there's a chasm between being elected and passing new laws. Research I've read and conversations we've had on CNBC suggest that the next two years in Washington, D.C., will be flush with finger-pointing, investigations into the president and his family, and posturing ahead of the far-more-important 2028 presidential election. S&P Global doesn't exactly agree with me, saying that Democratic control of either chamber would bring "tougher oversight of agency decisions" and could impact things such as tax incentives and "other policies underpinning long-term energy investments." A Democratic Congress could be good for offshore wind, an energy source the president seems to hate with the white-hot passion of the sun. Speaking of the sun, a shift blue could also be positive for the continued growth of solar, perhaps via new tax incentives. Though both are growing rapidly. If the Republicans maintain control over one or both houses, we keep doing more of the same, albeit with more urgency. S&P Global adds that "a continued Republican majority would give the administration more room to pursue expanded domestic production, faster permitting and environmental deregulation, though narrow margins could limit major legislation." Any change in control of Congress is also unlikely to make a big difference around the Iran conflict. Once any new Congress begins in January, things will have either ramped up, stayed the same, or cooled down. A new Congress could try to use its authority under the War Powers Act. The team at Piper Sandler agrees, writing that "elections matter, but will likely not change the direction of things" as Trump focuses more on his own legacy. That's a polite way of saying that the President is going to do largely what he wants, Congress be darned. On the state level, the midterms may matter a little bit more, particularly as they relate to energy-hungry data centers. In Texas, a change in the statehouse could bring a change in sentiment around data centers. Candidate Gina Hinojosa has a policy to "end data center madness" and supports a moratorium on new builds. Amy Acton also supports a "conditional moratorium" on new data center builds in Ohio. Vivek Ramaswamy is also calling for conditions on new data center construction. The issue is a big deal in many states. Yet even if those candidates, or candidates with similar views on big new energy projects, win, they'd still have to enact meaningful change. Which could happen, of course. So let's say it does happen. New governors enter office and use their power to throttle or even stop new projects. Even if some of the big new projects are stalled or stopped, power demand, at a minimum, would stay at current levels. Which means demand for power production inputs such as natural gas, nuclear, and yes, even coal, would remain at current levels. As far as power-hungry utility stocks go, Bank of America agrees with my election take above - mostly. Its team writes that it thinks the "2026 cycle matters for utility equities in far fewer states than the headline count suggests," but that committee appointments in each state will matter. The BofA team says that, regarding the election and utility stocks, five states matter most: Georgia, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, and Texas. Texas is the "most consequential," as state environmental regulators have halted data center permits. That state's Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) has actually stopped electronic permitting to make sure any permit is unrelated to data centers. To my point, that's already known information. It matters, but markets are already aware of it and have priced it in.

events.title: Owners of banned NDIS company allegedly funded Ferrari and football club
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Owners of banned Perth NDIS company Adachi allegedly purchased Victorian NDIS business Topic: Business and Industry Regulation Adrian Mtungwazi bought Daily Living Disability Services in 2024 with his wife Chiedza Mtungwazi. ( Supplied: LinkedIn ) The directors of a banned NDIS business in Perth have allegedly been able to buy another NDIS provider in regional Victoria. Both companies have gone into liquidation with significant debt, leaving regional clients without care and staff without jobs. The NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission is investigating and no charges have been laid. The NDIS watchdog is investigating after the directors of a banned NDIS company that racked up a $6.8 million debt bought another NDIS business in Victoria's Latrobe Valley. Perth-based NDIS operator Adachi Disability Services was banned in February 2024. According to the liquidator's report, its directors allegedly used company funds to pay for a Ferrari, overseas property and fund a Zimbabwean football club called Adachi FC. The liquidator's report revealed that despite the ban placed on Adachi, its directors Adrian and Chiedza Mtungwazi were able to purchase Daily Living Disability Services (Daily Living) in Traralgon using Adachi funds. Daily Living collapsed overnight in March 2026, leaving its clients without care and owing its staff and the Australian Taxation Office an estimated $1.2 million. The closure has left NDIS advocates questioning how the directors were able to purchase the company despite the ban on Adachi, and calling for more checks and balances in the scheme. Peter Earnshaw took his son Liam to Daily Living Disability Services for five years. ( ABC News: Tara Whitchurch ) When Daily Living suddenly went into liquidation in March 2026, Gippsland families like Peter and Liam Earnshaw were completely blindsided. Mr Earnshaw's non-verbal autistic son Liam relied on Daily Living services for five years, five days a week and overnight. "It gave him something to look forward to every day," Mr Earnshaw said. "He loved it, all of his friends were there." Clients were left without care and all staff lost their jobs overnight. As a single dad, Peter had to take two weeks off work to find alternative care for Liam, but finding another provider was difficult. "Being in a small town, it's hard to find a provider that's a good fit," he said. The former office of Daily Living Disability Services in Traralgon. ( ABC News: Lily Kristanto ) Mr Earnshaw said the directors should not have been able to buy another NDIS business if their original company was banned by the NDIS. He said the government should have noticed the "multiple red flags" when the directors allegedly bought another business. "There's no checks and balances," he said. "So what they do, they open up under a different company name. It's just too easy." Liam Earnshaw was devastated when Daily Living Disability Services closed down. ( ABC News: Tara Whitchurch ) A Ferrari, overseas property and a football club In his report, liquidator Andrew Yeo from Pitcher Partners, said Adrian Mtungwazi and his wife Chiedza took out "director loans" of $2.3 million. Mr Yeo alleged the couple used company money to buy assets that were "purely for the Directors personal use, including a Ferrari motor vehicle". The liquidator found Adachi company funds were sent to overseas bank accounts in South Africa, the Philippines, United Kingdom and Zimbabwe. Mr Yeo said his investigations indicated "Adrian may also have been providing funds to a Zimbabwe-based football club called 'Adachi FC'." The report stated in 2021 the NDIS watchdog, the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission, was aware of alleged "regulatory issues" and alleged Adachi was "mismanaging client complaints". In February 2024, the NDIS watchdog placed a banning order on the company , which Mr Yeo said in the report was due to compliance issues. However in April 2024, the report revealed the directors used company funds to purchase an NDIS service provider in Traralgon, Victoria. When the Mtungwazis bought Daily Living Disability Services, Mr Yeo said they purposefully wanted to avoid being listed on ASIC records. Mr Yeo said the director of Daily Living was a former employee of Adachi and the Mtungwazis informed Mr Yeo that they held shares in the business for the Mtungwazis. "[The Mtungwazis] informed me that the purchase of the business was purposefully structured in a way that neither Chiedza or Adrian would be appointed as a director or shareholder on the ASIC records," Mr Yeo said.

events.title: Hackers behind $6.3bn Binance heist ‘used malware and bogus job interviews’
events.summary: Firm reveals details about how its cryptocurrency exchange was compromised, saying operation began in June The hackers behind the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance heist used bogus job interviews, malicious software and an internal AI tool, the company has revealed. The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange was compromised in an operation that began with an inadvertent download of malware in June, led to a recruitment scam in September and then a raid last week of “hot wallets” where billions of dollars worth of crypto-assets were taken. The FBI has blamed North Korea for last week’s heist but Pyongyang, a prolific crypto-hacker , described the accusation as “absurd rhetoric” on Tuesday. According to an update Binance released on Tuesday, the hackers got their first foothold in the summer when a company engineer inadvertently downloaded malware that exposed the employee’s role and that of others in the team that looked after Binance’s cryptowallet infrastructure. A fake project director then contacted a different engineer on a legitimate job-hunting platform, leading to a first-round video interview with a sham HR representative and a second-round interview – on a chat app – with the “chief executive” of a fictitious company. It was during the second interview that the engineer was tricked into downloading malware on to his computer. On 20 October, the attacker used the compromised computer plus an internal AI tool to gain control of the engineer’s system and that of a second wallet developer on the same team. Then on 29 October, the attacker used the second developer’s computer, using stolen ⁠credentials from the first engineer, and triggered a malicious script to ​launch the attack. Binance said $2.85bn of the $6.34bn drained from cryptowallets in the attack had been frozen or intercepted. Deepfake job interviews are a known part of North Korea’s cyber-arsenal , but normally from the other side of the process – where bogus IT professionals apply for jobs as a means of funnelling money back to Pyongyang. “This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance said in the update. The FBI said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the hack. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning But Kim Yo-jong, the influential sister of the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un , said on Tuesday that the allegations proved Washington remained hostile towards Pyongyang, according to North Korea’s state news agency, KCNA. “The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK [the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea] as a ‘cybercriminal state,’ claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organisation ‘supported’ by the DPRK was involved in the incident,” KCNA quoted her as saying. “But the US assertion ‌is absurd rhetoric and nothing new,” said Kim, a ruling party official. “It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cybercrimes in different parts of the world are our deeds.”

events.title: IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts
events.summary: To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society ’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series. The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple , software company Tavant , and cybersecurity concern Zscaler . Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar . Technical discussions grounded in engineering Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work. Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples. The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations. Extending access through a virtual format The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel. For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace. Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community. Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization. Examining governed AI agents The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala , a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle. The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows. Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam , a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar. Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly. Building a continuing technical program Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations. Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems. Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community. Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

events.title: Ferrari raises 2026 guidance after Q3 earnings beat
events.summary: Ferrari raised its 2026 guidance after its third-quarter results topped Wall Street's expectations. The sports car maker cited stronger customer personalizations, lower-than-expected currency headwinds and its Formula 1 championship position as reasons for the guidance raise. Ferrari shipped 10,170 vehicles through the first nine months, 318 fewer than a year earlier, even as revenue and earnings increased. Ferrari on Tuesday raised its 2026 guidance after the sports car maker slightly beat Wall Street's third-quarter expectations. Here's how Ferrari performed in the third quarter compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 2.44 euros ($2.77) adjusted vs. 2.37 euros expected Revenue: 1.9 billion euros vs. 1.89 billion euros expected Ferrari raised its guidance to revenue of 7.65 billion euros, up from 7.6 billion euros; adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization to 3 billion euros, up from 2.97 billion euros; and adjusted EPS to at least 9.85 euros, up from at least 9.68 euros. The automaker also upgraded its expectations for industrial free cash flow to up to 1.65 billion euros, up from previous expectations for at least 1.55 billion euros. This is the second consecutive quarter Ferrari has raised its 2026 guidance, despite vehicle shipments being lower by 318 units through the first nine months of the year, at 10,170 vehicles, compared with last year. The decline is led by fewer shipments to the Americas and China, Hong Kong and Taiwan. Ferrari said Tuesday that the guidance improvements were a result of stronger-than-expected customer personalizations, lower than anticipated currency headwinds and a second place finish in the Formula 1 championship. "Our order book now reaches into 2028, and we still have two more launches to come this year. In addition, we continue to create engaging events around the world to further tighten the bonds with our clients and partners across Racing, Sports Cars and Lifestyle," Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna said in a release. RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan said Tuesday that Ferrari's results were largely in line with Wall Street expectations. However, he said shares may be "under slight pressure given some were hoping for a bigger guidance raise, but expect it to get better once folks realize these results are healthy." Ferrari's U.S. shares initially declined on the results before turning positive and were up roughly 4% during midday trading.

The Luce, Ferrari’s first electric car and one of its most polarizing models, isn’t just selling. It’s selling out. The five-seater EV designed by Jony Ive, Apple’s longtime design chief, was mocked and widely panned when it debuted in May, sending Ferrari’s stock price lower. But all that criticism hasn’t dampened demand, according to CEO Benedetto Vigna. The 2027 production run of the Luce, which starts at about $615,000, is “fully allocated,” Vigna said Tuesday during the company’s third-quarter earnings call, meaning every car Ferrari plans to build next year already has a buyer. “If someone comes, he has to wait one year to get the cars,” Vigna added. The first deliveries of the Luce are expected to begin in the fourth quarter. Just how many Luce cars that represents is unclear. Ferrari has never publicly disclosed how many Luce vehicles it plans to produce. Financial Times reported earlier this year, citing unnamed sources, that Ferrari planned to sell just under 500 units this year. The company’s longer-term target is to sell 2,500 units by 2030, or about 600 a year, according to Financial Times. Speculation on who these buyers are — ahem, the founders of multibillion-dollar AI labs, perhaps? — will have to remain just that until Luces are spotted in the wild. Vigna wouldn’t provide a breakdown of who these Luce customers are, only noting it was a “good mix in terms of client, it is a good mix also in terms of geography.” He later added that there is no specific pattern or demographic of Luce buyers. While Luce deliveries have yet to begin, Ferrari’s existing lineup and growing demand for personalized options helped fuel its financial performance in the third quarter . Revenue from customizations, which executives said accounted for more than 21% of revenue from cars and spare parts, helped boost profits. The company said deliveries of the F80, its limited-run hypercar , and customization reflect its clients’ “ever-deepening desire” to make each Ferrari uniquely their own. As a result, the company raised its full-year guidance, saying it now expects adjusted earnings of at least €3 billion ($3.36 billion), up from €2.97 billion. Ferrari, which enjoys some of the highest profit margins in the auto industry, reported third-quarter revenue of €1.9 billion, up 7% from a year earlier, and net income of €431 million, up 13%. Operating profit was €563 million, for an operating margin of 29.7%, meaning the company kept roughly 30 cents of every dollar of revenue as profit from its core business. events.title: Binance hackers used fake job interview in US$6.3 billion attack
events.summary: The attack on Binance has raised questions about how hackers breached the world’s largest crypto exchange after years of North Korea-linked attacks. Fake job interviews are a well-known hacking technique. Binance said hackers used a fake job interview and a tampered advert tool to reach engineers’ computers, then stole US$6.3 billion in crypto in a record attack. The breach began in June and grew through September and October, exposing wallet developers’ systems before the Oct 29 theft. Binance said it apologised and will repay users. The attack raised fresh fears over crypto security and North Korea-linked hacking. Binance is boosting AI detection and plans a security research fund with AI firms. PARIS/DETROIT - Hackers used a bogus job interview and software hidden in an advertisement to compromise the computers of two Binance software engineers before using a third’s computer to drain US$6.3 billion (S$8 billion) worth of crypto in last week’s record heist, the exchange said on Nov 3. In its initial report on how hackers pulled off what could be the largest-ever financial theft, Binance detailed a multi-stage hacking endeavour that began in June and set off a series of security breaches culminating in the theft on Oct 29. Even as Binance scrambled to lock down its system and freeze withdrawals after detecting the attack late on Oct 29, the hackers were still making off with crypto from the exchange nearly four hours after the first theft, Binance said. The FBI has blamed a North Korean hacking group, a claim North Korea has rejected. Binance has said it is repaying all customers whose funds were stolen. The attack has raised questions about how hackers breached the world’s largest crypto exchange after years of North Korea-linked attacks - which have grown in ambition and frequency - and renewed questions about the vulnerability of digital assets to cybercrime. Cybersecurity experts and government officials have for years warned about North Korean and other hackers using phony job interviews to target employees at companies of interest, said Michael Barnhart, a researcher with cybersecurity firm DTEX. Fake job interviews are a well-known hacking technique. Binance said it had detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyberthreats in 2026. That shows Binance is “just getting barraged,” Barnhart said. “This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance said in its report. Binance said the attack began in June when an employee on its wallet developer team downloaded a tool from the internet that hackers had tampered with. The exchange said it detected this afterwards, replaced the device and changed credentials, but the employee’s role and those of others on the wallet team were exposed. A person familiar with the incident said the tool’s malicious version had been placed in an advertisement, which meant it appeared higher in a search engine than the real version. Then in September, a second software engineer seeking a new job downloaded a “malicious code repository” onto the person’s computer after interviewing for what they thought was a legitimate role, including meeting virtually with the CEO of a fictitious company, Binance’s report said. On Oct 20, the attacker used the compromised computer plus an internal AI tool to gain control of the wallet developer’s system and that of a second wallet developer. Nine days later, the attacker used the second wallet developer’s computer, with stolen credentials from the first wallet developer, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack. A limited number of engineers at the company have direct access to wallets – which store or trade crypto – the person familiar with the hack said. The attack unfolded quickly on Oct 29, removing 233.46 million XRP – a cryptocurrency – from five Binance hot, or internet-connected, wallets to an attacker-controlled address in just four minutes, before attackers withdrew other cryptocurrencies including bitcoin, the exchange said in its report. Binance said it received an internal alert about large transfers and began investigating. It moved to suspend withdrawals, freeze affected tokens and remove unauthorised permissions, resulting in about $2.85 billion of frozen assets, but suspending withdrawals alone could not stop all unauthorised asset movements. Attackers used 50 signing transactions to manipulate the account, while Binance said it was forced to build new procedures to revoke authorisations, slowing its response. The final unauthorised transfer was at 2356 GMT (7.56am the next day in Singapore), Binance said, nearly four hours after the attack began. Binance said as a result of the hack, it was increasing investment in AI-enabled detection and working on establishing a security research fund and targeted initiatives with leading AI companies. events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Netflix announced on Tuesday that it’s rolling out a new “AI Discover” tab where users will be able to experiment with new ways to find their next watch. The first experimental feature launching under the tab will allow users to get recommendations based on what they’re currently in the mood for. Users can choose from curated themes featuring clips from shows and movies, based on their mood, viewing preferences, how much time they have, or what’s new and trending. Themes include “something light,” “scare me,” “family movie night,” “quick watches,” and more. The addition of the new tab suggests that Netflix wants to make its growing library easier to navigate while shifting discovery away from an experience where users are endlessly scrolling through titles toward a more personalized and AI-powered experience. Netflix says AI Discover is powered by a new intelligence layer it’s been building that responds to what users tell the platform in real time and keeps learning. Once users pick a theme, they’ll see matching recommendations. They also have the option to select more specific themes so they can keep searching until they find something they’re interested in, or choose the “something different” option to start over. Each title features a “Tune Your Recommendations” button beside “Play” and “My List” to allow users to save recommendations they like or exclude titles they don’t want suggested again. “There’s more to enjoy and discover on Netflix than ever, but what sounds right for a quiet night in may look different for family movie night or a few spare minutes,” Netflix wrote in a blog post . “We’ve spent years refining how you discover, with recommendations tailored to your tastes, from what you Thumbs Up to what you add to ‘My List.’ Now, AI Discover joins the mix as a new way to explore.” Netflix describes AI Discover as its “test kitchen,” where it will “try out new recipes for discovery.” The company says users’ feedback will help it decide which features to keep or improve before bringing them over to the main Netflix experience. AI Discover is starting to roll out in the U.S. to users who use Netflix in English on supported TVs. The company plans to bring the new tab to additional users in the coming weeks. If users have access to the new feature, they’ll see a “Discover” button with a red gem icon and a “New” label in the top navigation bar on their TV. events.title: Binance co-CEO Richard Teng says hackers used fake job interviews, AI tool to steal $6.3 billion in crypto
events.summary: Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange. The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop. "In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction." He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets. Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group. Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker." As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance. Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack. The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges. As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street." "We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. "We're working around the clock with law enforcement agencies and with industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen funds for that front."

events.title: Meta seeks to raise up to $25 billion in debt sale as AI spending jumps
events.summary: Meta is aiming to raise between $20 billion and $25 billion in a bond sale as the company ramps up spending on infrastructure and AI models and services. The sale is expected to be two-thirds U.S. dollars and one-third in Euros, according to people familiar with the matter. On Friday, S&P Global Ratings revised the company's outlook from AA- stable to AA- negative. Meta is seeking to raise between $20 billion and $25 billion in a bond sale on Tuesday as the company ramps up its spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure along with AI models and services. The debt sale is expected to be two-thirds in U.S. dollars and one-third in euros, according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be named because the details are private. Final pricing for the bond sale should come Tuesday afternoon, the sources said. Meta declined to comment. Bloomberg News first reported on Meta's plans. Meta's bond sale comes days after S&P Global Ratings revised the company's outlook from AA- stable to AA- negative, citing "uncertainty" about its hefty capex spending and negative free cash flow. In its third-quarter earnings report last month, the Facebook parent revealed that its full-year capex will come in between $135 billion to $145 billion, representing a $5 billion increase to the low end of its previous guidance. Meta posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion for its latest quarter, joining Alphabet and Amazon in reporting a negative figure. Meta previously raised $25 billion in an April bond sale, and said last week that it plans to raise $95 billion in an effort to fund its AI initiatives. Of that, Meta intends to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, and an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program. Meta's stock rose 2.7% on Tuesday after dropping in 12 of the prior 14 trading sessions and closing out October with its worst month in four years. events.title: UK’s King Charles expresses ‘sorrow’ in Antigua over slave trade
events.summary: Caribbean nations call for reparations as King Charles stops short of issuing an apology for colonial-era slavery. King Charles III has said at the official opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda that the transatlantic slave trade fills him with “horror” and “the most profound personal sorrow”. The British monarch said on Tuesday that the slave trade “still casts a shadow over these [Caribbean] islands and other members of our Commonwealth”, and that the Royal Navy had played “a leading role” in ending it. list 1 of 3 Does the UK have a legal obligation to redress the harms of slavery? list 2 of 3 King Charles’s Caribbean tour: Will he discuss slavery reparations? list 3 of 3 King Charles on Caribbean tour as calls grow for slavery reparations “We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles said. “We can, however, learn from the past.” The king said he was seeking ways to address the wrongs by improving access to education, investing in jobs, encouraging trade among Commonwealth countries and pushing for climate resilience. He ended the speech short of the apology that many Caribbean and African countries had hoped for. He offered no measures to address the economic and social damage of slavery. Buckingham Palace had said the king would not issue a formal apology for slavery during his Caribbean tour, which also took him to the Bahamas and Guyana. Guyanese President Mohamed Irfaan Ali said in an interview that an apology should be the king’s next step. The dispute surfaced at the last Commonwealth summit in Samoa in 2024, when leaders called for discussions about reparations despite opposition from then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer. Last week, current British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK was open to a formal apology , while ruling out financial reparations. Burnham, writing in The Guardian, said he wanted “to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people”. He also proposed leading a programme of debt restructuring to help the Commonwealth’s poorest countries. Ahead of Charles’s speech on Tuesday, a small group of protesters outside the venue held signs reading “Acknowledge the wrong. Commit to repair.” “Technically, we’re free, but mentally a lot of us aren’t,” said Shana Michelle, from Antigua. “You have to apologise, yes. That is where we start with the repair.” Leaders, including Burnham, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, were among those in attendance on Tuesday. The Commonwealth has 56 member nations. Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne said, “No nation should be forced to mortgage its future simply to survive its present.”

events.title: TasWater bosses blame regulator for 'miscalculation' that saw massive bill hikes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts TasWater leaders privately blamed regulator for 'blatant' sewerage charge 'mistake', internal documents show Tasmania's Economic Regulator approved a new pricing structure from July this year. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) In September, some of TasWater's business customers, such as sporting clubs, reported enormous jumps in their fixed sewerage charges. Internal emails, secured through right to information, show TasWater leaders blamed the increase on an "error" by the Office of the Tasmanian Economic Regulator. TasWater says some customers' bills have already been amended while others are paused as the utility works on a solution to the bill increases. Senior leaders at TasWater privately blamed the state's economic regulator for a "blatant mistake" that threatened to cost some Tasmanians tens of thousands of dollars in extra charges, documents show. In September, the ABC spoke to TasWater customers whose bills skyrocketed after the Office of the Tasmanian Economic Regulator approved a new pricing structure, valid from July 2026 to June 2030. It introduced a new way of billing some non-residential customers for the fixed component of their sewerage bill — basing it on water connection size, rather than on their estimated demand on the sewerage network. One business owner said the change saw their bill rise from $630 a month to $3,800 a month, while another sporting association said it copped a $1,400 monthly increase. A TasWater document from September 30 said the price hike may have impacted 33 sporting fields and 62-mixed use sporting facilities. ( ABC News: Georgia Hogge ) Before the change took effect, TasWater had predicted the change could disadvantage some customers and had proposed a solution — some customers with larger pipes would instead be charged as if they had a smaller 20mm connection. But the regulator knocked back the remedy, saying it would create inconsistencies. Businesses, clubs left reeling after change in TasWater pricing Businesses have been hit with hefty bill increases by Tasmania's water provider, leaving some wondering if they can remain open. When the billing changes came in, it led to outcry and an intervention from Premier Jeremy Rockliff, who called on TasWater to pause the billing structure and work with stakeholders to find a more sustainable way forward. But now, documents released to the ABC under right to information (RTI) laws show how TasWater's leadership internally reacted after the blowback, laying the blame on the regulator. TasWater leaders also initially argued that any attempt to reduce the bills must be matched with pricing increases elsewhere, to minimise the impact on its budget. For its part in knocking back the potential remedy, the regulator argued: "the potential for broader impacts across non-residential customers, which have since arisen, was not brought to [its] attention". It also said it only set the maximum amount TasWater could charge, but the water utility was free to charge less. Internal emails, secured through the RTI process, show the premier's media release was promptly forwarded to TasWater leadership, including chair Kevin Young and CEO George Theo. TasWater CEO George Theo believed the price issues were a regulatory matter. ( Supplied: TasWater ) Sep 10, CEO George Theo to chair Kevin Young: "Politics being played where the Premier is asking TW [TasWater] and the Councils to reconsider price increases. "We should consider our response, what he is asking for is not for us in my opinion its a regulatory matter." Mr Young wrote back to Mr Theo the same day. Sep 10, chair Kevin Young to CEO George Theo: "I think it would be worthwhile for the premier and/ or treasurer to write to the economic regulator pointing out the major problem from the price determination and asking the regulator what can be done to correct the error? "I think it is a blatant mistake and miscalculation that needs to be corrected." The Office of the Tasmanian Economic Regulator says while it sets the maximum amount TasWater can charge, the water utility can charge less. ( ABC News: Georgia Hogge ) On September 11, Mr Theo again wrote to Mr Young, saying if the bills were to be reduced, those costs must be recouped.

events.title: What the 2026 midterm elections could mean for Trump's final two years
events.summary: Tuesday's midterm elections will decide who controls Congress for the remainder of Donald Trump's presidency. If Republicans win, Trump could spend another two years facing little congressional resistance and pushing through major policy packages. If Democrats win one or both chambers, the president's remaining legislative priorities would be severely kneecapped, and even the basic functions of government could become gridlocked. Tuesday's midterm elections will at their heart determine control of Congress for the remainder of Donald Trump 's presidency. U.S. voters will decide whether Trump will maintain his Republican iron grip on Washington or recede into lame-duck status after a Democratic triumph. Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm elections If Republicans win, Trump could spend another two years facing little congressional resistance and pushing through major policy packages . If Democrats win one or both chambers, the president's remaining legislative priorities would be severely kneecapped, and even the basic functions of government could become gridlocked . Oddsmakers and public polls placed Democrats in a favorable position ahead of Election Day, especially for flipping control of the Republican-held House. Still, the balance of power will not be decided until ballots are counted — a process that could take days or, in some cases, weeks to complete. The Senate is expected to be particularly close, and if the balance of power comes down to Alaska, the nation may have to wait while the state counts. "The election results could trigger an immediate market reaction, particularly as the Senate outcome becomes clearer," the Washington Policy Strategy Group of Stifel wrote Sunday in an analyst report, where it predicted Democrats will win the House while the Senate remains too close to call. "However, the market's knee-jerk trade could reverse as investors recognize that gridlock remains the most likely policy outcome in either case." Midterm elections 2026 live updates: Economy, inflation and voter concerns 5 things to watch on Election Day as Democrats push for control of Congress Midterm elections could jolt stocks if Democrats sweep Congress Defense, healthcare, crypto and AI: How the midterm election could affect stocks What the 2026 midterm elections could mean for Trump’s final two years Nine Senate races may help determine the fate of Social Security Stock market after midterm elections: What S&P 500 history shows Republicans also control the Senate and with a larger majority than in the House. If Democrats capture one chamber of Congress, Washington policymaking would become significantly more gridlocked. Single-party budget reconciliation bills, the procedural vehicle for most major spending and policy changes in the current status quo of tight congressional margins, would become impossible. Bipartisanship would be required to advance legislation, making must-pass bills such as government funding packages, defense spending and the looming debt ceiling hike more important — and more contentious. In a divided Congress, the party that doesn't control the White House typically uses moments including government funding and debt-ceiling hikes to extract concessions from the majority party, a practice that can lead to brinksmanship. "If Republicans defy the conventional wisdom and maintain their Senate majority, then we would expect a relief rally in the sectors that might react negatively to a Democratic victory," Stifel wrote. "Democrats would still govern the House and gridlock would prevail. In this scenario, Senate Republicans would act as a check on both the Democrats and many of Trump's populist impulses." Democrats are also widely expected to use any majority in Congress to launch investigations into the White House and businesses that have worked with the Trump administration. The majority party gains subpoena power in congressional committees. Polling indicates a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate is possible. In that case, Democrats may more aggressively pursue party-line reconciliation measures that wouldn't become law but would give the party a megaphone ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Trump would still have the ability to veto legislation that Congress passed, severely limiting Democratic bills' prospects of becoming law. Must-pass legislation would be slightly easier to get through Congress if Democrats controlled both chambers. But deals would still need to be brokered with the White House, and the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold could still prove a hurdle that requires bipartisanship. Whichever party gains Senate control is highly unlikely to have at least 60 seats. Democratic lawmakers in both the House and Senate would jump at the chance to lead investigations of the White House and business if given the opportunity.

events.title: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks as Melania Trump prepares to host ceasefire meeting
events.summary: Putin aide Vladimir ​Medinsky is set to serve ⁠as Moscow's chief negotiator ​at peace talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Nov. 10-11, Russia confirmed Tuesday. Separately, first lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House to discuss a local ceasefire in Kherson, the White House said. The Kremlin also hopes to finalize plans for a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, the U.S. and China in the coming days, Russia's Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday. Russia on Tuesday confirmed that peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. will go ahead next week in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, while also signaling that a meeting between Presidents Vladimir Putin , Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to end the conflict was on the table. Putin aide Vladimir ​Medinsky will serve ⁠as Moscow's chief negotiator ​at the talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a conference call, according to Reuters. Separately, first lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House to discuss the local ceasefire in Kherson, the White House said Tuesday. Monday saw the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region to allow for evacuation of residents, in a pause of hostilities that the White House said was brokered by the first lady. Ukraine on Monday accused Russia of using the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city. The first lady's summit on Thursday will be "an extraordinary moment in American history," the White House said, but did not name the representatives who will attend. Melania Trump will deliver remarks on the Oleshky ceasefire at 11 a.m. ET on Thursday, it added. Peskov also said Tuesday the Kremlin hopes to finalize plans for a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, the U.S. and China in the coming days. The comments follow earlier reports that these countries were planning to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table. Zelenskyy has said that any negotiations over Ukraine's future must include Kyiv. events.title: An NYC Marathon runner died suddenly at 24. Her family says the cause was rhabdomyolysis, a rare risk that can even affect fit athletes.
events.summary: A woman died after collapsing at the New York City Marathon from a rare side effect of hard exercise called rhabdomyolysis. kena betancur / AFP via Getty Images A New York City Marathon runner died after collapsing at the finish line near Mile 24. Her family said the cause of death was rhabdomyolysis, a rare side effect of hard exercise. Rhabdo can afflict even experienced athletes and cause life-threatening symptoms if left untreated. A 24-year-old woman who died after the New York City Marathon on Sunday was suffering from a rare side effect of exercise called rhabdomyolysis, her family said. Rachel Apa, an experienced D1 field hockey athlete who spent months training for the race, collapsed near mile 24 in Central Park and was taken by ambulance to the hospital, her father told The New York Times . Apa was a product manager for an electronic manufacturing company. Earlier this year, she posted on LinkedIn that she was running the marathon to raise money for the Parkinson's Foundation, in honor of her grandfather. The New York Road Runners, the group that organizes the marathon, and Apa's family did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Rhabdomyolysis, known as rhabdo, is a risk of extensive strenuous exercise caused by muscle tissue breaking down and overloading the kidneys. Without prompt medical treatment, it can be life-threatening. Here's what to know about rhabdo, including the symptoms to look out for and how to prevent it. What is rhabdomyolysis and what causes it? Rhabdomyolysis can occur after severe muscle injury or intense exertion. As damaged muscle tissue breaks down, it releases compounds into the bloodstream that the kidneys typically filter out. In rare cases, those byproducts can overwhelm the kidneys and lead to kidney damage or acute kidney failure. About 26,000 cases of rhabdo are reported in the US each year, research suggests. Anyone can suffer from rhabdo, but factors like hot environments and dehydration can increase the risk, according to Cleveland Clinic. While it's generally not common, cases of rhabdo are often caused by high-intensity exercise or long endurance sessions without rest. For instance, research has previously linked cases of rhabdo to marathons (particularly during high temperatures) and vigorous spin classes . It's also increasingly a concern for the military, which is working to spot rhabdo in troops more quickly. What are the symptoms of rhabdo? Symptoms of rhabdo include fatigue, muscle cramps or unexpected pain, and dark-colored urine, which can show up hours or days after exercise, according to the CDC. Rhabdo can be diagnosed with a blood test and treated with IV fluids to help flush out the waste products. To prevent rhabdo, avoid pushing too hard during exercise, take breaks as needed, and drink plenty of water, especially in hot, humid weather. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The 'poison pill' ballot measure that could kill the California billionaire tax
events.summary: California voters will decide Tuesday on Proposition 40, known as the Billionaire Tax Act, which would impose a one-time tax of 5% on the total net worth of Californians worth over $1 billion. The tax is one of the most widely watched ballot measures this election season, since it taps popular anger over the rising power of tech billionaires. The strongest challenge to California's billionaire tax could be Proposition 42, a competing ballot measure that bans state taxes on retirement accounts, say tax experts. Get Inside Wealth directly to your inbox The Inside Wealth newsletter by Robert Frank is your weekly guide to high-net-worth investors and the industries that serve them. The California billionaire tax could face a stiff challenge from a competing ballot measure that would ban state taxes on retirement accounts, according to tax experts. California voters will decide the fate today of Proposition 40, known as the Billionaire Tax Act, which would impose a one-time tax of 5% on the total net worth of Californians worth over $1 billion. The so-called "billionaire tax" is one of the most widely watched ballot measures this election season, since it would be the first state tax on net worth and taps popular anger over the rising power and wealth of tech billionaires. Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm elections The tax requires a simple majority to pass. Since it would only tax the state's roughly 250 billionaires, many political experts initially predicted easy passage. Yet a recent poll by the Public Policy Institute of California shows it falling short, with 46% supporting and 52% against. Supporters of the tax blame a $300 million ad blitz funded by tech billionaires and business groups opposing the measure. Many of the ads claim the ballot measure would allow the Legislature, with a two-thirds vote, to expand the tax to everyday Californians. Yet tax experts cite another potential roadblock to the tax: Proposition 42. One of two ballot measures that would act as poison pills against the billionaire tax if they get more votes, Prop 42 calls for a permanent ban on any statewide tax on property of all Californians. The ballot measure "Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer's past activities." The official California Voter Information Guide explains the "pro" argument by saying that Prop 42 protects Californians from double taxation by "prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings." The "con" argument, according to the voter guide, is that Prop 42 is "just another billionaire-funded trick." Propositions 41 and 42 were created and submitted by Building a Better California, a political action committee funded by tech executives and several California billionaires opposed to the billionaire tax. Political and tax experts say voters' fears about protecting retirement accounts will be a powerful motivation to vote "yes" on Prop 42, thus nullifying the billionaire tax. As much as they may want to tax billionaires, their retirement accounts may be more important. "Both Proposition 41, which prohibits new taxes from disregarding voter-approved spending limits, and Proposition 42, which prohibits new taxes on retirement accounts and personal property, could win majority support," said Jared Walczak of Walczak Policy Consulting.

events.title: AI is on the ballot. Data centers are a major political issue in the midterms. But the implications of today’s vote for AI go much further
events.summary: Hello and welcome to Eye on AI. In this edition: AI is on the ballot. Anthropic discloses its Q3 results and even more massive spending plans. Investors push Anthropic to lower valuation target as its IPO math looks tough . Palantir reports record revenue growth. Report: U.S. intelligence believes Chinese spy targeted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. A new way to ‘program’ AI models. AI lab employees offer chilling video testimonials on the tech’s big risks. It’s election day in the U.S., of course, and in many places AI is on the ballot. Voters in dozens of states and local municipalities from California to Maine are deciding on measures that could impact the construction of hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of data center projects. Bloomberg has a great breakdown of the measures by type and state. Overall, there are at least 41 ballot initiatives involving data centers, according to election tracking site Ballotpedia. My native Ohio has the most pending, with 21 measures in total, including 11 that would either ban construction or force a pause in further data center developments. Among the most closely watched municipalities is Piqua, a 20,000-person city in west central Ohio, where Meta is planning to spend $1 billion to construct a data center with a capacity of up to 1.4 gigawatts. Meta promises the project will bring 1,000 construction jobs to the area, but local opposition is running high. Voters there will be deciding today whether to recall the mayor and two city commissioners who have supported the project. There’s also a $2 billion AWS data center project on the ballot in Sunbury, Ohio, as well as a $10 billion AWS project on the ballot in Adams County, Ohio. With a majority of Americans being more fearful than hopeful about AI, according to a recent Pew Research Center poll , many data center projects could be in trouble. In the second quarter of 2026 alone, at least 45 data center projects worth some $68 billion were disrupted due to local opposition, according to a report from Data Center Watch, a research project run by the company 10a Labs. These trends could spell trouble for the leading AI companies, which are increasingly compute constrained, as well as for the neocloud companies that have sprung up to provide AI compute. (For more on the risks facing the neoclouds, see my colleague Beatrice Nolan’s essay in last Thursday’s Eye on AI.) Many AI industry leaders are belatedly saying data center developers made a mistake in trying to rush many of these projects to market without doing enough to ensure political buy-in from the communities in which they are located. OpenAI has recently been trying to convince people to support data center projects by rebranding them as “compute campuses” —although it’s not clear that alone will do much. When Bea and I recently sat down with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in London, he told us, “before we bring in massive amounts of investment into a small community, I think we have to go first and let the community know what we’re planning to do. Partner with the community, invest in the community, and if the community really doesn’t want us to be there, find another community.” He said that he thought the industry now realizes this and has changed its approach. “Everybody is much more mindful about it,” he said. “I’m hoping we turn the tide on [data centers].” But this belated “hearts and minds” strategy from the AI industry and its data center partners may be too little, too late. All of this certainly heightens tensions around Anthropic’s upcoming IPO. In an updated prospectus made public on the SEC website yesterday, the company disclosed even more infrastructure and compute commitments than it had in its initial S-1 filing, with the figure now totaling some $895 billion. The company also revealed that it had to spend $5 billion in the third quarter to source short-term computing capacity to meet demand, saying that the added spending was one of the major reasons its adjusted operating margin fell to 15% from 19% in the prior quarter. Anthropic wants to lock in data center capacity on a longer-term basis, and even build out its own data centers through its new “Anthropic Direct” project , to lower some of these costs. But there’s a debate about whether the data center capacity Anthropic and its rivals such as OpenAI need will actually be available on the time scales they require, due to problems getting data centers built and connected to the grid. In fact, some think that Anthropic may be committing to buy more capacity from neoclouds than it actually needs precisely because it is assuming some portion of it won’t ever get delivered. A vibe shift on Capitol Hill—but what will make it into law? If the midterms result in a Democratic-controlled Congress, as seems possible, even likely if the polls prove correct, then AI policy could shift dramatically. The Democrats are far more likely to try to enact some kind of federal AI regulation. Before the election, the bipartisan Frontier Act looked like the bill that had the best odds of passing. But a new Congress will rejuggle that calculus and could open the path to other bills. Of course, any legislation that Congress does pass faces a likely veto from President Trump, who has been steadfast in his opposition to AI regulation. That means it will still require a bipartisan bill with very broad support to have any hope of garnering the two-thirds majority in both houses needed to override a veto. This probably still favors a bill that looks like the Frontier Act, but you never know. Another thing we may see in a Democratic-controlled Congress: a new wave of investigations into the leading AI companies and the safety and security protocols they’re implementing. Already Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) has written to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to demand answers to questions about the risks the company disclosed in its IPO prospectus. Expect much more of this if the Democrats retake the Senate. Will AI play a role in trying to manipulate the vote? Another thing to watch for in the midterms will be what role, if any, AI plays in attempts at election interference, political misinformation, and manipulation. For years, experts have been concerned about deepfakes and other AI-generated content being used in this way. Increasingly, AI is being used to create political advertisements, as well as satirical social media memes, that can influence, or at least reinforce, people’s perceptions of candidates. But in most cases, it is clear that this political communication is AI-generated and the effort is aimed more at persuasion than deception. So far, in U.S. elections, true deepfakes have not proved decisive. events.title: Google’s Gemini-powered Home Speaker is already on sale for 20 percent off
events.summary: We’re big fans of the Google Home Speaker’s design. | Photo: Jennifer Patison Tuohy / The Verge If you’re looking for a good smart speaker, the Google Home Speaker is down to around $79 ($20 off) in all four colors at Best Buy , Walmart , and Target . That’s the best price we’ve seen for the Gemini-powered speaker, which launched in June and represents Google’s first smart speaker in several years. Google Home Speaker Where to Buy: $99.99 $79 at Walmart $99.99 $79.99 at Best Buy $99.99 $79.99 at Target In her review , my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy noted that Google’s new Home Speaker offers a nice balance of sound quality, size, and design. It’s smaller than the prior-gen Nest Audio , making it easy to place anywhere in your home. However, despite its small size, it produces loud, clear audio with 360-degree sound. Our own David Pierce even found it sounded cleaner, louder, and sharper than Amazon’s similarly priced Echo Dot Max , though Tuohy preferred the latter’s fuller sound and stronger bass. The older Nest Audio still sounds better overall, but Google’s latest speaker takes up less space and costs slightly less. The Google Home Speaker also offers a few useful smart home upgrades. It supports Matter and includes a Thread border router, allowing you to connect and control a wide range of compatible smart home devices. It’s also the first Google smart speaker that can double as an audio output for the Google TV Streamer 4K , letting you play TV audio through one or two speakers instead of your TV’s built-in speakers. Tuohy found it worked well and delivered clear dialogue, though sound quality varied depending on what she was watching. One of its most notable features is support for Gemini, which is also available on older Google speakers and is much better at understanding natural language and complex requests than the old Google Assistant. In her testing, Tuohy found it could handle multiple smart home commands at once and respond to conversational requests, like turning down the air conditioner when she mentioned feeling too hot. It’s also particularly impressive at answering general knowledge questions, though it can be slow and unreliable at times. Keep in mind, too, that some features require a $10-a-month Google Home Premium subscription , including Gemini Live, which lets you have extended conversations with the assistant without repeating the wake word. events.title: Greenland parliament approves security deal with US, Denmark
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Lawmakers vote 16-0 for trilateral agreement signed in September, while seven abstained. Trump plans for ‘massive’ resource exploration in Greenland Lawmakers in the semi-autonomous Danish territory of Greenland have approved an agreement with Denmark and the United States aimed at bolstering security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The deal was passed 16-0 on Tuesday, with seven lawmakers abstaining. list 1 of 3 US signs ‘tremendous’ security deal with Denmark and Greenland list 2 of 3 Why does Greenland matter to the US? list 3 of 3 Greenland’s delegation gets hero’s welcome after signing US-Denmark pact The agreement was signed in September by US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. It followed months of negotiations behind the scenes amid growing tensions over Trump’s repeated threats to seize the vast, resource-rich Arctic island. Greenlandic Foreign Minister Mute Egede said the ratification was another important step for the self-governing island. “The road to this point has been ⁠a difficult one for us as ⁠a people. But we have stood firm on our fundamental principles, chosen dialogue and taken responsibility for our country’s interests,” he wrote in a ⁠post on Facebook. “This is about all of us. The Greenland we love. ⁠About our security. And about our ⁠right to shape our own future,” he said. Located between Europe and North America, Greenland is the world’s largest island, with a population of 57,000 people. Trump’s refusal last year to rule out a military invasion had caused fear among Greenlanders, the majority of whom rejected US control, according to opinion polls. The trilateral deal paves the way for more US bases on Greenland. It also allows the US to “modernise and expand” its activities at the Pituffik Space Base, a remote US military installation in northwest Greenland. Under its terms, Greenland will remain under Danish control – but the agreement would still apply if the island eventually chooses independence. The deal stipulates it will only “enter into force” once the “necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland, have been completed”. Danish lawmakers are set to debate it later this month, while no approval is required from the US Senate.

events.title: Midterm elections could jolt stocks if Democrats sweep Congress
events.summary: Investors are not yet fully accounting for the Democrats winning both the House and Senate, a blue wave scenario that could weigh on share prices in the short term on Wednesday. History says any dip should be bought as the post-midterms market move is usually upward. But big gains already this year, may have stolen that momentum. Big Democrat gains could further weigh on an already-ailing AI trade on fear restrictions on data centers gain traction nationwide. The stock market is not yet pricing in a Democratic sweep of Congress — despite some polls and most prediction markets pointing that way — so that scenario could weigh on share prices Wednesday, according to investors and analysts. Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm elections Republicans managing to keep control could cause a short-term relief rally, they said. Short-term moves aside, the typical post-midterm pattern in the months ahead is bullish. But some wonder if the market could buck the positive historical trend this time because the S&P 500 is already up so much this year going into the election. As far as certain stocks to watch, a big Democratic win on Tuesday night — especially in the Texas governor race — could add fuel to an artificial intelligence stock sell-off on the notion that more data center restrictions would gain momentum nationally. Defense stocks could come under pressure on fears of limits on spending. Polls are pointing to a Democratic victory in the House and a toss-up in the Senate. Prediction markets have been more favorable to Democrats, calling for a blue sweep . While investors are signaling "begrudging acceptance" to a base-case scenario that there will indeed be a Democratic sweep, that's not how they're positioning, said Tobin Marcus, head of U.S. policy and politics at Wolfe Research. The firm's recent survey data among more than 100 institutional investors suggests they are not strongly positioned for any particular result. "Investors seem to have a significant dose of skepticism about whether the final outcome is going to be quite as favorable to Democrats as the polling suggests," Marcus told CNBC, noting that the firm shares the view that the "polling is likely overstating Democratic strength." JPMorgan sees a blue wave knocking the S&P 500 by about a half percent on Wednesday. On the other hand, if Republicans end up retaining both chambers of Congress, that could spur a rally, said Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at the Wells Fargo Investment Institute. "From a certainty standpoint, the market knows what to do with Republicans holding both chambers," he said. Citigroup strategists said Monday that Republicans losing the House but managing to keep the Senate could be "a tailwind for equities into year-end." JPMorgan traders predict up to a 1% pop on Wednesday if Republicans hold on to that chamber. Looking past any short-term move, stocks tend to rally after the midterms have concluded. In fact, the S&P 500 was up one year out after all midterm elections going back to the early 1980s. But the S&P 500 has already recorded double-digit gains so far in 2026, so some on Wall Street worry that investors are being overly complacent heading into this year's elections. During midterm election years, the S&P 500 has typically averaged a 14% drawdown at some point in the second half of the year found Jonathan Krinsky, chief market technician at BTIG. "The reason stocks often perform well in November during midterms is because [the S&P 500] typically is weak INTO the elections. We have the opposite setup this year," Krinsky wrote last week. "Therefore, while consensus is that we see a post midterm rally, we think the opposite is actually more likely." It's not helping that the broader market has recently come under significant pressure due to turbulence in the artificial intelligence trade, which led the Nasdaq Composite to post its worst day since June on Friday. AI shares led the market lower again on Monday. A strong showing from Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections could pressure the trade even more . At the state level, increased Democratic control is probably a headwind for stocks associated with data centers and technological capital equipment, analysts said. "It [would solidify] the early kind of cautionary signs in different states around the advancement of AI infrastructure," Rob Rains at Washington Analysis told CNBC. Goldman Sachs strategists said this week that a Democratic Congress "might limit data center tax incentives, but a national moratorium looks unlikely in any election outcome." One example would be Texas — a key hub of the data center buildout. A surprise loss there by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has the "potential to spook" the market in the short term, Wolfe's Marcus said. A blue wave might pressure defense shares, while boosting healthcare stocks, analysts and investors said.
