events.title: Ghosted after a job interview? There's a website for that—and thousands of frustrated job seekers have weighed in
events.summary: Work AI is making a mess of how humans interact at work Work Use this 4-word phrase to stand out after a job interview: 'It can be really powerful,' says career coach Work Some job seekers are refusing to do AI interviews, even in a tough market Work How AI is ruining job interviews Work Ex-Google recruiter: Why this common mistake makes your resume 'invisible' Gary Meyer didn't intend to become a ghostbuster. But his website, Did They Ghost You , has become an outlet for thousands of frustrated job seekers who have been ghosted by employers. Based on anonymous reports — 2,888 at last count — the site tracks and ranks the companies that are most often accused of abruptly ceasing contact with candidates, including some of the biggest names in the S&P 500. Ghosting is a widespread issue. A recent report from hiring platform Greenhouse found that 45% of job seekers who made it to the interview stage of a hiring process said they were ghosted by an employer afterward, based on a survey of 1,200 U.S. candidates conducted in September 2026. Meyer, 42, an artificial intelligence-focused marketing consultant who lives in Toronto, created Did They Ghost You in June after listening to his friends vent about interviewing with companies and then never hearing back. He never intended for the website to be more than a "fun little side project," but when he shared a link to his site on LinkedIn, the reports started pouring in. He says that within the first few days, the site received more than two million visitors: "Clearly, it struck a bit of a nerve." Meyer, who reads and approves each report himself, says he fielded five or six new submissions every minute at the height of the site's popularity over the summer. To protect people's identities, Meyer typically doesn't publish the contents of the report, and his site doesn't track personal information. Each report contributes to an overall tally of ghosting incidents. "Was told that I was the preferred candidate by the Director of HR in a debrief immediately following the final interview and then just didn't hear back," one report featured on the site said. "Ghosted, then reposted their ad a week later," said another. Meyer's definition of being ghosted by an employer doesn't include applying for a job and never hearing back — unfortunately, "that's part and parcel" of the job market today, he says. His website is for people who make it through several steps of the hiring process and then never hear from the company again. "These are people who have gone through multiple rounds of interviews, met with people, flown to various states or cities for the interview and then right at the end, just nothing, no response, nothing," he says. Part of the reason he created the site is to let those job seekers know they're not alone, he says. "I think a huge part of what makes it hurt so much when you get ghosted is the assumption is that you've screwed up so badly that you're not worth responding to, that you're not even worth an email," he says. It's easy for job seekers to blame themselves when they get ghosted, according to career coach Phoebe Gavin, but it's really a failure on the company's part to practice "basic etiquette" in the hiring process. "The hiring process requires a great deal of unpaid labor from candidates, and it is a reasonable expectation that you will receive some sort of communication, that you will be treated with some sort of dignity," she says. Although it doesn't excuse their actions, there are a few common reasons that a company might ghost a candidate, Gavin says. Especially at small companies, managers are often tasked with supervising the hiring process on top of their regular duties. While juggling all those responsibilities, it's easy for a candidate to get "lost in the shuffle," she says. Another possibility is that there could be some behind-the-scenes factors that the hiring manager can't share with an external candidate, like a budget cut, hiring freeze or leadership turnover, Gavin says. Still, "candidates deserve to hear from hiring managers regardless," she says. Meyer says he doesn't intend to turn Did They Ghost You into the next Glassdoor. The site's popularity "got a little bit overwhelming," he says, and he currently has a backlog of reports to read and approve. He plans to keep running the website, but "the best case scenario is that this problem gets fixed, and there's no point in having the site anymore." events.title: Gas policy consultants worked for industry and government at same time
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Consultancy ACIL Allen advised on government gas policy while working undisclosed for gas industry The Future Gas Strategy committed to expanding Australia's investment in gas. ( ABC News: Chris Lewis ) Consulting firm ACIL Allen helped to develop the government's Future Gas Strategy while also doing undisclosed work for the gas industry. Climate Integrity said its investigation had revealed conflicts of interest that the consultancy should have disclosed to the energy department. Greens senator Steph Hodgins-May says the government and energy department must explain why perceived conflicts of interest were missed. A consulting firm hired by the federal government to help develop its Future Gas Strategy was simultaneously doing paid work for the gas industry and did not disclose that conflict of interest to the energy department. An investigation by advocacy group Climate Integrity found ACIL Allen did not disclose that while it was working on two reports for the government, it was also undertaking work for Gas Energy Australia, the Australian Pipelines and Gas Association and the Business Council of Australia, which represents several gas giants as members. Consultancy ACIL Allen was commissioned to assess proposed reforms to the east coast gas market in late 2023, at the same time it was working for three gas industry groups to produce reports about the benefit of gas to the economy and its role in Australia's transition to net zero emissions by 2050. Months later, ACIL Allen was hired by the government again to provide advice on Australia's gas needs, to be fed into the government's landmark Future Gas Strategy — the policy plan for how Australia will transition away from gas towards net zero emissions. "This will inform an understanding of energy security, whether other sources of firming can perform this role and whether government action is needed," a department official wrote about the ACIL Allen contract, in emails released under freedom of information (FOI) laws. Tender records and documents obtained under FOI show ACIL Allen's work for government and industry over 2023 and 2024 directly overlapped. Madeleine King delivered the Future Gas Strategy in 2024. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The ABC attempted to reach ACIL Allen, including in questions sent by email. When the ABC spoke to an unidentified ACIL Allen representative by phone, he responded, "Yeah, no, I don't want to talk to you, thank you," before hanging up. ACIL Allen also did not respond to questions put by Climate Integrity several months ago. Future Gas Strategy promised plan for gas beyond 2050 The Future Gas Strategy delivered by Resources Minister Madeleine King in 2024 concluded that "the analytical findings are clear … natural gas is needed through to 2050 and beyond", with the policy committing to expand Australia's gas investment. Labor backbench 'blindsided' by Albanese gas strategy Labor backbenchers say they were caught off guard by the government's new gas policy, which the resources minister says will keep the fossil fuel in Australia's energy mix until 2050 "and beyond". It prompted a revolt on Labor's back bench, with several MPs at the time telling the ABC they had been blindsided by the policy , and its focus on expanding gas and continuing it beyond 2050. Climate Integrity executive director Claire Snyder said the gas industry had obvious financial interests in shaping the Future Gas Strategy, and ACIL Allen should have been clear it was also doing work for them. "The gas industry clients of ACIL Allen have a direct financial interest in the outcomes of the Future Gas Strategy and of the gas policies that ACIL Allen is working on for the government. So to us that is a clear conflict of interest," executive director Claire Snyder said. "What we have is a consultancy with undeclared ties to the gas industry advising the government on consequential gas policy. "Our analysis has also shown that the body of work produced by ACIL Allen over that period of time consistently overstated the cost of zero emissions alternatives to gas, and it entirely omitted the climate cost of developing new gas supplies. The result of this is it advantaged the case for gas." As an example, Climate Integrity pointed to modelling based on up-front capital costs of energy projects, rather than system costs comparing expense over a project's lifetime, as a methodology that advantaged gas. Greens deputy leader Steph Hodgins-May said the non-disclosure called into question the government's Future Gas Strategy. "It has no integrity.

events.title: CrowdStrike to shell out nearly $500M for 2 AI security startups as the market for securing agents takes off
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike is buying two AI security companies that expand its products to more broadly monitor, test, and cover AI models and agents, as companies across industries start rolling out AI agents and models wholesale. CrowdStrike said it will buy Fiddler AI , which makes observability software for monitoring AI agents inside enterprises, and Dreadnode , which helps companies automate security testing specifically aimed at detecting flaws in AI models, apps, and agents before they are set live. The company is paying around $400 million for Fiddler AI, and about $95 million for Dreadnode, according to The Wall Street Journal . The deals are happening at a time of significant upheaval in the cybersecurity space, especially as companies’ policies and processes lag behind AI adoption within their walls. Teams and individual employees alike are experimenting with AI tools, automating workflows, vibe-coding custom apps, and deploying armies of AI agents to do their bidding, which is understandably causing headaches for security teams. CrowdStrike, whose products are used widely across enterprises and governments, is clearly trying to leverage its already significant heft and presence to capture a share of this quickly burgeoning market . It’s not alone, of course, as we’ve already seen several startups and cybersecurity vendors raising dozens of millions in funding to solve issues for companies, though most of these approaches are essentially based on the conviction that existing security software isn’t enough to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, or usage. The company has itself been building detection and response controls , dubbed Falcon Guardian, to help companies see and understand what agents are doing on their devices, and these acquisitions seem to further flesh out its offerings. Fiddler AI is going to be part of CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform as Falcon Observe, where it’ll ostensibly help the company’s clients evaluate agents before they’re deployed, understand their actions, and monitor what they do, and feed that information as telemetry into the broader platform. Dreadnode, meanwhile, will be integrated into the Falcon Guardian product , to which the startup’s software will feed its testing results as security policy recommendations. Founded in 2018, Fiddler AI has raised a total of about $99 million to date, according to PitchBook. Dreadnode, founded in 2023, has raised $14 million so far. As the global body representing the mobile network industry, the GSMA claims that severe storms and floods already cost operators $1.7 billion annually to repair damage to cell radio sites, and it believes that figure could nearly double to more than $3 billion a year by 2050, under the climate conditions expected then. The GSMA sets out its findings in a six-part research series, Futureproofing Connectivity: Climate Risk and Resilience in Telecommunications , alongside a separate document outlining its Policy Principles for Mobile Network Resilience . The report identifies weather-related risks that can affect telecoms networks, along with the associated restoration costs. Towers, masts, and rooftop sites are particularly exposed to wind and storms or lightning, for example, while ground-level equipment at mobile sites can be inundated in flooding incidents. High temperatures can cause radio equipment to overheat, while heavy rain can degrade wireless signal strength, and infrastructure in coastal locations may be exposed to storm surges. However, the report fingers the electricity supply as the biggest vulnerability. If that gets knocked out, the network could go offline once any backup power is exhausted, which may take anywhere from a few hours to considerably longer, depending on the site. Under current climate conditions, the cost of damage to cell sites is estimated at $1 billion associated with severe storms, while river and coastal floods account for $577 million and $124 million, respectively. Based on projected mid-century climate conditions, the GSMA expects costs due to severe storms to rise significantly to about $2.37 billion, accounting for three-quarters of all damage. The report asserts that cell network resilience requires a whole ecosystem approach, pointing out that if severe weather impacts power networks, then that also affects the telecoms infrastructure. The GSMA says that network firms have traditionally managed the operational risks that may affect network availability, but claims they face barriers in conducting full assessments of those associated with climate change. Some of these barriers are internal, such as lack of shared information between departments. Other barriers are in the different regulatory reporting frameworks, with infrastructure rules tending to focus on service continuity, while climate disclosure frameworks focus on governance, financial exposure, and reporting for investors and other stakeholders. The report lists separate recommendations for network firms and for policymakers and regulators. Operators are advised to embed resilience by design, using modeled projections for severe weather and future risk scenarios. They are also told to plan and test resilience across the wider ecosystem, engaging with others such as public authorities. When it comes to policymakers and regulators, the report asks for resilience frameworks to be developed through consultation with the operators. It also advises coordination among mobile operators, electricity and fuel providers, and emergency services to help maintain vital communications during major disruptions. And as if that isn't enough to chew over, the separate policy document sets out five principles for governments and regulators.

events.title: States take steps to secure vote after federal pullback
events.summary: State officials have largely taken securing the 2026 midterm elections into their own hands after nearly two years of federal program and funding cuts during the second Trump administration. Why it matters: The reduction in federal support has come as AI tools threaten to make it easier for hackers to uncover software vulnerabilities, launch cyberattacks, and spread disinformation that undermines trust in election results. Reality check: Just because a security flaw exists doesn't mean hackers can exploit it to manipulate election results. Nearly all U.S. elections maintain paper records that can be used to verify electronic tallies. Threat level: Election officials are preparing for everything from cyberattacks and AI-generated disinformation to physical threats, logistical disruptions and legal challenges. The big picture: State election officials relied on homeland security agencies, fusion centers, police, National Guard units and private cybersecurity firms to prepare for the midterms, John Milhofer, a spokesperson for the National Association of Secretaries of State, told Axios. That group and the National Association of State Election Directors are helping states exchange threat intelligence and connect with federal agencies and private sector experts. Catch up quick: State resources have become more important after the Trump administration scaled back federal election security assistance. CISA cut election security personnel and services in 2025, while federal funding for the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center, a key information-sharing network for election officials, ended that year. Election officials are receiving fewer election-specific threat briefings and less direct technical assistance, even after CISA outlined plans to restore some services in September. Zoom in: Michael Moore, chief information security officer for the Arizona secretary of state's office, told Axios that the state has been without a dedicated CISA cybersecurity adviser since March 2025. The Arizona Department of Homeland Security has helped fill the gap, providing security tools and monitoring services to smaller counties. On Election Day, Arizona is bringing together its state cybersecurity team, National Guard, the FBI and a representative from CISA's Region 9 office to coordinate responses to potential threats, Moore said. Moore's team has spent years conducting tabletop exercises covering cyberattacks, AI-generated impersonations of election officials, suspicious packages and other disruptions. Between the lines: Arizona is also getting threat intelligence from former CISA personnel who work in the space, election security nonprofits and officials in other states. Moore said his relationship with New Jersey's election security officials is particularly useful because his East Coast counterparts can warn him about threats hours before they might emerge in Arizona. What they're saying: A CISA spokesperson said in a statement that the agency will provide state and local government officials, including election officials and election vendors, "no-cost voluntary services" like vulnerability scanning and technical expertise, when they request it. "We are committed to supporting state and local elections officials to protect election infrastructure and safeguard our democracy," the spokesperson added. Yes, but: Moore said he still wants CISA to return to its 2024 staffing levels — and then double them. "If we are literally experiencing a cyberattack from a nation-state, it shouldn't be Arizona versus that nation-state," Moore said. "We're the United States of America. It should be a unified response." David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, told reporters during a briefing Thursday that states have hired vendors and built their own networks to compensate for the federal retreat. "They might not be able to replace everything," Becker said. "They're not going to get the same bird's-eye national-level view of potential disinformation or potential cyber events." The bottom line: Election officials said they're prepared for disruptions, even if they can't prevent every attack. "The goal is prevent as much as we can, detect and recover," Moore said. "We're going to have some amount of disruption.... We're going to recover."

events.title: AI-generated 'slopaganda' in political ads puts internet platforms on alert
events.summary: Tuesday's midterm elections follow record spending on AI-generated political ads. There's no federal legislation mandating disclosure of AI use in such ads. The midterm election cycle has been dominated by "slopaganda," or campaign ads featuring AI-generated clips and images, creating another challenge for Instagram, YouTube and X as they attempt to monitor their platforms. The term slopaganda dates back to early last year, when a group of AI experts used it in a paper to describe a new phenomenon combining generative AI slop with propaganda and misinformation. There's no comprehensive federal law governing the use or disclosure of AI in political ads. And while there are some 30 state laws with different requirements about AI use and disclosure, candidates don't always abide by them. On the leading internet sites run by Meta , Google and Elon Musk's SpaceX , users run into AI-generated ads and AI-generated posts shared by politicians, alongside authentic videos and clips. More than $187 million has been spent on nearly 300 ads generated or enhanced by AI, according to an analysis released last week by the Wesleyan Media Project . That's almost certainly an undercount, the organization says, because so many ads don't contain disclaimers. Over 90% of the spending came from Republican candidates, a Republican party committee or a Republican-leaning group, the report found, and most don't include disclosures. CNBC found a number of AI-generated ads running online without disclosures, including a fake video of New York Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul that was posted by her opponent, Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman. In Texas, Republican senatorial candidate Ken Paxton created an AI-generated video showing Democratic opponent James Talarico making controversial statements, with a three-second disclosure flashing in the middle. It's being shared as organic content on YouTube and X by Paxton's campaign. The Blakeman and Paxton campaigns didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. YouTube told CNBC that the company applies "prominent labels to realistic AI content." "For organic content on YouTube, political candidates can request removal where their face appears to be altered or generated by AI," the company said. "For advertisers, we require disclosure when an election ad contains synthetic or digitally altered people or events to provide viewers with transparency." YouTube parent Google also requires political ads to complete its election ads verification process and include "paid for by" disclosures. X says advertisers must comply with applicable laws, putting the responsibility on the advertiser, not the platform. The company didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment. Meta referred to its guidelines on political ads, including restrictions on their use in the week prior to the election. The company also mandates "paid for by" labels and maintains an ad library of political ads. In June, the company ramped up its labeling, adding a new "about this ad" tool for ads that Meta detects have been created with third-party AI tools. Last month, Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. Cambridge Analytica, which was a political consulting firm, allegedly accessed the information of 87 million Facebook users in improper fashion. One risk the tech platforms face with generative AI is being asked to create misleading images and videos. The Brennan Center for Justice tested ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Claude, Perplexity and DeepSeek for their willingness to facilitate deceptive content. The study from August found that many models may avoid generating content around familiar conspiracies, but can generally be manipulated into creating misleading material. A retest of those platforms in October found that ChatGPT had made progress. It had started redirecting prompts for harmful election images into illustrations so they look like comics, or refusing to take action on them altogether. A number of national politicians are trying to address the issue. The Protect Elections from Deceptive AI Act , backed by senators from both parties, would prohibit knowingly distributing materially deceptive AI-generated video or audio about federal candidates. Other bills are being led by Democrats in Congress, including the AI Ads Act , which is looking to expand current bans on campaign misrepresentation to include generative AI content. None of the proposed bills have advanced out of committee. WATCH: AI challenge is lack of compute in the marketplace

events.title: Improved asteroid deflection model runs faster, reveals more doomsday worries
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Anthropic BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters “We expected aim to matter ... What surprised us was how much,' says Sandia physicist Nathan Moore Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth 3 days ago Voyager 1 gives controllers the silent treatment 4 days ago NASA ponders a Hubble servicing mission or a controlled deorbit 4 days ago Boffin's software found a possible dwarf planet - a result so rare he thought it must be a bug 5 days ago China's spaceplane bears striking resemblance to America's X-37B 6 days ago Researchers at Sandia National Laboratories have developed a method to make asteroid deflection modeling faster and more detailed. Their simulations also demonstrated just how much asteroid shape and orientation can complicate efforts to deflect a threatening space rock. Sandia researchers, led by staff physicist Nathan Moore, were looking for a way to better model how X-rays from a nuclear detonation near an asteroid can change its trajectory, as explained in a recently published research paper . “Before, the calculations were so time-consuming, one could not do very many of them,” Moore told The Register . “So it was very difficult to explore different scenarios, different asteroids, or different mission concepts.” The complexity of those calculations forced earlier researchers to make compromises, often modeling asteroids as spheres or simplifying the physics involved. Perfectly spherical asteroids are rare, and their irregular shapes present an additional challenge for those keeping an eye on the skies to avert a potential asteroid apocalypse. To overcome the computational problem and enable better modeling of irregular asteroid shapes, Moore and his team combined two high-fidelity simulation codes already in use at Sandia: ALEGRA, which models radiation heating and high-energy material dynamics, and SPARTA, which simulates the behavior of low-density gases. As Moore explained to us in an email, both codes are good at one particular part of asteroid impact modeling, but bad at the other. “ALEGRA … can very accurately simulate the vaporization of the rocky surface, but the calculation becomes more inefficient for matter at low densities,” Moore told us. “This is a problem for asteroid deflection simulations, because as the gas expands around the asteroid, the calculation time goes up.” Earlier asteroid simulations using ALEGRA typically modeled asteroids as spheres to reduce calculation times. “SPARTA is more efficient at low gas densities,” Moore said. “The problem is, conversely, SPARTA gets more difficult to run at high gas densities. So the key here was using both codes.” In Moore’s model, ALEGRA handles regions of high gas density, while SPARTA tackles the more dilute regions of an irregular shape. The result is two codes handling the parts of the problem they're best suited to solve, reducing the overall computational burden. The combined approach is more than 1,600 times faster than earlier methods, Moore said in a Sandia press release , while retaining sufficient accuracy to predict deflection in irregularly shaped asteroids. The improved simulations reveal just how much asteroid shape and orientation can complicate attempts to calculate the outcome of a nuclear deflection. “We expected aim to matter,” Moore said. “What surprised us was how much.” Deflection simulations using detailed models of three well-studied asteroids – Golevka, Bennu, and Itokawa – found that irradiating different sides of the same asteroid with X-rays from a nearby nuclear detonation could produce as much as a fivefold difference in the resulting velocity change. Bennu, the most symmetrical of the three, still showed nearly twofold differences in deflection velocity depending on which side faced the blast. In other words, we need to be incredibly precise about where we detonate a nuclear device near an asteroid, or we risk giving it a much smaller shove than intended.

events.title: What’s at stake as Nebraska voters decide whether to legalize online sports betting in the midterms
events.summary: Nebraskans will vote on two ballot measures that can reshape the state’s gambling industry and bring mobile sports betting to bettors across the state. Measures 440 and 441 on Nebraska’s midterm ballot would collectively legalize and regulate online sports wagering, allowing people located in the state to place bets on professional and college sporting events. The measures come at a time when sports betting has become one of the fastest-growing segments of the American gambling industry. Since the Supreme Court cleared the way for states to legalize sports wagering in 2018, sportsbooks have expanded into dozens of markets, turning professional sports into a lucrative business for gambling operators, advertisers and media companies. And the state has much to gain from legalization—the biggest selling point being the possibility of generating additional tax revenue. What are the initiatives, exactly? The two initiatives are designed to work together, but they address different parts of the legalization process. Initiative 440 is a proposed constitutional amendment. It would amend the state’s constitution to authorize legislation allowing people to place sports wagers through internet-based platforms operated by authorized gaming operators connected to licensed racetrack casinos. “We know Nebraskans are already wagering on sports through illegal and offshore platforms or driving to a neighboring state where wagering is legal,” supporters of the measures wrote in the Nebraska secretary of state’s informational pamphlet . “This means millions of dollars in tax revenue leave our state every year. Initiative 440 keeps the money in Nebraska through a legal, regulated and secure marketplace that is projected to deliver more than $166 million in direct property tax relief to Nebraska homeowners, farmers, ranchers and small businesses over the next ten years.” Initiative 441 is the accompanying statutory initiative. It would establish the legal framework for online sports wagering and authorize the Nebraska Racing and Gaming Commission to regulate operators and adopt rules governing the industry. “This initiative requires that 70 percent of all wagering tax revenue goes directly to Nebraska’s Property Tax Credit Cash Fund,” the supporters wrote. A vote in favor of only one measure would not be enough to establish legal online sports betting. Both must pass for the proposed system to take effect. Nebraska already permits some forms of sports gambling, however. Voters approved casino gambling at licensed racetracks in 2020, and sports wagering became available at racetrack casinos in 2023. But residents have to visit a licensed facility to place their bets. According to the Nebraska Racing and Gaming Commission, sportsbooks generated approximately $9.28 million in gross gaming revenue in 2025, nearly double the $4.71 million recorded in 2024. And that existing market has already contributed to property tax relief—Nebraska taxes gross gaming revenue at 20%, with 70% of the resulting gaming-tax revenue directed to its Property Tax Credit Cash Fund. events.title: A New York Giants co-owner says the NFL can reach new fans in 2 key ways
events.summary: Carolyn Tisch Blodgett is bullish on flag football and international expansion for the NFL. Carl Timpone / BFA New York Giants co-owner Carolyn Tisch Blodgett sees room for the NFL to grow. International games are crucial, Tisch Blodgett said, since there "isn't enough room to continue to grow in the US only." The sports investor is also optimistic that flag football will bring in new fans. The NFL is America's favorite league, and a New York Giants co-owner says there are ways to keep it growing. Carolyn Tisch Blodgett , whose family owns a 45% stake in the Giants, said flag football and international games are the two biggest avenues for the NFL to build on its massive audience. "There just isn't enough room to continue to grow in the US only. You have to be thinking about international growth too," Tisch Blodgett said at Business Insider's The Long Play event. Tisch Blodgett, who runs sports-focused venture capital firm Next 3 and Gotham FC in the National Women's Soccer League, said that playing games abroad is crucial to the league's long-term success, as it helps build a younger, more diverse audience. "A sports fan today in 2026 looks different than a sports fan did maybe 100 years ago," Tisch Blodgett said. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has made international contests a key cornerstone of his tenure for the last two decades. The league has played games abroad every year since 2007 (except for 2020), going from one game a year in London to nine this season across the globe in places like Melbourne, Rio de Janeiro, Paris, Madrid, Munich, and Mexico City. Tisch Blodgett has seen championship-caliber teams with Gotham FC and the New York Giants. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images Flag football, which will be an Olympic sport in 2028, is another way for the NFL to connect with new fans abroad and in the US, Tisch Blodgett said. That includes girls who may not have the opportunity to play tackle football. Playing a sport is correlated with fandom, Tisch Blodgett said. She's bullish that kids who try flag football will develop a lifelong affinity for the NFL. "If we know we need people to be playing to be a fan, we're going to invest in flag so that we continue to grow that fandom," Tisch Blodgett said. Flag football participation among high school girls surged 49% last year to over 100,000 — making it one of the 10 most popular sports for that demographic, according to a recent survey by the National Federation of State High School Associations. The NFHS said that four years ago, fewer than 16,000 high school girls played flag football, making it the fastest-growing high school sport in the years since. Tackle-free football leagues are also open to boys whose parents may not want them to risk getting concussions, which have been an area of focus for the NFL in the last decade. The NFL is investing in flag football, and its efforts include launching Premier Flag — a new pro flag football league that will start next summer. "As tackle football has declined, they didn't just sit back," Tisch Blodgett said of the NFL. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Xbox Nano has a hidden cloud secret
events.summary: Microsoft is about to launch its new Xbox Nano controller tomorrow, and the tiny device has a little secret. events.title: Protect Poundland from predatory capitalism, MPs tell government
events.summary: Budget retailer and 12,000 jobs at risk after US owner fails to accept buyout offers MPs have called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping. The fate of the retail chain and its 12,000 staff remains uncertain after it filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court last Thursday. The board of Poundland has lined up the advisory company AlixPartners to run the process after the owner, US restructuring specialist Gordon Brothers, ceased providing funding. In an urgent question in the House of Commons on Tuesday, Gareth Snell, Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent Central , asked the government what could be done to “send a message to Gordon Brothers that the predatory capitalism that they are putting into this company will not be tolerated, because we in this country will always stand with people before profit”. Another Labour MP, Antonia Bance, asked what measures the government would use to “hold Gordon Brothers to account”, and if it would “establish an urgent review of whether our corporate governance and insolvency frameworks give sufficient protection against asset stripping and short term financial engineering, at the cost of jobs and our high streets?” The Green party MP Hannah Spencer said the “scandal” of Poundland “exposes a very serious problem, that our economy is vulnerable to private equity vultures who swoop in and prey on our high street brands by loading them with debt and then trying to ditch them for a profit”. Kate Dearden, the minister for the future of work, told parliament that government officials had held talks with Gordon Brothers on Monday night and she would meet Poundland’s management team along with Usdaw, the shop workers’ union, on Wednesday. She said Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, would meet Gordon Brothers again later this week as political pressure mounts on the company to accept a solvent bid for Poundland. Liam Byrne, the chair of business select committee, has also asked Gordon Brothers to answer its questions about Poundland on Wednesday next week. Dearden said the government could not involve itself in the “commercial negotiations” with potential buyers or comment on individual bids. However, she said the government was “taking a responsible approach not to sit by and do nothing” and was putting pressure on Gordon Brothers to accept it had “responsibilities as well as rights” over Poundland and its employees. Gordon Brothers is understood to remain in talks with at least two potential buyers for the whole company, including a fully funded offer from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group. Another offer from Innovest, an investment group understood to be advised by former Reform election candidate Charles Bunker, is believed to have partial funding in place. The chance of Poundland avoiding mass store closures and job losses is shrinking by the day because suppliers have held back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade . Gordon Brothers is believed to be unwilling to accept Martin Property’s offer of about £15m, only half of which would be paid immediately, because it falls short of repaying a £30m shareholder loan. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The prime minister’s spokesperson said: “We continue to stay close to what’s an extremely worrying situation for Poundland staff, their families and communities. “Gordon Brothers need to explain why they haven’t accepted any offer to keep the company going. That’s the case. It appears they’re not acting in the best interests of their loyal UK staff and stores.” In a letter to the government, reported by Sky News, Gordon Brothers executive Mark Newton-Jones defended its approach, saying it had “supported Poundland with £85m of additional financing” since acquiring it for £1 last year and the chain had returned to underlying profit. However, the letter added: “Like other high street retailers, the company faces multiple economic challenges, including rising inflation, increasing staffing costs and shrinkage from severe levels of shoplifting, which means it is still not cash-generative at a sustainable level despite the turnaround efforts.” Dozens of MPs from around the UK have called on the government to reassure their constituents that action would be taken to stop Poundland’s collapse. Bradley Thomas, the Conservative party business spokesperson, blamed the government for Poundland’s demise. He said: “The current economic landscape is hostile to British business.” Earlier on Tuesday, the founder of Poundland, Steve Smith, told the Guardian that staff at the chain could be out of work for years if it collapsed. Gordon Brothers was approached for comment.

events.title: Food suppliers in UK hit by cyber-attacks after freezers targeted in Europe
events.summary: Cybersecurity experts say national impact ‘minimal’ but incidents may represent the ‘foothills’ of a wider threat Food suppliers in the UK have been hit by cyber-attacks after hackers raised the temperatures of supermarket freezers across Europe . The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NSCS) said it was working with the affected companies but the national impact was minimal. Speaking at the launch of the NCSC’s annual review on Tuesday , its director of operations, Paul Chichester, said: “We’re aware of those incidents in the UK, and obviously we’re working with the affected organisations. We’ll keep monitoring that. At the moment, the impact is minimal.” Cybersecurity experts meanwhile reported that attacks on “dummy” fridge controls – deliberately placed online to lure would-be hackers – displayed characteristics similar to malicious operations linked to Russia. Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday – with some rising to as high as 50C (122F) – and several companies confirming they had been hacked. Similar incidents were reported in France last month . It has emerged that the cyber-attack on French supermarket fridges involved legacy technology connected to the internet with default passwords. No UK grocery chain has been directly affected so far. Chichester said the NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, was working with organisations to identify loopholes in their technology and close them before hackers exploited them. He said the NCSC was not able to comment on who might have carried out the attacks, but that they were not AI-enabled and had used vulnerabilities that had been “out there for a long period of time”. The NCSC’s chief executive, Richard Horne, said the fridge attacks represented the “foothills” of an enlarged cyberthreat that companies and the public faced as AI systems highlighted flaws in IT networks that owners were not aware of or had neglected to patch. “There are so many vulnerabilities out there that … you could say are waiting to be exploited,” he added. The agency’s chief technology officer, Ollie Whitehouse, said everyday domestic devices connected to the internet would be susceptible to hackers in certain situations. He said manufacturers needed to be encouraged to make their technology safer, and consumers needed to accept paying more for safer equipment. The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers said some of its more than 300 members had been affected after becoming “collateral” in the hack. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters The industry body said no meat had been lost in the refrigeration hacks but the incidents were a “reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets”. One meat supply company saw its cold units rise to up to 100C while another two reported their units had started to defrost. The association said the affected units were empty at the time. A fruit and vegetable wholesaler in London was also affected but prevented the attack from escalating by pulling the internet connection to its cold storage units out at the wall. Alex Pearce, managing director of Langridge Organic, said the hackers had changed the parameters on a number of units, setting them to defrost for more than four hours at 150C. However, Pearce and his staff intervened before any stock could be damaged. “It clearly must have been easy to get in [to the system] because the simple solution was to unplug ourselves from the internet,” he said. Pearce said Langridge uses the same fridge control system, developed by a US software company called Copeland, that was involved in the French supermarket incidents. The Grocer news website first reported the Langridge incident. Copeland said it is talking to affected customers and has recommended software fixes. Cybersecurity researchers said attacks on dummy Danfoss fridge controls – whose systems were also targeted by the hackers in mainland Europe – were similar to recent operations linked to Russia . Xavier Bellekens, the chief executive of the cyberdefence firm Lupovis, said it had recorded 256 attempted attacks from 91 different sources between 20 October and 30 October after setting up online “honeypot” traps that are indistinguishable to attackers from real Danfoss fridge controllers. The attackers attempting to take over the dummy controls remained anonymous, but most of the authentication attempts used the manufacturer’s publicly documented factory-default username and password credentials. They also used what Bellekens called “bulletproof” hosting, which means using internet service providers that are particularly tolerant of malicious activity, often ignore abuse complaints or make it difficult for authorities to disrupt their customers’ operations.

events.title: I tried Ina Garten's easy chicken chili. It's a delicious, hearty dinner that's perfect for chilly temperatures.
events.summary: I made Ina Garten's chicken chili, and it was easy, healthy, and so comforting. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I tried Ina Garten's chicken chili recipe. Garten came up with the recipe while running her Barefoot Contessa store in the Hamptons. She swapped beef for chicken, and it became even more popular than the original. Ina Garten served traditional chili to her customers for 20 years while running her Barefoot Contessa store in the Hamptons. One day, Garten decided to tweak the recipe and swap the beef for chicken. It became even more popular than the original dish. The Barefoot Contessa store is long gone, but Garten's chicken chili recipe still lives on — and it's perfect for fall . Ina Garten's chicken chili features plenty of spices. Ina Garten appears on Sunday TODAY with Willie Geist in October 2018. Mike Smith/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images To make Garten's chicken chili for six, you'll need: 4 split chicken breasts, bone-in, skin on 2 (28-ounce) cans of whole-peeled plum tomatoes in puree, undrained 4 cups of chopped yellow onions 2 red bell peppers, cored, seeded, and large-diced 2 yellow bell peppers, cored, seeded, and large-diced ¼ cup of minced fresh basil leaves ⅛ cup of good olive oil, plus extra for chicken ⅛ cup of minced garlic 2 teaspoons of kosher salt, plus more for chicken 1 teaspoon of chili powder 1 teaspoon of ground cumin ¼ teaspoon of dried red pepper flakes, or to taste ¼ teaspoon of cayenne pepper, or to taste Freshly ground black pepper Chopped green onions, for serving Corn chips, for serving Grated cheddar cheese, for serving Sour cream, for serving While these are Garten's recommended measurements, I should note that I doubled some of the seasoning and added 2 teaspoons of chili powder, 2 teaspoons of ground cumin, ½ teaspoon of dried red pepper flakes, and ½ teaspoon of cayenne pepper. I wanted the chicken chili to pack a punch, and doubling these spices turned up the flavor without making things too hot. I prepped my ingredients and preheated the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I chopped my onions and bell peppers and minced the garlic. I misread Garten's recipe and cut my bell peppers a bit smaller than she recommended, but their shape still held up well in the chili. I think larger pieces might actually be too chunky for this dish because there's so much chicken in the chili, so I recommend going with a smaller dice for the bell peppers instead. I cooked the onions in olive oil for 15 minutes, then added the garlic. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider "You want to cook the garlic for just a minute so it doesn't get really bitter," Garten explained in a "Barefoot Contessa" episode while demonstrating the recipe. I added the bell peppers and seasoning. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I threw in the chili powder, cumin, red pepper flakes, cayenne, and salt, and cooked everything for one minute. Then it was time to add the tomatoes. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider "I always make this with canned tomatoes; life's too short to peel a tomato," Garten said in the episode. According to the recipe, you can crush the tomatoes by hand or throw them in a food processor. If you opt for the latter, Garten recommends adding them in batches and pulsing the processor six to eight times. I don't have a food processor, so I crushed the tomatoes by hand. I also threw the leftover juice into the pot. After adding basil, I brought my chili to a boil and then reduced the heat to a simmer. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's recipe is designed so the chicken and chili are ready at the same time, so she recommends cooking the chili for 30 minutes. I had some extra time on my hands, so I allowed the chili to simmer for a little longer to give the flavors more time to develop. While my chili simmered, I roasted the chicken. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider During the "Barefoot Contessa" episode, Garten said she cooks the chicken with the skin on because she found it "really keeps it moist." She also noted that she roasts the chicken instead of boiling it because it makes the meat taste better. I rubbed my chicken breasts with olive oil and generously seasoned them with salt and pepper before throwing them into the oven for 35 minutes. Garten said the chicken breasts should be "just cooked" when you take them out of the oven. Once my chicken had slightly cooled, I separated the meat from the bone and started chopping. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider "Tear off the bone with your hands; it's the best way to do it," Garten said in the "Barefoot Contessa" episode. Garten then recommended cutting the chicken into ¾-inch chunks so the meat can be "really delicious and chunky." I added the chicken to the chili and continued simmering it uncovered. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's recipe calls for the chili to simmer with the chicken for 20 minutes. While the chili was simmering with the chicken, I prepped my toppings. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Since I bought pre-grated cheese, all I needed to do was chop my green onions. Garten's chicken chili made for a fantastic dinner. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's chicken chili is so hearty and comforting. The rich tomatoes paired really well with the tender, juicy chicken, which soaked up so much delicious flavor, and the bell peppers and green onions added great texture. I also enjoyed the extra hit of acidity and creaminess from the sour cream. I made this chili for my friend Kayla, who was also a huge fan. "This chili is reminiscent of a chicken tortilla soup, but it's so much heartier!" she added. "It makes you feel so warm and cozy." As temperatures continue to drop, Garten's comforting recipe will definitely satisfy your chili cravings. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Palantir sinks 2% after earnings as analysts point to slowdown in total contract value
events.summary: Palantir shares fell on Tuesday after the software company reported Q3 earnings. The software company saw a slowdown in U.S. commercial total contract value growth. Apple shares also sank as the company reckons with a global memory crunch and a scramble for computer components. Palantir shares fell on Tuesday after the software company reported third-quarter earnings and analysts pointed to signs of a slowdown in total contract value and other "forward indicators." U.S. commercial revenue topped government for the first time, but the company closed $1.5 billion in TCV in the segment, up 11% from last year. In Q2, Palantir closed a record $2.1 billion worth of TCV in the segment, which was up 153% from the prior year. Investors will "no doubt be looking for evidence in subsequent quarters that 11% growth in U.S. commercial TCV bookings is a fluke of duration and not something structural," a Piper Sandler note from Monday said. "We believe that is the case and demand for PLTR's solutions still very much outstrip supply." In a Tuesday note, Goldman Sachs analysts noted that the company attributed some of this to shorter contract durations. "The key will be converting shorter duration contracts into longer duration commitments, which Palantir has done successfully in the past," the analysts wrote. Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time, Palantir said in its earnings report. The iPhone maker reported better-than-expected revenue in its fourth-quarter earnings, but fell short of estimates on iPad sales and issued a margin forecast that disappointed investors. Apple 's statement marked the first earnings report since John Ternus took over as CEO from Tim Cook in September. The stock fell more than 2% on Tuesday. The company is reckoning with a global memory crunch and a scramble for computer components. Memory costs were higher this quarter than in the June period, the company said Monday. Despite the price surge, Ternus said Apple had just capped off its "best fiscal year ever." He told CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos that Apple's growth came despite supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds. "The concern is profitability," said Violeta Todorova, senior research analyst at Leverage Shares. "Management pointed to memory as the main pressure, together with the cost of rolling out Siri AI. Memory shortages are also expected to limit Mac and iPad supply, as demand has run ahead of plans." Apple shares have risen 25% in 2026, ahead of other big tech names, but that premium leaves "little room for disappointment," Todorova added. events.title: South Carolina shrimpers weigh costs, vote in crucial US midterms
events.summary: Shrimpers worry about fuel costs, tariffs and Trump’s proposed cuts to the agency that provides vital weather data. Mount Pleasant, South Carolina – For Mark Marhefka, the weather can be the difference between a profitable fishing trip and a dangerous one. As a shrimper and fisherman for 49 years, Marhefka relies on forecasts, weather buoys and data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to decide when it is safe to take his boats offshore. With storms and warm water temperatures disrupting this year’s fishing season, he worries that President Donald Trump’s proposed funding cuts could further reduce the services fishermen depend on. list 1 of 3 China to suspend imports of Japanese seafood amid diplomatic row: Reports list 2 of 3 Trump administration aims to cut regulations on US commercial fishing list 3 of 3 Lobster industry caught in Maine’s political headwinds before US midterms “They’ve already started cutting back on NOAA, and they’re looking to do more in this next fiscal year,” Marhefka, who owns Abundant Seafood, told Al Jazeera. “It’s definitely something that we need to fight against.” Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, NOAA has lost roughly 20 percent of its workforce, according to an analysis of federal employment data. The administration’s proposed 2027 budget would cut funding for ocean monitoring and terminate a programme supporting regional ocean observations. But the weather is only one of the pressures facing South Carolina shrimpers as they head to the polls on Tuesday for the US midterm elections. Rising fuel prices, equipment costs and competition from imported shrimp are weighing on people who make their living from the water. Marhefka believes Democrats could address these pressures better than Republicans. “Fuel costs have doubled since Trump has been back in office,” said Marhefka. “I voted Democrat because I really think Annie Andrews is going to help South Carolina.” At an election-eve rally in Charleston on Monday, the state’s Democratic Senate candidate, Annie Andrews, sought to appeal to voters like Marhefka, arguing that her campaign would address the financial pressures facing coastal communities. “I’m fighting for a South Carolina that we can afford,” Andrews said to the crowd. “I’m fighting to lower the damn diesel for our farmers and our fishermen and our shrimpers.” Although shrimpers make up a small share of South Carolina’s electorate, their concerns raise bigger questions about the cost of doing business and retirement planning. John Henry Middleton, an 81-year-old fisherman who has been shrimping for about 50 years, is an undecided voter. He says he is frustrated with both parties, arguing that politicians make promises but fail to work together on issues affecting common people. “I want to see them get together and work for the good of the people,” he told Al Jazeera. His concerns as he heads to the ballot box on Tuesday include the cost of living and whether he will have enough money to support himself in retirement. He said he has paid taxes and worked for decades, but still has to work at 81. Kevin S, who declined to give his last name, works at Geechee Seafood on Shem Creek and said he plans to vote Republican on Tuesday. He said many people in the fishing industry lean Republican because they see government regulation as an obstacle to making a living. “It’s a pretty regulated industry. A lot of red tape, a lot of extreme permits,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that some fishing permits can cost thousands of dollars. Kevin added that rising fuel prices have increased the cost of running his business, but he doesn’t closely follow the factors driving those increases. When asked whether the war in Iran was contributing to higher prices, he said he didn’t know enough about the issue to say. Instead, he pointed to Trump’s efforts to increase domestic energy production as a reason he thinks Republicans are better placed to address fuel costs. He also believes many blue-collar workers share this view, but emphasised that industry support for Republicans does not necessarily mean enthusiasm for the party. “I just don’t really trust Democrats as much to make the best financial decisions,” he said. “It’s not that a lot of people love the Republican Party. It’s more of a lesser of two evils.” The pressures facing shrimpers are also evident in the dwindling number of businesses around Shem Creek, a historic fishing area near Charleston. Cindy and Taylor Tarvin, co-owners of Tarvin Seafood, estimate that only about eight shrimpers remain in the area. They say the decline reflects how difficult it has become to make a living in the industry. “Younger captains can make a living, but not a lavish one,” Cindy Tarvin told Al Jazeera. The Tarvins said their diesel costs rose sharply this year. They started the year paying $2.71 per gallon (3.78 litres), but by late September they were paying $5.99 per gallon.

events.title: AI isn't on the ballot, but it's still being tested
events.summary: Stephen Maturen/Getty Images This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Americans are casting their votes in an election cycle that could reshape Washington's power structure. The GOP's control of both the House and Senate seems likely to break, according to most forecasts. Democrats are favored to win the House, with a shot at the Senate if they can net four seats while defending their own. BI's Brent D. Griffiths and Madison Hoff broke down everything you need to know — from the key topics to the closest races — for the 2026 midterm elections . Throughout the day and into the evening, we'll also have updates on the tightest races and the business world's reaction, so keep checking our homepage . Today's results could serve as a litmus test for AI on multiple fronts. Affordability remains a top concern for most voters . But one aspect of AI turned into a hot topic on the campaign trail. Data centers were a major talking point for politicians . The vast majority of Americans previously said they don't want them built where they live . Politicians responded with everything from outright moratoriums to calls for additional safeguards to address data centers' impact on water supply and electricity costs. Midterm results could offer more color on the public's appetite for AI infrastructure, shaping how tech companies try to appeal to voters going forward. OpenAI is already thinking about the next major election cycle. A memo from its top lobbyist, obtained by Politico, shows it pitching 2028 hopefuls on how to talk about AI . Others aren't waiting to make an impact. Elon Musk has donated nearly half a billion dollars, the largest amount for a non-candidate to spend in a single election cycle, according to the New York Times . A good chunk of that money is supporting Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's Senate campaign, a key race for the GOP. AI's unofficial home state could also face a shake-up thanks to one proposal on the ballot. California's proposed billionaire tax has already sent some AI-focused billionaires packing, with many relocating to Florida . Meta's Mark Zuckerberg considered leaving the state over the tax before the tech giant stepped in to ease his concerns (and his potential tax bill). The proposal is a one-time 5% tax on current billionaires, but its approval could prompt hopeful billionaires to reconsider staying in the state. events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Seoul National University -led researchers published “Resolving the Kay–Dunn limit and the speed–endurance dilemma in ferroelectric Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 for DRAM-class sub-volt capacitors.” The first author, Geun Hyeong Park, Ph.D., summarizes the work here: “Fast, frequently rewritten memory requires low operating voltages, rapid switching, and high cycling endurance. In ferroelectric capacitors, however, accelerating polarization switching often requires higher voltages that can shorten device lifetime. This work addresses this tradeoff through TiN electrode and interface engineering, reducing interfacial voltage loss and facilitating polarization reversal. Key experimental results include: 42.1 ns polarization switching at 0.6 V. 8.1 ns polarization switching at 1.0 V. Hundreds of billions of switching cycles at 0.6 V, using a 20% polarization-loss criterion. Cycling tests also reached 10^12 bipolar cycles without hard electrical breakdown. Beyond the capacitor measurements, the researchers propose a common-plate ferroelectric RAM (CP-FeRAM) architecture using one transistor and one capacitor per cell, and evaluate its readout through circuit simulations. The architecture explores polarization-based sensing after stored charge has decayed, offering a potential route to reducing refresh requirements in DRAM-like memory.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: The NYC Marathon costs more than $300 to enter. Here's what it's like to run it.
events.summary: The 2026 TCS New York City Marathon took place on November 1. David Schwartz Nearly 60,000 runners participated in the 2026 NYC Marathon, starting from Staten Island. Entry to the NYC Marathon is tough, with a 1% chance in the general drawing. Business Insider reporters who participated in 2026 take you inside the iconic race. On Sunday, November 1, nearly 60,000 runners took part in the 2026 NYC Marathon, starting in Staten Island and crossing the finish line 26.2 miles later in Central Park. It's not easy — or cheap — to get in. The odds of gaining entry through the general drawing are about 1%. New Yorkers can secure a spot through the "9+1" program, which requires completing nine NYRR races and volunteering at one. Charity bibs are another option, often requiring runners to raise thousands of dollars, and a select few can earn a spot with a qualifying time. If you're lucky enough to get your hands on a bib, registration will still cost upward of $300. In 2026, the fee was $333.11 . It is also a major feat of preparation and training in the months leading up to the event. My colleague Noah Sheidlower and I were among the runners who took on the five-borough race this year. Here's what it was like. The TCS New York City Marathon begins in Staten Island. Courtesy of Noah Sheidlower Transit to the start begins as early as 5 a.m. The race falls on the first Sunday of every November, coinciding with the end of daylight saving time. The extra hour of sleep makes a difference when your alarm is set to go off in the 3s or 4s. Noah and I take a bus from Midtown. The lines are long, but organized. Runners board the Midtown Manhattan bus before the sun comes up. Noah Sheidlower There's also a bus from MetLife Stadium, and many runners take the Staten Island Ferry. The ferry ride, while cold, offers an epic flyby of the Statue of Liberty. After arriving in Staten Island and going through security, we have a few hours to kill before the gun goes off. This year, temps are in the low 40s at the start. Runners bring blankets and wear layers they can shed at the start line. Runners bundle up to stay warm in the starting village. Volunteers may even lend you a pair of gloves if you ask. Kathleen Elkins There's coffee and bagels in the starting village — and bathroom lines that can last half an hour. The sun rises over the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, which runners cross during the first mile of the NYC Marathon. Noah Sheidlower There are five start waves, with Wave 1 beginning at 9:10 a.m. and Wave 5 at 11:30 a.m. Runners head to their assigned corrals about 30 minutes before their wave begins. Runners wait inside the starting corrals before walking to the start line. Noah Sheidlower As we approach the start line, the vibes are immaculate. Music plays as runners make final preparations, take photos, dance, and high-five one another. Just before the starting cannon fires, the soundtrack shifts to Frank Sinatra's "Theme From New York, New York." This is my seventh time running the race, and that exact moment — as soon as I hear, "Start spreading the news" — still sends goosebumps down my arms. The first mile takes you over the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, from Staten Island to Brooklyn. It's the steepest part of the course — and one of the most picturesque, with lower Manhattan in the distance. Runners cross the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, the steepest climb of the whole course. Noah Sheidlower After climbing for about a mile, we're rewarded with a downhill that spits us out in Brooklyn. We spend the next 11 miles running through New York's most populous borough. Lafayette Avenue, through Clinton Hill and Fort Greene, is particularly rambunctious, with block parties and live music. Passing through Williamsburg also feels like crashing a house party. From Brooklyn, we cross the Pulaski Bridge into Queens around the halfway mark. We then run through Long Island City before approaching the dreaded Queensboro Bridge. It's steep, silent, and soul-crushing — the only part of the course where spectators aren't allowed. But once we reach the apex and begin descending, we start to hear what's known as the "wall of sound": spectators waiting with open arms — and beer cans — at mile 16. Their energy is contagious, making it easy to forget that you still have a lot of running ahead. The author, absolutely leaning into the Mile 17 crowd. Summer Conner The crowd carries us up First Avenue and into the Bronx, where we're greeted with hip-hop music and some tricky hills. If your name hasn't yet fallen off your shirt — as happened to one of the authors — strangers cheer for you personally. That can help if you hit the infamous mile-20 wall, when your legs start to feel like lead. We reenter Manhattan around mile 21, and prepare to face the 5th Avenue hill starting around 23. It's brutal. As NYC Marathon veteran Casey Neistat described the course, it's "not the hardest, it's the meanest." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Travel + Leisure (@travelandleisure) The final three miles are the toughest, but the crowds are thick. They make sure you reach the finish line. Runners cross the NYC Marathon finish line in Central Park. Noah Sheidlower Crossing the finish line is emotional. Happy tears at the finish line are inevitable. Kathleen Elkins Almost as iconic as the finisher medal is the bright orange poncho volunteers wrap you up in. It keeps you warm — and guarantees enough "Congrats!" from strangers for the rest of the day that you can't help but wonder if this is what it feels like to be Jalen Brunson. Noah Sheidlower Despite the stiff legs and lost toenails, most runners — including yours truly — already can't wait for next year. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Photos from the 2026 NYC Marathon, from celebrity sightings to record-setting finishes
events.summary: More than 240,000 people applied for this year's drawing, and about 1% received a spot. Reuben Ingber/Business Insider The New York City Marathon, the world's largest marathon, took place on November 1. Over 60,000 runners finished the 26.2-mile-long race that weaves through all five boroughs. Several celebrities joined in on the race, including Casey Neistat, Jennifer Connelly, and more. New York City traded Halloween costumes and candy for running shoes and bibs as the five boroughs transformed into a racetrack for the city's annual marathon. The 26.2-mile race, which drew over 2 million spectators on November 1, is the world's biggest marathon. There are a handful of ways to get in, but probably the best-known is the lottery system. Runners apply in one of three pools: those who live within 60 miles of the city, US residents outside the metro area, and international applicants. The application opens in February, and the drawing takes place in early March. Of the 240,000 people who applied this year, only about 1% received a spot — yet it saw more finishers than ever before. Beyond the lottery, runners can get in by raising money for charity, meeting qualifying time standards, participating in New York Road Runners programs, or booking through an approved international travel operator. NYRR is the nonprofit that organizes the race. From Halloween costumes and celebrity sightings to record-setting runs and emotional finishes, here are some of the best photos from the 2026 New York City Marathon. The New York City Marathon celebrated 50 years of its five-borough course in 2026. Participants enter a hall to pick up their bibs at the marathon expo in New York City, United States, on October 30, 2026. (Photo by Michael Yanow/NurPhoto via Getty Images) Michael Yanow/NurPhoto via Getty Images While the first New York City Marathon began in 1970, the first marathon to weave through all five boroughs took place 50 years ago in 1976. Runners pay between $255 and $358 to race, depending on where they live and if they're an NYRR member. The race starts in Staten Island and ends in Central Park. NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 1: An aerial view as runners cross the Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge during the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon on November 1, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Paul Seibert/Back Left Media/New York Road Runners via Getty Images) Paul Seibert/Back Left Media/New York Road Runners via Getty Images Runners start at Fort Wadsworth on Staten Island, cross the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge into Brooklyn, then continue through Queens, Manhattan, and the Bronx before finishing in Central Park. With the earliest start time at 8 a.m., racers braved the cold morning air as they arrived. Reuben Ingber/Business Insider The professional wheelchair, women's professional, and men's professional divisions began between 8 and 9:05 a.m. The general public waves followed, starting at 9:10 a.m. and continuing through 11:30 a.m. The temperatures at the start were in the low 50s. By the afternoon, temperatures reached the mid-60s under sunny skies. Exactly 61,529 people started the race, and 61,146 finished — the most ever in any marathon. Runners pass through Central Park as they compete in the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon. Kena Betancur / AFP via Getty Images The 2026 New York City Marathon set a world record for the most finishers for the third straight year, and became the first marathon to see more than 60,000 people complete the race. The second-largest marathon is the Paris Marathon , which attracts between 50,000 and 60,000 runners each year. Runners from all walks and stages of life completed the race — the youngest participant was 18, and the oldest was 90. Runners celebrate after competing in the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon in New York City on November 1, 2026. The 26.2-mile race passes through all five boroughs, beginning in Staten Island and finishing in Central Park. (Photo by TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images) TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images The oldest finisher was Danil Farkash, 90, from the US, with a race time of 11:24:18. The youngest was Lucy Weld, 18, from the US, who turned 18 on race day. Her race time was 4:12:06. The runners represented 153 countries. Italy had the highest number of non-US finishers this year, followed by France. Celebrities, including Jennifer Connelly and Casey Neistat, ran among the participants. Reuben Ingber/Business Insider Neistat, a famous YouTuber, completed his 10th New York City Marathon—and his 30th marathon overall — on Sunday. He's called the city's marathon " the meanest " of all marathon courses because of its hills and hard surfaces. Spectators across all five boroughs showed their support with signs and cheers. Reuben Ingber/Business Insider Signs ranged from supportive slogans to funny messages. Taking place on the day after Halloween, several racers chose to run in costumes. Reuben Ingber/Business Insider Other costumes included runners dressed up as bananas, slices of pizza, and a Trojan War-era soldier. Tracy Morgan was the marathon's official Grand Marshal. Grand Marshals Tracy Morgan and Estee Stimler participate in the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon. Bryan Bedder/New York Road Runners via Getty Images As Grand Marshal, the " 30 Rock " star joined spectators in cheering runners at the finish. Sheila Chepkirui won the women's race, crossing the finish line at 2:24:36. Kenya's Sheila Chepkirui crosses the finish line to win the women's race at the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon in New York City on November 1, 2026. The 26.2-mile race passes through all five boroughs, beginning in Staten Island and finishing in Central Park. (Photo by TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images) TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images Her time translates to a pace of roughly 5:30 per mile. The women's professional field also included Julia Paternain, who holds Uruguay's women's marathon national record, among others. Andreas Almgren won the men's race, crossing the finish line at 2:06:01. Sweden's Andreas Almgren crosses the finish line to win the men's race at the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon in New York City on November 1, 2026. The 26.2-mile race passes through all five boroughs, beginning in Staten Island and finishing in Central Park. (Photo by TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images) TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images His time translates to a 4:48-per-mile pace. The men's professional field also included Edward Cheserek, who holds one of the world's fastest mile times, and Joe Klecker, a professional runner for On. Catherine Debrunner and Marcel Hug won the wheelchair division race, respectively.
