events.title: Anthropic is still grappling with the economics of compute
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. There’s a lot of mystery around the finances of major AI labs, and as Anthropic inches towards it IPO, we’re starting to get some answers. In particular, the company is finally disclosing more about the economics of compute, and how much of Anthropic’s skyrocketing revenue is being lost to compute costs. In a new filing on Monday , Anthropic released data that showed those margins on compute actually getting worse. The filing was an update to the S-1 released last week — but where that filing’s financial disclosures only covered through June 30 of this year, the new data extended to disclose results through an extra quarter, to September 30. Broadly, Anthropic had a good quarter: revenue reached $17 billion, up from $11.5 billion in the previous quarter, suggesting durable growth. But the operating loss grew at the same time, thanks in large part to growing compute costs. Looking at the compute margins makes the picture even worse. In the new quarter, compute took up 58% of the company’s revenue, up from 48% the quarter before. At a moment when the company could win over IPO investors by showing margins improving, they’re getting worse. A chart in the filing shows this even more clearly, tracking the company’s revenue for every dollar spent on compute. Since the start of 2025, it’s been steadily growing, peaking at just over 2x this past quarter, then falling back down to 1.72x. Many indications imply that this shift in compute margins is more of a blip than a long-term problem, but it still tells us important things about the business of running a major lab. Trying to keep up with demand, Anthropic’s compute bill shot up to $10 billion for the quarter, including, as the filing notes, “$5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments.” Basically, demand was growing so fast that Anthropic had to scramble for compute, which meant paying higher rates. Some of those deals have already played out in public. Anthropic has been paying SpaceX $1.25 billion a month for compute, alongside multibillion-dollar deals with Nscale , Akamai , and Volta . In the parlance of the industry, these are neoclouds rather than hyperscalers — smaller outfits that offer more flexible compute deals at higher rates. Anthropic’s margins got worse in Q3 because of deals like these, and there’s no sign they’ll be able to do without them anytime soon. As the new filing puts it, “We expect compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain our largest operating expense for the foreseeable future as additional committed compute becomes available to us under multi-year arrangements with CSPs, and as we continue to invest in additional compute.” Anthropic is still trying to lower its compute costs. In particular, the company talks quite a bit about its efforts to build its own compute base under a project it calls “Anthropic Direct.” But with demand growing so fast, those efforts aren’t going to be able to keep pace, and the neoclouds will continue to be the best option they have. In a sense, these are champagne problems. As long as revenue is growing at nearly 50% a quarter, few investors will worry about high compute costs — and the moment demand slows down, investors may be comforted by a compute picture that has gotten a lot sunnier. But it’s a reminder of how much AI labs still depend on the trillion-dollar infrastructure buildout — and how vulnerable they are to hiccups in that process. It’s easy to imagine the data center buildout slowing down over the next year if bond markets get skittish or local opposition gets more intense. There’s not much Anthropic can do to address either of those risks, and either one would make a messy compute picture a whole lot messier. In the meantime, the future of Anthropic and other labs will be at the mercy of compute prices. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

events.title: Disney plans several thousand layoffs, asks some managers to cut costs by up to 20%
events.summary: Disney expects to lay off several thousand employees, according to people familiar with the matter. This is the latest round of job cuts since Josh D'Amaro became CEO earlier this year. Disney is planning to cut several thousand jobs, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. Some managers at the entertainment giant have been asked to reduce costs by up to 20%, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. It marks the latest round of layoffs since CEO Josh D'Amaro took the reins earlier this year. The update comes after separate plans in April to cut as many as 1,000 employees , predominantly in the marketing department, and in September to cut about 300 employees , many in human resources and technology divisions. Bloomberg was first to report the latest round of layoffs. Company executives warned of the possibility of more reductions in its August earnings report. "We remain highly focused on reducing costs across the enterprise to create incremental capacity to invest for growth and are evaluating a variety of levers," D'Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston wrote in an Aug. 5 letter to shareholders . "We are mid-stream in this work and will provide future updates on our progress." Disney introduced plans in August for an early retirement program for some employees. "This is one of several actions we're taking to reshape our organization, including involuntary staff reductions that have already begun in some areas and will continue into next year," Chief People Officer Sonia Coleman wrote in a letter to employees on Aug. 24. Disney had about 231,000 employees as of the close of its fiscal year 2025, which ended in September of that year, according to the company's annual financial report. Disney is not the only entertainment company looking to reduce costs. Netflix said in a memo last month that it would lay off roughly 6% of its workforce . Skydance , the newly combined company of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, is also expected to cut staff in an effort to realize $6 billion in synergies over three years. Disney will report its fiscal fourth-quarter earnings on Nov. 17.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Shonky awards handed to ticketing giants, Virgin, Sony and a 25-hour washer-dryer Choice has handed out its 2026 Shonky Awards to the worst products and services of the year. ( ABC News: Eric Hao Zheng ) Consumer group Choice has handed out the 2026 Shonky Awards to the worst products and services of the year. Ticketek and Ticketmaster were named for "fleecing fans with tricky ticket tactics" while Virgin claimed its first Shonky for pocketing $75 million worth of expired flight credits. Protein chips, a pet insurer, Sony, and a washer-dryer that takes 25 hours also made this year's list. Two ticketing companies, an airline, and a washer-dryer that takes 25 hours are among the recipients of the one award no business wants. Consumer group Choice has released the winners of its 21st annual Shonky Awards, handed to the worst products and services of 2026. Ticketek and Ticketmaster have been awarded their second Shonky. ( Supplied: Choice ) Ticketek and Ticketmaster have won their second Shonky, this time for "fleecing fans with tricky ticket tactics", called out for using dynamic pricing and "in demand" tickets. Tickets sold by Ticketek this year for a John Farnham Tribute concert had prices up to $1,650. NRL fans purchasing through Ticketmaster were asked to pay $50 more for "in demand" seats just one row or bay apart from regular seats. A Ticketek spokesperson said variable pricing was used on less than 7 per cent of the John Farnham Tribute and this did not apply to the $1,650 tickets. "Where it is used, fans are notified about potential price changes before they enter the on-sale," they said. Ticketmaster has been called out for the use of "in-demand" tickets. ( AP: Phelan M Ebenhack ) Changes to Australian Consumer Law from July 2027 ban dynamic pricing under certain circumstances where it unreasonably manipulates customers or distorts their decision-making. Choice editorial director Mark Serrels said there was heightened awareness around ticket prices. "I think it was really exacerbated by these big events like the Oasis reunion," he said. A Ticketmaster spokesperson said it did not use surge pricing and "for in-demand tickets" and that "event organisers set the prices of sought-after seats closer to market value and may review these over the sales period." This year, Choice gave Qantas a break and awarded Virgin Australia its first Shonky, for pocketing $75 million worth of expired flight credits. The airline cancelled several flights between April 2020 and July 2022, at the height of the COVID pandemic, holding about $93 million in unused flight credits as of February this year. Virgin Australia has earned its first Shonky Award. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Customers were forced to book trips by June 30 this year, with a deadline to fly by May 27, 2027. Virgin notes in its 2025/26 annual report that $75 million worth of expired COVID-19 credits "impacted" its underlying net profit of $404 million. A Virgin Australia spokesperson said more than 93 per cent of COVID credits were redeemed. "We regularly communicated the expiry date and later extended the fly-by date to 27 May 2027, giving guests almost another year to travel," they said. Hisense earned its first Shonky for releasing an 8-star energy-rated "super energy efficient" washer-dryer. The catch? That rating is tied to the machine's eco settings that take 12 hours to wash and 13 hours to dry — 25 hours for a load of laundry. Mark Serrels says Hisense's 25-hour washer-dryer cycle could be a form of "greenwashing" — pun intended. ( Supplied: Choice ) Mr Serrels said the energy rating system was due for an overhaul, with almost all white goods manufacturers exploiting it. Also claiming a Shonky are Quest Nacho Cheese Protein Chips priced at more than $20 per 100g — 886 per cent more than a pack of Doritos without the protein label. Quest Protein Chips will help get you ripped (off). ( Supplied: Choice ) Mr Serrels said this was a difficult decision with an influx of added-protein goods hitting store shelves, noting some of these goods were ultra-processed with very little additional protein and a much higher ticket price. While the entire pet insurance industry has won a Shonky, with insurers not covering pre-existing conditions the main issue, this year Petcover has earned its own for taking things further. One of its policies requires customers to enter a new policy every 12 months, which classifies all conditions the pet has previously experienced as pre-existing, therefore excluding them from the cover.

events.title: Darfur survivors vow to tell story of those killed after Sudan camp attacks
events.summary: Survivors of attacks on displacement camps in Darfur recall the lives they built, and the violence that forced them to flee. In a small house in Omdurman, Hassan Saber Jumaa, a senior administrator at the Zamzam displacement camp in Sudan, sat on a simple wooden chair. He scrolled through his phone, looking for any photograph he might have of Zamzam, which is near el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, and once sheltered hundreds of thousands. He found nothing. Jumaa explained that his old phone was looted during last year’s attack by Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces on the camp. Pointing to the bare walls around him, Jumaa said that all he has left are his memories of the camp, and the people who once called it home. list 1 of 3 Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopia list 2 of 3 Sudan’s displaced return to new challenges in war-battered Khartoum list 3 of 3 Drone attacks extend campaign targeting Sudan’s power system Zamzam, established in 2004, was home to generations of people displaced by western Sudan’s Darfur war, which began in 2003 and continued for nearly two decades. Alongside Abu Shouk camp and al-Salam camp, Zamzam formed part of one of Darfur’s largest concentrations of displaced people. Jumaa recalled a bustling community, with its market open every day, and children walking to school. Zamzam continued as a refuge for civilians until Sudan’s current war, which began in 2023. The RSF, fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces and its allies, captured the camp in April 2025, after months of attacks. Famine had been confirmed in the camp in August 2024. Mukhtar Musa, a survivor of the assault, watched the community he knew descend into starvation and violence. He said restrictions on the movement of goods had exhausted food supplies, leaving some residents with little choice but to eat animal feed and peanut shells. Umm Kulthum Ali Saleh described the months before the final attack as the hardest of her life. The RSF siege on Zamzam stopped goods from entering. She searched for food every morning, and recalled seeing women cooking grass and mixing mud with flour to bake bread. Saleh believes the blockade was not merely a military measure, but a deliberate way to weaken the camp’s residents in advance of the final offensive, and Zamzam’s fall. On April 11, the RSF launched a three-day assault using cars, camels, and horses, burning straw homes and health facilities. A United Nations Human Rights Office report documented at least 1,013 civilians killed, including 319 who were summarily executed in homes, markets, schools, clinics, and mosques. The report documented other abuses, including rape, gang rape, sexual slavery, and other forms of sexual violence, particularly targeting the Zaghawa community. Musa was a witness to some of those mass killings, and said he saw RSF fighters kill civilians while chanting religious slogans. He described seeing bodies scattered around the main market and near schools, and said fighters continued pursuing civilians along roads leading out of the camp. Saleh also recalled seeing bodies littering the roads, with only chickens, donkeys, and sheep wandering among the abandoned buildings. The attack forced tens of thousands to flee Zamzam, with many remaining in the el-Fasher area, and others fleeing south to Tawila and Dar al-Salam. The violence continued to engulf el-Fasher and its surrounding displacement camps over the following months. With Zamzam under its control, the RSF launched an attack on el-Fasher in August 2025, and soon captured the Abu Shouk camp. The UN Human Rights Office said at least 40 displaced people were killed inside Abu Shouk, while 19 others were injured. The International Organization for Migration reported that at least 500 residents fled the camp that day. The RSF captured el-Fasher itself on October 26, 2025. More than 6,000 people are believed to have been killed in the attack, in el-Fasher as well as on escape routes out of the city. The UN found that RSF fighters targeted civilians, including members of non-Arab communities, and committed acts amounting to war crimes. The RSF has previously denied targeting civilians in Zamzam and el-Fasher, while acknowledging that some fighters committed abuses. The survivors of Zamzam, al-Shouk, and el-Fasher focus on bearing witness to the tragedy they faced. Jumaa said the destruction of Zamzam marked not the end of the violence, but the beginning of another wave of displacement. For him, the camp survives in the memories of those who once lived there – even as they are now displaced elsewhere. Musa, meanwhile, said he cannot forget the first days of the siege, and the bodies he saw on the streets. “Whoever survives must tell the story of what happened,” Musa said.

events.title: Chipotle's COO says he looks for this problem-solving skill in future leaders
events.summary: Chipotle's COO looks for problem-solving skills in the workers he promotes. Chipotle, Ana Altchek; Alyssa Powell/BI Today's tip to get better at work: Get better at showing you have leadership potential. Chipotle's chief operating officer, Jason Kidd, said he looks to promote workers who solve problems. Instead of coming to your boss with what went wrong, go into conversations with a solution. Get better at: Showing leadership potential Today's move If you want to get promoted, don't just bring your boss problems — come to them with possible solutions when something goes wrong. Jason Kidd , the chief operating officer at Chipotle, visits roughly a dozen restaurants every week and he uses team dinners in every location as a way to scout talent for promotions. He said he looks for four qualities in the people he promotes, including how they respond when things go wrong. Why it works At any company, including a fast-moving restaurant like Chipotle, problems are bound to arise. Kidd looks for leaders who can anticipate issues, take ownership, and find a solution. Those employees show they aren't waiting around for problems to land in their lap. They're actively taking initiative to improve the workplace. Try it today The next time an issue comes up at work, take a few minutes to brainstorm possible solutions. When you approach your manager, tell them what went wrong, a couple of possible solutions, and your recommendation for what to do next. That demonstrates leadership and initiative. The bottom line You aren't directly responsible for every problem that comes up at work. However, by showing your boss that you're actively working to avoid adding another task to their to-do list, you're helping make their job easier and showing them that you can handle more responsibility. Source This insight is based on Business Insider's reporting about how Chipotle's COO Jason Kidd promotes workers, and the qualities he looks for. events.title: Shopify falls 7% after Q3 revenue and merchandise volume miss estimates
events.summary: Shopify reported Q3 earnings before the bell on Tuesday. The e-commerce platform beat earnings expectations but posted revenue just below LSEG estimates. Gross merchandise volume and subscription gross profit missed estimates. Shopify reported before the bell Tuesday and posted adjusted earnings of 49 cents per share, topping LSEG estimates of 46 cents per share. Overall, quarterly revenue of $3.74 billion came in just below LSEG estimates of $3.75 billion. Shopify said it sees revenue growth in the "low thirties" range year over year for the fourth quarter, versus LSEG estimates of 32.1%. Gross merchandise volume, which came in at $119.15 billion, missed analyst estimates of $120.03 billion for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. Subscription gross profit also missed estimates by nearly $20 million, coming in at $661 million compared to StreetAccount estimates of $680.3 million. Merchant gross profit beat estimates. Shopify president Harley Finkelstein called the GMV results "consistent" and "durable" in comments to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Tuesday, and noted it was the thirteenth consecutive quarter of GMV growth above 20%. "We're really proud of the print, and we're going to keep building for the long term and ignore the noise day to day," Finkelstein said. Subscription revenue of $836 million also missed analyst estimates of $848.1 million, according to FactSet. Merchant revenue beat estimates. Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents OpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest round Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are covered Why AI is boosting Meta’s ad business while hurting Google search Meta released its consumer-facing artificial intelligence agent Muse during the third quarter, and Shopify was an early partner. The partnership allows Muse to browse and purchase items on Shopify's platform within the Muse app and allows customers to check out with Shopify's payment service, Shop Pay. Finkelstein addressed concerns about potential pricing pressure as AI agents negotiate prices and cost compare on behalf of users. "We're not seeing that prices are being lowered," he said. Instead, Finkelstein said AI agents are driving new traffic to Shopify's business and are helping consumers find new brands and products. "Brands like the Tin Can phone, a screenless phone for kids, are seeing incredible success because of agentic-based commerce, where a consumer is being very specific and using very merit-based results and using Shopify catalog. It is presenting these great products to consumers that there's no way they would have found otherwise." Finkelstein acknowledged some economic pressure on consumers heading into the holiday season, but said businesses are optimistic and agentic shopping could have a breakthrough moment. "I do think this is the first holiday season where AI-assisted shopping capabilities will become mainstream, especially with the rise of personal agents," he said.

events.title: We downsized from a one-bedroom NYC apartment to a 38-foot sailboat. Life changed, but not for the better.
events.summary: Although living on a sailboat sounded incredible and had its perks, it ultimately wasn't for me. Carly Miller In 2024, my partner and I left our NYC apartment and moved onto a sailboat with our dog. The lifestyle wasn't as affordable as I expected, and I felt like we were constantly making repairs. It was tough always having to be alert at sea. After about a year, I wanted a stable home on land. In 2024, my partner, Guy, and I had just landed back in our East Village apartment after a month in London when we asked each other, "Where to next?" I was still unpacking my luggage when an idea struck me: "We should live on a boat ." To most people, that sounds like a joke. For us, that was a perfectly reasonable idea. Guy was a lifelong sailor who had always dreamed of owning a boat , and to me, it sounded like an adventure I wanted to be part of. We both worked full-time remote jobs , and Guy had a fairly successful startup that made it possible for us to afford the boat. A month later, we moved onto a 38-foot sailboat with our dog. We imagined saving lots of money, seeing incredible sights, having complete freedom, and connecting with nature. Our ultimate goal was to cross the Pacific Ocean . However, it didn't take long for me to realize boat life was anything but the romanticized dream I had envisioned when I gave up my apartment. Instead of chasing adventure, I spent my time and money on maintenance and repairs Owning a boat can get expensive. Carly Miller Since we were downsizing from an apartment in one of the most expensive cities in the US , we thought we'd easily be saving money by living on a boat. Although we no longer paying NYC rent, we still had tons of expenses. The guy who sold us the boat had joked that the letters in "boat" stand for "Bust Out Another Thousand." Turns out he wasn't really kidding. Almost overnight, every day became overwhelmed by a list of things that needed fixing. We spent more time than we wanted making repairs on the boat. Carly Miller There was the $1,000 alternator, followed by a plumbing failure that left our toilet out of service. We spent two months trying to fix the problem ourselves before bringing in a professional. When our autopilot broke, we couldn't afford the roughly $3,000 replacement. One of us had to stay at the wheel when we sailed, which made balancing work and travel especially difficult. Those repairs came on top of expenses like fuel and marina slips, which could run more than $100 a night. Every day seemed to bring another expense or something to add to the to-do list. I didn't mind having fewer possessions or living in a smaller space . What wore me down was the endless work and expense of keeping that space functioning. I underestimated the stress of living on the water Living on a boat wasn't as peaceful as I expected. Carly Miller I expected living so attuned to nature would bring me peace. Instead, I found it difficult to relax. Clocking out of my full-time job didn't mean I could switch off. I was always "on" at sea. We had to monitor forecasts, wind direction, and currents to decide when we could sail and where we could safely anchor. We took turns waking up every hour to check that our anchor was holding and we weren't drifting. There are a lot of factors to monitor when you're sailing. Carly Miller Life at anchor was also surprisingly inactive. Sometimes bad weather kept us confined to our 38-foot boat for days. The sailing community could feel frustratingly isolating, too. At marinas, people often seemed to defer to Guy for decisions, and he seemed to more easily garner respect, too. Part of me felt like it was because he was a man. I was learning to be a boater, but I didn't always feel accepted or treated as an equal. At times, it was hard to be far from loved ones. Carly Miller The isolation also meant being far from family. When my family's dog died, I was stuck in a mangrove forest in the Bahamas and couldn't get home in time to say goodbye. Although we had the freedom to reach remote places, there was a constant catch: I also worried about how easily we could leave them in case of an emergency. I still love sailing, but I don't love owning a boat Sailing can be rewarding and fun, but owning a boat can be challenging. Carly Miller Despite the drawbacks, there were mornings that reminded me why I'd wanted this: We'd wake up before sunrise, coffees in hand, watching dolphins play at the bow. I love the magic of sailing. There's no roaring motor, just the wind in the sails and the creak of the ropes. When the boat heels over and everything lines up, we hit that perfect speed and glide over the water. It's euphoric. Nothing else comes close to that feeling. But I do not love being a boat owner . We made a lot of fun memories, but I'm glad we no longer live on a boat. Carly Miller After about a year aboard, we left the boat in the Bahamas and flew to Portugal to see family, then to Hawaii to see friends. We'd planned to head to Panama and the Pacific afterward, but I was burned out. For the first time in my life, I wanted routine and stability. So, we decided to just sail the boat back to New York City . Part of me still regrets not crossing the Pacific Ocean. If I get the opportunity, I'd like to make that crossing as part of someone else's crew. For now, though, I'm perfectly happy to have a home on land again. events.title: Israel political deadlock leaves Netanyahu’s future hanging in the balance
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections With neither bloc near a majority, Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties hold the key to Israel’s next government. Israel’s election results are due to be certified on Wednesday, but with both leading blocs falling short of a parliamentary majority, negotiations remain deadlocked. As things stand, the right-wing coalition of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured 53 seats in the October 27 vote, while the self-styled Zionist opposition alliance led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot had 48. A majority requires 61 seats in the 120-strong Knesset. The 19 remaining seats went to the two Arab-led lists – the Joint List and Ra’am, or the United Arab List. list 1 of 4 Israel election: When will government be formed, who will lead it? list 2 of 4 Israeli officials say results stand as Netanyahu claims election ‘stolen’ list 3 of 4 The future of the Palestinian vote in Israel list 4 of 4 Arab parties back Eisenkot: What’s the latest in Israel’s coalition talks? Netanyahu’s camp has been accused of seeking to delegitimise the results after launching a series of largely discounted claims that the vote for the Arab parties, which scored their best-ever electoral performance, had been manipulated by foreign interference. Despite their historic showing that was boosted by an unprecedented surge in voter turnout, the two Arab-led lists remain politically isolated. And while there have been indications that they would be prepared to support, or at least not oppose, an Eisenkot-led government, their backing remains contentious within the opposition – a broad and increasingly fractious alliance that also includes parties led by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, left-winger Yair Golan and right-winger Avigdor Lieberman. After a meeting on Tuesday, the main opposition leaders issued a statement announcing that they were preparing to “act immediately” to replace Netanyahu’s governing coalition “with a national emergency government and translate the clear parliamentary majority in the Knesset into action”. Yet, the statement did not specify how they would reach the majority that would ultimately depend on them allying with either the Arab-led lists or two ultra-Orthodox parties, which have historically supported Netanyahu in return for shielding some of their members from military service. “Essentially, we’re both on track to a government, and nowhere near being able to form one,” Israeli pollster Mitchell Barak told Al Jazeera. Though informal negotiations are widely reported to have begun, official talks on establishing a governing coalition will start only after the results are certified on Wednesday. Netanyahu’s Likud party has already mooted refusing to recognise the results, citing its continuing claims of irregularities in the Arab vote. Those allegations have been investigated and discounted by police, while a separate probe by the internal security service, the Shin Bet, remains ongoing. Once the results are certified, President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with all the parties to determine which member of the Knesset, not necessarily a party leader, is best placed to form a government. Herzog, who lost to Netanyahu after an especially bitter contest in 2015, has found himself in the unusual position of having to decide who should be given the first opportunity to form a government, while simultaneously considering the prime minister’s longstanding request for a pardon in his ongoing corruption trial . One of Herzog’s options is to ask the Arab parties to recommend Eisenkot. If selected, the leader of the centrist Yashar party will initially have 28 days to assemble a coalition, a period that can be extended by 14 days. Should he fail, Herzog can then invite another candidate to try. For his part, Netanyahu on Monday argued that Likud’s first-place finish, with 27 seats, gave him a mandate to lead the next government. “We aim to form a broad government with our partners and with any other party that wishes to join, provided they do not support terrorism,” he said. Still, it is unlikely he will be able to command a majority without entering an alliance with the Arab parties that he has consistently vilified, or a large-scale wave of defections from the opposition. Whatever the state of the negotiations, the new Knesset is due to be sworn in on November 10. Barak said coordination within the opposition appeared minimal, while personal animosities between Netanyahu and Herzog further complicated already fraught negotiations. “It’s really not clear who’s talking to who,” he added. “Earlier this week, they named [Bennett’s running mate] Lapid as their choice of speaker, which was apparently news to both Eisenkot and Bennett. Equally, Netanyahu now has to appeal to his political rival, Herzog, both to be given the responsibility of forming a government and to be pardoned before any conviction,” Barak continued.

events.title: Rivian spinout Also was working on an e-moto project in Kenya — until it walked away
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Also, the micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly started and then walked away from an electric two-wheeler pilot project in Kenya earlier this year, as it sought to focus its resources on its consumer e-bike and autonomous vehicle ambitions, TechCrunch has learned. The project received grant funding from the Shell Foundation, an independent charity established by the British oil and gas giant Shell plc. A section of the Shell Foundation’s website that has since been removed said the project’s goal was to “enable and de-risk global OEM entry into Africa’s EV market by piloting a locally integrated electric two-wheeler platform in Kenya, with potential to scale across East Africa.” According to the deleted section, Also was expected to work on modular battery designs and distributed EV charging, and planned on “developing a purpose-built electric motorcycle for African riders.” The opportunity for electric motorcycles seems ripe on the continent, which has a massive two-wheeler market. African mobility company Spiro recently said it has more than 130,000 electric motorcycles operating across seven countries, along with 2,500 battery-swapping stations. This boom has drawn interest from Chinese mobility companies and investors, which are pouring resources into the space . In a September email, Also told TechCrunch that it had “explored this project” with an unnamed partner, but ultimately “decided to focus on its core roadmap” after completing only “some early-stage work.” Also said the grant funding it received from the Shell Foundation “will follow the project to support its ongoing development,” but declined to offer specifics. The Shell Foundation told TechCrunch in an email that the project was “intended to generate evidence on driver income uplift potential, operational performance and commercial viability to deepen the company’s understanding of the market opportunity.” But when TechCrunch asked for more specifics, the Shell Foundation declined, citing a nondisclosure agreement with Also. Days later, the project disappeared from the Shell Foundation’s website. During an interview last month at TechCrunch Disrupt, Also co-founder and president Chris Yu said the Kenya pilot project initially made sense given Also’s mission to build small, purpose-built vehicles that are “first and foremost cost-optimized to do the job that needs to be done in a particular market.” But other projects took precedence, Yu said, especially the development of small autonomous vehicles — which Also is working on as part of a partnership with DoorDash . “We piloted and ultimately decided, largely because of just urgency and pace around autonomy, frankly, that our attention would be best, in the near term, served fully focused” on that, he said, adding that he thinks there’s a “high chance that autonomy will show up first, and at a broader scale in these types of purpose-built smaller vehicles than at scale in passenger vehicles.” Also walked away from the Africa project during a somewhat rocky first year of independence. Supply chain problems forced the company to repeatedly delay deliveries of its first product, a premium e-bike called the TM-B, frustrating customers who had reserved one. What made matters worse was Also’s relative silence. The company said little for much of 2026 about when the bikes would arrive — a communication failure its leadership now acknowledges was a mistake. “I think we did a pretty poor job communicating to our reservation holders through the summer when they were all waiting, and we got called out for that,” Yu said in the interview. “But I think it’s actually great. It’s really hard to earn the opportunity for people to care, and to tell us what they think, and to help us improve.” Getting its first product launch back on track is crucial for Also, which has ambitions far beyond e-bikes. The company plans to sell commercial cargo bikes to companies like Amazon , including four-wheeled models, and has the partnership with DoorDash. These products are next in the company’s pipeline, Yu said, and represent bigger revenue opportunities. But the TM-B comes first. It’s Also’s most visible product to consumers, and its striking design has drawn plenty of curiosity. Yu said no single problem was responsible for delaying the bikes, which finally started shipping to customers in early October. Instead, Also spent much of the year playing supply chain Whac-A-Mole, a particularly difficult challenge given the TM-B’s complexity. Yu described the bike as “kind of a computer on wheels.” At one point, Also found itself competing for the same raw materials used to make printed circuit boards for AI data centers. At other times, the company struggled to navigate certification requirements with different government agencies.

events.title: Keeping mortgage interest relief approved
events.summary: The States agreed to phase the tax relief out in 2015, but it was frozen between 2024 - 2026 A move to keep tax relief on interest paid on mortgage payments has been approved. Deputy Aidan Matthews, who brought the amendment to the Budget in Guernsey, said it was currently the "worst possible time" to consider phasing out the tax relief. It also meant that the phased withdrawal of the relief, which was agreed in 2015, would also stop, it was confirmed. The relief allows homeowners to apply for tax relief on any interest paid on the mortgage of their principle residence of up to £3,500 a year. Speaking against the move, Deputy Neil Inder said that, while the idea was right in isolation, if all amendments were approved, it would add "£20m to the budget". Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Alderney representative Alex Snowdon said the timing of the amendment was "important". He said: "There is a lot of Guernsey and Alderney people will be working two to three jobs that are really struggling to try and support the mortgage and their families. "I think this sends a strong message that we are trying to do a little bit to try and help people who are going through a very difficult time. "Some might say [these are] normal interest rates, but we've had money so cheap for so long that we are getting back to more difficult interest rates because house prices are going up so much people are borrowing so much more money." Deputy Jayne Ozanne said in the debate that she was "very split" on the amendment because it was an "unfair advantage" to homeowners over renters. "This will not solve the crisis of people leaving the island," she said. "They can not afford to save for a deposit for a mortgage because they are paying such high rents," she said. "Their monthly outgoings does not allow them to create the capital egg that they need to put a deposit down. This will not help that; it may help them once they've got a mortgage to decide to stay. "I'm wrestling because I feel there is an inequality here... the average rent in the island is over £2,000 per month while the average mortgage, I believe, is £1,000. "But two wrongs don't make a right. I recognise that families are feeling squeezed." Follow BBC Guernsey on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . events.title: Primark brings forward home deliveries plan by two years as profits slide
events.summary: Retailer acquires robot-assisted warehouse and intends to have UK service up and running before end of 2027 Primark is to begin making home deliveries by the end of next year as it aims to win new shoppers after a slide in profits. George Weston, the boss of the cut-price fashion chain’s owner Associated British Foods (ABF), said it had brought forward the launch of Primark’s home delivery plans by about two years. The company was able to speed up the process by snapping up a robot-assisted warehouse in Sheffield from Debenhams, the owner of Boohoo, PrettyLittle Thing and Karen Millen. Primark will take over the warehouse by the middle of next year and is working on preparing its suppliers to provide stock suitable for sending out to individual shoppers as well as the usual bulk orders for stores. Primark already offers a click and collect service in the UK which it has gradually rolled out since 2022 . The service is not available to its stores in mainland Europe. The chain, which has 511 stores across 21 countries, will launch home deliveries in the UK by December next year. It intends to offer the service in mainland Europe after that, but has not set out a timeframe. Primark has previously said it could not make money by selling fashion for home delivery, but Weston said the economics had changed with delivery and returns charges that could cover most of the logistical costs now common across the industry. He added that the group’s research had shown it could attract new customers, rather than just substituting a sale in store for a less profitable one online. “We now know there’s a group of shoppers who don’t reject Primark but just don’t use us very often as they are too far away from a store or prefer to shop online,” he said. The move comes as Primark faces tough competition from the rise of cut-price online specialists such as Shein as well as the supermarkets’ clothing ranges and the likes of H&M and Zara, all of which sell online and in stores. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Weston insisted that Shein was not grabbing more than a “little bit” of market share from Primark, and that there was more competition from those who could mix online and stores. Sales at Primark rose 4% to £9.8bn in the year to 12 September led by new store openings. Sales at established UK stores rose just 0.5% and sales at established stores in mainland Europe slumped 4.7% and in the US were down 2.6% as shoppers reined in spending on clothing amid higher energy and fuel bills. Primark said performance in the UK had been helped by improved ranges, action to cut prices and more marketing, tactics that are now being rolled out across Europe. However, that action saw profits drop 10% to £1bn. ABF intends to spin off Primark in December 2027, separating it from its sugar and food business that includes brands such as Twinings teas, Blue Dragon flavourings and Jordans cereals.

Google announced on Tuesday that it plans to disable AI tools for K-12 students next year unless school administrators explicitly turn them on. The tech giant says the change follows consultations with schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers. As a result, Google is revising its approach across Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. The decision means that schools choosing to restrict AI altogether will no longer be able to access Google Search, as AI features are now integrated into the search engine. Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” which means that if a school chooses to restrict AI altogether, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.” The change raises an issue for schools. Although teachers may not want students to use AI Overviews in Google Search to conduct research or complete assignments, they likely still want them to be able to have access to the search engine to find sources and other learning materials. However, Google Search and its AI features are now inseparable. Given the dominance of Google’s suite of apps in classrooms and the widespread use of Chromebooks, the decision underscores the company’s influence over the education sector. Schools that want to continue to have access to Google Search will have to accept its AI features. “We’ll share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition,” Phillips wrote in a blog post . “Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit.” Google announced the upcoming change alongside the launch of Guided Learning in schools. The tool, which was unveiled earlier this year, sort of functions like an AI tutor, as it’s designed to help users build a deep understanding instead of just getting answers. The launch comes amid concerns that AI chatbots undermine the learning process because they spit out direct answers. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: How political candidates charter jets to travel across battleground states during election cycles
events.summary: Philippe Reines, Hillary Clinton's 2016 presidential campaign advisor, speaks to members of the traveling press aboard the campaign plane. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Campaign travel is a niche corner of aviation that moves political candidates across the country. DC-based firm Advanced Aviation Team served Susan Collins' and Hakeem Jeffries' campaigns in 2026. Each trip involves carefully coordinating aircraft, crews, press, and — sometimes — armed security. It's been a busy year for campaign travel as state and federal lawmakers — and their challengers — crisscross the country for rallies and fundraisers for the 2026 midterm elections. But moving candidates and their staff, donors, press, and, in some cases, armed security, from one stop to the next isn't as simple as booking a commercial flight. Political travel has become a niche of its own within aviation. One pro in that realm is Gregg Brunson-Pitts, the founder and CEO of Advanced Aviation Team. Founded in 2015, the Washington, DC-based firm arranges VIP travel for ultrawealthy families, celebrities, and corporate C-suites, with a particular specialty in campaign travel. Gregg Brunson-Pitts founded Advanced Aviation Team after working for former President George W. Bush. Courtesy of Gregg Brunson-Pitts Brunson-Pitts' company manages every step of political travel — from scheduling flights and sourcing crews to branding planes, coordinating security, and adapting to rapidly changing itineraries. Advanced Aviation handles hundreds of thousands of dollars in contracts over a single election cycle and describes itself as nonpartisan. This year, Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings show it received roughly $58,000 from Sen. Susan Collins' leadership PAC and $66,000 from Rep. Hakeem Jeffries' campaign committee for 2026 travel, among others. All 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats (including two special elections), 36 governorships, three territorial governorships, numerous state offices, and thousands of state legislative seats nationwide will be on Tuesday's ballot. "We are hyper-focused on client satisfaction, which means seeing around corners, being problem solvers, and being solutions-oriented," Brunson-Pitts told Business Insider in early 2026. "We're seeing organizations plan earlier and lock in travel support sooner, because once the calendar tightens, capacity disappears quickly." A firm run by former White House travel directors Brunson-Pitts previously ran the White House Travel Office for eight years under former President George W. Bush. He said a charter jet carrying the White House press corps, Secret Service personnel, and other staff would almost always fly in tandem with Air Force One . President George W. Bush and first lady Laura Bush board Air Force One in June 2004 PETER MUHLY/AFP via Getty Images That experience — blending chartered aircraft, armed security, and government protocols — helped him build a specialty focused on the logistical demands of modern campaigns: "Our approach allows us to support clients affiliated with any party," he said. Unlike charter operators or fractional owners such as NetJets or Flexjet , which operate and maintain their own planes, Advanced Aviation Team functions as a broker with access to contracted aircraft. "We can source smaller private jets, but we can also do group travel for 100 or more people and customize an airliner," he said. "Not a lot of brokers can do that; that's what sets us apart." Brunson-Pitts said he built a team drawing from inside and outside the aviation industry, bringing together experience in politics, campaign travel, logistics, and private aviation chartering , brokerage, and sales. For example, Peter Newell, the former director of the White House travel office under President Barack Obama, joined as company president in March. Meanwhile, before joining Advanced Aviation, company vice president Jonathan Tasler organized the McDonnell Douglas MD-83 chartered by Mitt Romney's 2012 presidential campaign. The MD-83 campaign plane that Republican candidate Mitt Romney chartered in 2012. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images This logistical expertise is imperative to a successful campaign, as winning can come down to how fast, cheaply, and visibly candidates can move across battleground states. "The campaign plane is an important tool to help candidates safely meet with voters and get out their message. Down the homestretch, it becomes a working office and a home away from home," Brunson-Pitts told Business Insider ahead of the midterms. "Our team works behind the scenes coordinating crews, airports, ground transportation, security and last-minute changes so the candidate can keep moving ." Campaigns can rent smaller jets and full-sized airliners Brunson-Pitts' client list spans two decades of election cycles and includes officials from both parties. Beyond Sen. Collins and Rep. In 2024, the firm worked with Doug Emhoff, the husband of former Vice President Kamala Harris, and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, Harris' 2024 running mate. He has also handled contracts for politicians such as former President Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton, John Kerry, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, and "many more." events.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy hopes Abu Dhabi talks will open path to Putin meeting
events.summary: Ukrainian president meets Germany’s Merz in Berlin as chancellor says Russia is yet to engage seriously in peace efforts. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he hopes upcoming United States-mediated talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi will lead to a three-way meeting of leaders that includes Russian President Vladimir Putin. Speaking in Berlin on Tuesday alongside German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Zelenskyy said the adviser-level talks, set for November 10 and 11 , were part of a broader diplomatic push to end the war. list 1 of 3 Russia detains minor over alleged Moscow attack plot after US warning list 2 of 3 Kherson braces for return of war as localised Russia-Ukraine truce ends list 3 of 3 Russian attack on Ukraine aid hub kills 31 as US announces new peace talks “We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders,” Zelenskyy told reporters. Asked about the Abu Dhabi talks, Merz said it was “important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement”. “I do not see that happening so far,” the chancellor said. Zelenskyy’s visit to Berlin was not announced in advance for security reasons. On landing, he said on X that diplomatic coordination, strengthening air defences and supporting Ukraine’s energy sector would top the agenda. US special envoy Steve Witkoff announced the new round of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US on Monday. He said the discussions would focus on “post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace”. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that a Russian delegation would attend, led as before by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, the state news agency TASS reported. The build-up to next week’s talks follows one of the most notable displays of cooperation between the warring sides since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Last week, human rights ombudsmen from Russia and Ukraine oversaw a local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to evacuate residents and deliver aid, in a mission brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Putin and Zelenskyy have had no direct contact since the invasion, and their representatives have held only a handful of rounds of talks. Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane, reporting from Berlin, said there was a clear sense from Zelenskyy and Merz that the Abu Dhabi meeting “is a step forward, and there was an element of positivity about it”. He said one journalist raised an important issue, saying “Europe and Ukraine are supposedly in lockstep with each other”, before asking, “why then are the Europeans not going to be in Abu Dhabi in those talks?” “There was not much of a reply there, but it’s clearly an issue, a thorny issue, perhaps, certainly for the Europeans,” Kane said. European governments have insisted on being involved in the negotiations but are unlikely to be at the table in Abu Dhabi. Instead, US envoys are due to meet representatives from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, NATO and the European Union in Brussels this week to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine and Europe’s post-war security architecture. Zelenskyy has said Ukraine needs an additional 70 billion euros ($77.5bn) from European countries next year. Kane said successive German governments had pledged their full support to Ukraine, financing its efforts to fend off Russian attacks and supplying weapons and ammunition. But he said Merz knows that “the financial aspect of helping Ukraine has become a real issue, given that the economy here and in other European countries is particularly threatened right now”. “The cost of living in this country for many voters has become a serious issue,” Kane said. He added that parties opposed to funding Ukraine, including the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing Die Linke, were “prospering in the polls and in elections”. Several summits are planned before year-end US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin may hold three-way talks on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 18 and 19 . Around the same time, the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of about 35 countries backing Ukraine, is due to meet in Berlin. The Group of 20 (G20) summit follows in Florida from December 13 to 15 , where it remains unclear whether Putin will attend for the first time since the invasion.

events.title: Montana voters take on Citizens United with a ballot initiative to strip corporations and nonprofits of their political spending power
events.summary: Sixteen years ago, the Supreme Court decided in the Citizens United case that corporations have a First Amendment right to spend money to influence elections. On Tuesday, Montana voters will decide whether their state can take that power away.  Initiative 194, also known as the Montana Plan , would strip corporations, trade associations, nonprofits, and other organizations of the legal power to spend money supporting or opposing a political candidate or ballot initiative in Montana. Backers say they’ve found a way around Citizens United , while critics argue the semantics of the ballot initiative still violate the 2010 Supreme Court ruling.  Rather than ban corporate political donations outright, I-194 would change the powers Montana grants to corporations and other entities it refers to as “artificial persons,” limiting them to only those powers that are “necessary and convenient.”  The measure would apply to entities that do business or hold property in Montana, but exempts political action committees (PACs), news and editorial content, and individuals. Organizations that violate this would forfeit the privileges Montana grants them to do business in the state, including limited liability, which protects owners from personal responsibility for business debts. A way around Citizens United At first glance, the language of the ballot initiative looks like it contradicts what Citizens United established—that corporations can spend money on elections. But Tom Moore, a former chief of staff to FEC Commissioner Ellen Weintraub and now senior fellow at the Center for American Progress (who also devised the legal theory behind the Montana Plan), told Fortune that states have authority over what corporations can do through corporate law. “When the state creates a corporation, it is starting from nothing and deciding what to give the corporation, and no case has ever held that they have to give local spending power to a corporation,” Moore said. He said I-194 would no longer grant corporations and nonprofits the ability to spend money on elections, which is different from banning them from exercising an existing right. “It’s not regulation; it’s redefinition,” Moore said.  He said he believes the measure would shut down dark money spending by preventing wealthy donors from hiding behind organizations that don’t disclose their contributors. For instance, a donor can give money to a nonprofit that then funnels it to a PAC, which would report the nonprofit as the donor rather than identifying the person. Moore said I-194 would cut off that route by preventing corporations, nonprofits, and trade associations from political giving, though individuals can still donate. “This is not going to stop Elon Musk from writing a big fat check to some election in Montana,” Moore said. “What it will stop them from doing is laundering the money through a dark money group.” But opponents of the ballot measure say the distinction between banning corporations from political giving and exercising their political rights is blurry. Bradley Smith, a former FEC chairman and professor at Capital University Law School, told Fortune states can’t sidestep the First Amendment by calling political spending a corporate power instead of a right. “The Supreme Court isn’t engaged in a semantic game,” he said.  Smith said states can set rules for corporations, but they can’t make them surrender constitutional protections in exchange for the benefits of incorporation.  “The core centerpiece undoubtedly is we’re going to deny all corporations in the state the right to speak about political affairs and about political candidates, and that’s just going to fail,” he said. Montana’s century-old fight against corporate interests Montana has tried curbing corporate influence in elections before. In 1912, Montanans passed the Corrupt Practices Act by initiative with 76% of the vote , angry at the political power of mining giant Amalgamated Copper, years after the state’s mining magnates, known as the Copper Kings , had bribed state legislators. The law barred corporations from spending money to influence elections, but the Supreme Court struck down the restriction in American Tradition Partnership v. Bullock in 2012 , ruling that it conflicted with Citizens United.  Montana also isn’t the only state trying to limit corporate influence over elections. Hawaii enacted a law similar to I-194, called Act 11 , in May. It’s now facing two federal lawsuits: one from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and another from the Grassroot Institute of Hawaii , which the Institute for Free Speech, an organization Smith founded, represents. The cases could help decide whether states can use corporate law to restrict political spending despite Citizens United .  Moore expects the issue to go up to the Supreme Court, whether through I-194 or the Hawaii lawsuits. If voters approve I-194, it would take effect Jan. 1, 2027, unless a court blocks it.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: A promising new drug could turn the tide against HIV
events.summary: Experts say that a promising drug that offers complete protection against HIV and requires only two shots a year isn't getting to enough people MBARARA, Uganda -- In the red light district in Mbarara, a city in western Uganda known in part for sex tourism, a sex worker named Lisa Mutoni insists on using condoms when men enter her room, to protect her against HIV and other infections. The problem: Some try to remove or tear the condom while having sex. She takes HIV-prevention medication called PrEP, or preexposure prophylaxis, which can come in the form of daily pills or periodic injections. But there’s a new option for her and millions like her — if they could only get it . It’s a drug called lenacapavir that studies have shown can offer nearly complete protection from HIV with just two shots a year. Mutoni said access to lenacapavir would benefit sex workers who sometimes shift elsewhere for months at a time. “If you know that you have that injection for six months, you feel like you are safe,” she said. “And then it is very good, nice because sometimes you can also forget, if it is the pill, you can forget to swallow.” But Mutoni says every time she tries to get what is commonly referred to as “lena,” it's not available. “They tell me that it is finished,” she said. Such is the promise and the frustration with lenacapavir, a drug developed by Gilead Sciences. Other PrEP options, including pills and an every-other-month shot of the drug cabotegravir, are very effective and widely available. But health experts say lenacapavir has the power not just to protect individuals but potentially even turn the tide of the HIV epidemic globally because of its long-lasting effects. But there are not nearly enough doses, in this East African country or the rest of the world. “The rate of growth (of lenacapavir rollout) isn’t fast enough. We need to be getting to the millions pretty soon,” said Andrew Hill, an expert in HIV treatment who is a senior visiting research fellow at the University of Liverpool in northwest England. That may start to change in the coming months. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has just tentatively approved a generic version of lenacapavir that could help speed the production and distribution of the drug to 120 low-income countries at a price of roughly $40 a year, far below the U.S. list price of $28,218. The approval was announced Monday. The hope, according to the Global Fund, is to get it to 3 million people by the end of 2028. Some, including Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, say this isn't nearly enough. The group is calling on Gilead to make cheap doses available to more countries and to sell it directly to MSF so it can help protect more people faster. “Gilead says it wants to end the HIV epidemic ‘for everyone, everywhere,’ but its actions say otherwise,” said Melissa Barber, MSF USA global health advocacy and policy adviser, in a recent statement. For now, people in Mbarara, where an estimated 10% of the adult population has HIV — double the rate of Uganda as a whole — have to settle for inferior choices. Julius Bampe, a polygamous man, was alarmed earlier this year when testing confirmed his younger wife had HIV. She was immediately given drugs to suppress her infection, while Bampe sought lenacapavir. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Parents and 2 young children among victims of Learjet crash in Florida, family says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say But when Bampe, an itinerant builder, went to get his injection, he found that there were no doses left. “When I got here, they said that is what they would have given me, but they said they didn’t have enough doses for everyone,” he said. The facility that Bampe goes to received 40 lenacapavir doses in April, with instructions to focus only on pregnant mothers at risk of acquiring HIV. The guidelines were later changed to include couples like Bampe and his wife, sex workers and others. That batch was quickly administered and another 70 doses sent in June were used up within 10 days, said Tarsisio Biryeija, a nursing officer working as a counselor at Mbarara Health Centre IV. Uganda has slashed its HIV rate over the past three decades, and it's far below that of some southern African countries. But like in many nations, health authorities in Uganda say infections are driven largely by transactional sexual encounters like those in Mbarara — and the type of transmission that lenacapavir could be so effective at stopping. Mutoni, the sex worker in Mbarara, gets counseling and other support, including condoms, from Immaculate Nyamwija, founder of a Mbarara-based organization known as Action for Improved Health and Wealth. Nyamwija offers HIV support services to women who would face discrimination elsewhere. “It is a challenge, because the demand is high and the doses are few,” she said.

events.title: I spent years trying to make family vacations perfect. Giving up made them fun again.
events.summary: The author said she always loved traveling and assumed not much would change when she had kids. She now admits she was wrong about one thing. Courtesy of Annabel Lee. I love traveling and was looking forward to bringing my kids along with me when I became a parent. But what we want in a vacation differs, and I spent years feeling exhausted by our family trips. I've changed my expectations for what family vacations should look like, and we're all much happier For years, when people have asked me how my family vacations were, I'd smile and say something along the lines of, "Great, but I need another one to recover." The truth was, while I'd been away to relax and have fun, I usually felt exhausted by the time I got home, thanks to conflicting expectations about what we all wanted to do. My husband, our kids (now 7 and 9), and I have tried trips to hotels in Cornwall, holiday parks in France, and cottages in Wales , but none were what I would describe as restful. Our trip wish lists are very different I adore traveling, and when I had children, I thought I would just bring them along and have similar experiences with them. My favorite trips involved beautiful hotels , European cities, sightseeing, lying on the beach, and long lunches at sidewalk cafes. When I had one baby, this was still fairly easy to accomplish. After all, babies are amenable and don't have strong views on where you go for dinner. We went to Italy and on road trips around the UK, and he wasn't too difficult to travel with. But as he grew into a toddler and we had another child, I realized family vacations would no longer be the same as my pre-children vacations. Our individual needs and ideas of what constitutes a good time differ greatly. While heaven for me is a late dinner and an Aperol spritz while sitting on a Roman street, my kids want pizza at 6 p.m., followed by cartoons back in the hotel room. I'd love a day looking around Pompeii or lying on the Amalfi Coast while they'd prefer to be engaged in soft play somewhere or splashing around in a family-friendly swimming pool. I want architectural arcades; they want arcade games. Vacations became more of an endurance test than a rest I spent years fighting our competing ideas, trying to make my kids fit my ideals of family vacations. They didn't love it. When we were on trips, they didn't want to pose for family photos or sit through pasta dinners at sunset. The author said she would prefer to linger streetside sipping on a cocktail, while her kids want a familiar meal of pizza while on vacation. Courtesy of Annabel Lee. I'd end up stressed out and annoyed that my ideas about what our trips should be like weren't coming to life. They'd be frustrated at having to do things they didn't want to do, like museum trips and sightseeing. None of us were getting what we wanted. This turned family trips into a challenge for all of us, and the experience felt more like an endurance test than a break, with me constantly trying to make things go according to plan I had formed and convince my kids to go along with my ideas. I returned home from our adventures frazzled and feeling like I needed a rest more than when I started. Changing my expectations became the secret to happy family vacations After many years of struggling with this, I have now realized the secret to enjoying my family trip: lowering my expectations. I'm no longer bothered by trying to do it all when we go away or making my kids fit into my ideas of what a trip away should be like. We now prioritize a child-led approach to plans and destinations. I'm happy to book less beautiful hotels and stay in places with pools, early dining options, and family-friendly activities. While I miss the aesthetics, I know that there will be time for gorgeous city breaks when they are older. For now, I'm prioritizing peace, ease, and comfort. This strategy has transformed how we travel, and it means that, for the first time, family trips feel like fun again. They aren't like they were before, but knowing my kids are safe, happy, and having a great time is worth it. I've learned a 6 p.m. pizza and Aperol Spritz can be a little slice of heaven, too. events.title: America's tech elite are holding their breath as they await California's billionaire tax vote
events.summary: Californians are voting on a proposal that could send a one-time, huge tax bill to the state's billionaires. Lester Cohen/Getty Images Californians are debating how to tax their ultra-rich neighbors. Silicon Valley is sweating it. It could bring in $100 billion to plug a coming Medicare hole — or lose billions in tax revenue. The debate has created fresh political and tech exec divides. Tune in to the latest episode of "How to Tax a Billionaire: California Edition" — it's filled with drama, tech celebrities, and there's a big pot of money at stake! Today, Californians are heading to the polls, where they'll be asked to answer "Yes" or "No" to Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time "5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion." The vote has started a showdown that's been shaking up Silicon Valley executives for months. Google cofounder Sergey Brin , former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Affirm CEO Max Levchin, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Kleiner Perkins Chairman John Doerr, and angel investor Chris Larsen have collectively poured millions into an opposition campaign . Brin himself has donated more than $100 million to the "No" team, per Cal Matters. State campaign-finance filings show committees opposing Prop. 40 had reported about $130 million in contributions through October 22, versus about $33 million for its supporters. Meanwhile, other tech executives are preparing, just in case they have to pay up. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg weighed moving out of the state. In October, the company created a new class of shares that would give Zuckerberg $20 billion in "immediate liquidity" if the vote passes — potentially allowing him to pay the tax without giving up some of his voting power. "I've got to tell you, I have not even thought about it once," Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, said during a January spot on Bloomberg TV. "We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it." The vote has also split some regular political alliances. Progressive Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders has backed the billionaire tax, while California's Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, opposes the measure. There are multiple paths to "No" If a majority of voters fill in the "Yes" bubble on Prop 40, roughly 200 people who were California residents on January 1, 2026, could face the one-time tax. That vote has two lurking trap doors — propositions 41 and 42 could ruin the "Yes" team's finale. Both countermeasures were designed to undercut Prop. 40 by imposing new auditor reviews and prohibiting taxes on certain assets. If either measure receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the billionaire tax could be stopped from taking effect, even if a majority of Californians vote for it. What California's billionaires could owe In broad terms, the measure would tax billionaires based on more than their salary. Taxable wealth would include ownership stakes in businesses, securities, investment accounts, art, collectibles, and intellectual property, among other assets. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be excluded. If the billionaire tax passes, it'll be due in 2027 — though taxpayers could spread out their payments across five years at a higher cost. Supporters say the measure could raise tens of billions of dollars over several years. A majority of the proceeds would go toward healthcare, with the remainder allocated to education, food assistance, and the operation of the tax program. The campaign has pitched the measure as a way to help backfill looming federal cuts to Medi-Cal. Overall, Prop. 40 backers have said the tax event would raise over $100 billion for the state. A National Bureau of Economic Research working paper from Stanford economists, published in October, warned that the results could be much less rosy . The initial tax event could bring in around $30 billion before prompting high-earning executives to leave the state, the paper said. That could lose California $38.9 billion over time, the paper warned. Read the original article on Business Insider

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Customers left wondering what's been compromised after vendor advises resetting passwords, 2FA and passkeys 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water 14 days ago '123456' password linked to Denmark data breach affecting 8.8M people 21 days ago UK.gov begins killing off passwords for 23 million users September 14, 2026 IT department put sticky notes on the laptops to help employees log in August 6, 2026 Law firm insisted on one password to rule them all July 16, 2026 Password manager mSecure has warned customers to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and potentially remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity, but it has not explained what happened or whether anyone's secrets were exposed. In an email sent to customers on November 3, seen by The Register , US-based developer mSeven Software said it launched an investigation after discovering something amiss with its password management application. "mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company wrote. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist." The company has yet to answer what the suspicious activity involved, when it occurred, or whether attackers accessed customer information. Its advice to customers, however, suggests that they should take this seriously. "Given the potential security implications, mSeven recommends that you immediately take steps to protect all confidential information stored within the mSecure password management application," the email continued. "This may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys." For anyone with hundreds of passwords stored in mSecure, that's potentially hours of work. And without knowing what happened, customers have no way of telling which credentials they actually need to replace. The warning has understandably gone down poorly with customers, who have taken to mSecure's support forum demanding answers. "Please provide more context to your email below advising there has been a security breach," one customer wrote. "It is not acceptable to offer the vague advice 'take steps'. Please state what remedial action is required, and what data was compromised." Others are wondering whether they're expected to spend the next several days changing every password they've ever saved. "I have over 800 passwords in mSecure, is the email saying I need to change all of them!" another customer asked. A separate user, who said they had more than 500 passwords stored in the application, questioned whether the warning applied to every two-factor authentication method and passkey associated with their accounts, or just those used to access mSecure itself. The confusion has also spilled onto Reddit , where customers have shared copies of the vague notification and questioned what might have happened. mSeven has yet to respond to The Register 's questions, leaving customers to guess whether their data has actually been compromised or the company is simply being cautious. That's not exactly reassuring from a business whose entire purpose is keeping other people's secrets safe. The company's email concludes: "We regret any inconvenience that this may cause." For customers contemplating hundreds of password resets, "inconvenience" may be putting it mildly.

Mayor of New York City Zohran Mamdani has criticized the owner of Madison Square Garden, one of the city’s largest entertainment venues, arguing that the company’s surveillance technology should not be allowed. Mamdani told Wired in an interview on Tuesday that surveillance technologies are “indicative of much that is wrong in our country today.” He added that City Council member Shahana Hanif introduced two pieces of local legislation aimed at banning the collection of biometric data , such as using facial recognition, in public places across the city. Mamdani said that the draft legislation is “an important response to this kind of an issue.” The comments come after a stream of reporting from Wired detailing how Madison Square Garden’s owner James Dolan relies on surveillance cameras and face-scanning technology to track people across and outside of its venues. In one report , Wired revealed that Dolan’s company keeps a database that, among other things, marks some visitors, including celebrity performers, as “LGBTQIA,” for reasons that are unclear. Dolan subsequently sued Wired over its reporting. In 2021, MSG made headlines after a woman was banned from Radio City, another Dolan-owned venue, after being recognized by facial recognition systems as an attorney at a law firm who was suing Dolan’s company but was not involved in the litigation. When reached by TechCrunch, Madison Square Garden spokesperson Mikyl Cordova said: “Wired’s reporting is inaccurate and false. MSG is pursuing legal remedies,” without providing evidence for its claim. Since 2021, New York City has required businesses to disclose when they are collecting biometric data from visitors.
