events.title: Gas prices could shape the midterms. See the US states where prices have risen the most.
events.summary: In 42 states, gas prices are more than $1 higher today than they were a year ago. Charles-McClintock Wilson/NurPhoto via Getty Images Rising gas prices since the beginning of the Iran War are a key issue during the 2026 midterms. Since last year, regular gas prices have increased by 40%, and diesel prices by 71% across states. Michigan, a key battleground state, saw the second-sharpest rise in gas prices after Wisconsin. For many voters, their choice in the midterm elections could come down to one thing: the pain at the pump . Since the Iran War began in February, higher fuel costs have become a growing pressure point for Americans. Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz , a critical global shipping chokepoint, have tightened global fuel supplies and pushed energy prices worldwide. On average, regular gas prices in the US today are nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA's  Fuel Price Tracker  as of November 2. In 42 states, regular gas prices per gallon today are at least $1 higher than they were a year ago. For diesel fuel , which is used in industries like agriculture and manufacturing , as well as for transporting goods, the rise has been even sharper. Across all US states , diesel prices have risen by 71% on average. Almost every US state recorded its highest-ever diesel prices this fall, with the exception of Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and New York, which saw higher prices in 2022, when Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent global fuel prices soaring. A White House spokesperson told Business Insider that once the conflict in the Middle East ends, gas prices will "drop drastically," adding Iran also "will not have a nuclear weapon." "Thanks to the exceptional work of the US military, more oil is now flowing out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran conflict began," the spokesperson said. To see how fuel prices have risen across the US, Business Insider used AAA data to compare today's gas prices with those a year ago. We ranked all US states by the percentage increase in regular prices, which most people see at the pump . We also listed the rise in diesel prices in each state to provide a fuller picture. events.title: UEFI bootkit infected fully patched Windows machines. Is Microsoft to blame?
events.summary: In 2023, malware tracked as BlackLotus became the first publicly documented in-the-wild UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11 systems. With the industry-wide chain-of-trust mechanism subverted, the malware was able to run malicious code before Windows was fully loaded and many security defenses were operational. Microsoft had already patched the vulnerability that BlackLotus exploited in 2022. In 2023 and 2024, Microsoft issued additional updates. The first added a new certificate that no longer trusted the vulnerable boot managers. The second provided the means to revoke trust in the digital certificate used to sign older vulnerable Windows boot managers. The organizations infected by the new bootkit, which is tracked under the name BlackX, had installed all of these patches. So how did they fall victim? UEFI bootkit refresher Before discussing the incident further, a brief review of BlackLotus and UEFI malware is in order. Short for Unified Extensible Firmware Interface , UEFI is firmware that runs immediately after a computer is turned on. One of its main jobs is to load system configuration settings, identify and initialize hardware components, and prepare the computer to start its OS. Read full article Comments

events.title: Taco Bell sales recover in the US after summer cyclospora outbreak
events.summary: Taco Bell’s U.S. sales are climbing again after a cyclospora outbreak tied to the chain slowed visits over the summer Taco Bell sales in the U.S. are climbing again after a cyclospora outbreak over the summer slowed business. Taco Bell’s same-store sales, or sales at locations open at least a year, have been outperforming the U.S. fast-food industry since the end of September, according to Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell. “We are really pleased with the rapid recovery,” CEO Chris Turner told investors Tuesday during a conference call. In mid-July, federal health officials identified lettuce from Mexico and served at Taco Bell locations in five U.S. states as the source of a widespread outbreak of the diarrhea-causing parasite cyclospora. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warned consumers not to eat shredded iceberg lettuce from Taco Bell restaurants in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia. Yum Brands is based in Louisville, Kentucky. Taco Bell’s U.S. same-store sales fell 4% in the July-September period compared with the previous year, while international sales climbed 5%. Turner said weekly app-based deals for Taco Bell’s loyalty members helped bring back core users. events.title: I launched a gluten-free bakery from my kitchen after leaving finance. It's on track to make $3M in revenue this year.
events.summary: Addison LaBonte is the founder of Sweet Addison's, a gluten-free bakery in Dallas. Desiree Rios for BI Addison LaBonte founded Sweet Addison's, a gluten-free bakery, after a layoff in finance in 2023. Sweet Addison's has seen rapid growth and is now on track for over $3M in revenue, employing a team of 10. Social media engagement helped the business expand with over 600,000 followers across platforms. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Addison LaBonte, the 32-year-old founder of Sweet Addison's, a gluten-free bakery in Dallas. It's been edited for length and clarity. Before launching Sweet Addison's in January 2024, I worked in finance and didn't love my job. I had an online audience of roughly 150,000 people who followed me for my recommendations on gluten-free desserts. As a content creator in the healthy baking niche, I thought there was a big gap in the market for a clean-ingredient, indulgent-tasting dessert. I've been gluten-free for 10 years now, so I wanted to create a product that would meet the needs of the gluten-free community. I played around with recipes in my kitchen, and then, through my online audience, I had a demand for it, and I thought, life is short; let's start a bakery. Nearly three years later, we're on track to do over $3M in revenue this year. LaBonte said her first customers were her social media followers. Desiree Rios for BI I was building my audience for about six years before I launched my bakery I had followers who were ready and excited to buy, and, thankfully, I earned their trust over time. When I did launch, they were my very first customers, and I'm so thankful for them. I was laid off from my finance job in 2023, about four months before I officially launched Sweet Addison's. I had a decent amount of savings and decided to go all in on my business. I started Sweet Addison's out of my apartment kitchen; it was very tight, and I had no idea what I was doing. There were cookies everywhere. LaBonte now leads a team of 10 out of a commercial kitchen. Desiree Rios for BI I knew I wanted this to become a really big business In the first month, we did around $8,000 in sales. It was pretty small, but it kept growing, and we've grown almost every month since then. I never wanted to just be a home baker. I had big dreams of building a national company, so that was always the plan. Looking back on the early days, it felt a little slow, but that was just because I was being impatient. Now, I have a team of 10, and we ship all around the country — that's the bulk of our business. Here in Dallas-Fort Worth, we're in about 10 coffee shops, and we're in four or five places in New York City. Since launching, I've continued to use social media to connect with customers On Instagram, we've scaled to over 325,000 followers; on TikTok, to 103,000; and on Facebook, to 203,000, for a total of over 600,000. The biggest thing is being consistent, posting every day, showing up, and answering all the DMs that you get. I also find that asking my audience what they're looking for and what would best serve them has been instrumental for us. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Addison LaBonte (@organicallyaddison) I let my customers choose the next flavor we launch I'll get on Instagram stories and ask, 'What flavor do you want to see next?' 'Vote for this or vote for that.' 'Which ingredients do you want to see?' It's a really fun way to get them involved. Being honest with them and asking them questions makes them feel like they're part of the brand. My advice for other small businesses is to be obsessed with their customers. Get to know them, talk to them, get their feedback, figure out exactly what they're looking for, and how you can better serve them. At the end of the day, I don't have a business without customers, so it's not about me. Putting the focus on them has been a game changer for my business. Getting customer feedback has been instrumental for success, LaBonte said. Desiree Rios for BI I chose to invest in our branding and our packaging The product has to stand out on the shelf, but even before we were in retailers, I wanted really nice packaging so that when people are posting about Sweet Addison's on Instagram, it would be eye-catching Still, one way we cut costs is by not doing any custom-branded shipping boxes. In my mind, when you order these cookies online, they'll still taste great, even if they're in an unbranded shipping box. The box doesn't make them taste better. There are certain other things that I would never compromise on, like the integrity of our ingredients. We spend a lot of money on high-quality ingredients. Having other people advocate for your brand gives you a leg up We've collaborated with a few influencers and brands, which has really accelerated our growth. If you can get people posting about your brand, it can really move the needle. When working with influencers, we'll send them cookies, and they'll post on our behalf, so the cost is just the cost of the cookies; we're not necessarily paying them to post about us. Brands and creators are different, but the outcomes have been relatively similar. Either way, we get our product in front of a lot more eyes, and it's been really fun. Sweet Addison's social media strategy includes influencer outreach and collaborations. Desiree Rios for BI I should've hired sooner As demand increased, especially during our first holiday season, I knew I needed to hire help , but I was so busy I almost didn't have time to interview, hire, and train someone. I had a two-week period when I was up till 3 a.m. every day working, and I thought there was no way I was going to get through Christmas on barely any sleep. I found the time and identified my first two team members who had commercial kitchen experience. Now that I lead a team of 10 every day in a commercial kitchen, I've been able to step back and focus on growing the business. I work 14 to 15 hours per day. I spend one to two hours on social media engaging with customers, posting, and answering DMs. I spend roughly five to six hours on admin tasks, plus another three to four hours per day on Zoom calls and meetings. I also still do new flavor recipe development and testing. LaBonte continues to test new flavors. Desiree Rios for BI I reinvest our profits back into the business Not much has fundamentally changed, but we have a really high repeat-order rate, which makes me very happy. We have a subscription too, so people can subscribe. The more people who find out about us, the more they buy and buy again, which has increased revenue. I'm so thankful for my business, and I would encourage people to go out and pursue their dreams because life is too short not to. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: US job postings jumped sharply in September, a sign hiring could pick up
events.summary: U.S. employers ramped up their job postings in September as stronger economic growth may be encouraging more hiring WASHINGTON -- U.S. employers ramped up their job postings in September as stronger economic growth may be encouraging more hiring. Yet voters are headed to the polls Tuesday largely gloomy over an economy beset by higher prices . U.S. job openings jumped to 7.5 million from a revised 7.19 million in August, the Labor Department reported Tuesday . It is the largest number of openings since May and up from a recent low of 6.9 million in March. The department’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) also showed that gross hiring — job gains before subtracting people who quit or lost jobs — rose and layoffs fell in September. The increases are a hopeful sign that hiring could improve, but the trend would have to continue for several months to suggest real improvement. Hiring has been sluggish for nearly three years, though layoffs have also been historically low, a sign of meager “churn” in the labor market. Low churn means those who are employed are enjoying relatively high levels of job security, but it is much harder than normal for those looking for work to find a job. The government will issue the October jobs report on Friday, which is forecast to show that employers added 65,000 positions last month, according to data provider FactSet. That would be an improvement from 29,000 in September. The unemployment rate is expected to stay at a low 4.2%. In September, layoffs fell sharply to just 1.64 million, the fewest since March 2025. The number of people quitting their jobs rose to 3.37 million, the highest in about 18 months, and up from 3.04 million. The rise in quits is generally a good sign because workers usually leave a job when they either have another lined up or when they are confident they can find new work. Sen. events.title: GhostBSD 26.2 takes the fright out of FreeBSD with a friendlier installer
events.summary: GhostBSD, the easiest-to-install flavor of FreeBSD for the daemon-curious desktop dabbler, is back with a fresh update. GhostBSD 26.2-R15.1p6 , to give it its slightly unwieldy full version number, is based on FreeBSD 15.1. It brings a new installer, full-disk encryption support, a smaller installation image, and fixes across its desktop tools. FreeBSD 15.1 was released back in June , and at the time of writing, it's the most recent point release of FreeBSD. The original plan was that FreeBSD 15.1 would include the option of installing KDE Plasma directly from the setup program, so that the OS would have a graphical desktop from its very first boot. However, this feature isn't ready just yet. That gap inspired Daemonarchy, which we covered late last month . But its Omarchy-derived, keyboard-driven tiling desktop can feel unfamiliar even to experienced Linux users accustomed to conventional desktops. GhostBSD has different goals. It brings Linux-like desktop convenience to FreeBSD: a live graphical environment to explore before installation, a graphical installer, and tools for managing software and updates. These conveniences are familiar to desktop Linux users, but a standard FreeBSD installation takes more work. Its text-mode installer leaves users to install and configure a graphical desktop themselves, if they want one. This is just how the BSD family does things, and most BSD users we've talked to regard it as standard operating procedure and see nothing wrong with it. For Linux users who are curious about how things are on the other side of the FOSS Unix fence, though, those extra steps can form formidable barriers. GhostBSD is an attempt to lay down a welcome mat. The standard edition of GhostBSD installs the MATE desktop, and the downloads page also offers a community-maintained version with Xfce instead. As the project said it would back in February, this release uses the XLibre fork of the X.org X11 server. That's one fewer desktop than when we last tried GhostBSD in August 2025 . That release also offered the Mac OS X-like Gershwin environment. There are practical hardware fixes too. The release notes list improvements for Intel AX200 Wi-Fi cards, open networks, password alerts, and non-ASCII network names, while USB HID support is enabled by default. Where has Gershwin gone? Gershwin remains in active development , so we asked project lead Joe Maloney why it wasn't included. "It has been difficult to find time to package for GhostBSD. It's the only distro I have ever packaged for," Maloney said. He added that rapid contributions from AppImage creator Simon Peter, known as probono, had made packaging increasingly difficult. He also pointed to the fact that GhostBSD project lead Eric Turgeon is developing his own environment too: the Mocka desktop . Mocka is still in its very early stages – alpha version 0.0.2 appeared early last month – but the plan is that when it's ready, it will become GhostBSD's default desktop. For now, the only available module is a dock for the MATE desktop, but the curious can follow its development on the GitHub project page . There may be no Gershwin included, but GhostBSD 26.2 offers MATE 1.28, and there's also a community-supported version with Xfce 4.20 instead. We tried the default MATE edition, and it works as well as ever. It defaults to a dark theme and the classic two-panel GNOME 2 desktop layout. The System menu in the top panel has an Administration submenu with a few of the project's own apps that aren't from upstream FreeBSD: "BE Station" for managing system boot environments, "Software Station" for browsing and installing applications, and "Update Station" for updates. We regularly hear from users growing tired of the Linux vendors' headlong rush into Rust, Wayland, systemd, containerized app formats, and so on. Some are curious about whether FreeBSD offers a usable alternative. GhostBSD is the easiest way to get a complete, ready-to-use graphical FreeBSD desktop. There is a price to pay for switching to FreeBSD: for a start, most proprietary Linux apps, from Chrome to Slack, are not available here. Hardware compatibility needs more checking than on mainstream Linux, especially with recent GPUs and Wi-Fi adapters. If Windows gaming is a priority, this isn't the obvious choice. But if you can live without those proprietary apps and find suitable open source replacements, FreeBSD is a viable alternative – and GhostBSD takes much of the setup work out of trying it. ®

events.title: AI Is Changing How Semiconductor Fabs Work — and Engineers Are Moving Faster Because of It
events.summary: Your browser doesn't support HTML5 video. Here is a link to the video instead. Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking. For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences. AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast. Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials. Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time. AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours. And digital twins let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a semiconductor manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. Engineers direct the work and make decisions based on their expertise while spending less time waiting for answers. Shorter Simulation Cycles Change What Engineers Can Explore Accelerated computing doesn’t just speed up individual calculations — it changes how many alternatives engineers can test before committing. Multiphysics simulations model interactions among physical effects, such as heat transfer, electrical behavior and mechanical stress. Using the NVIDIA cuDSS library, multiphysics software provider COMSOL is accelerating such simulations for semiconductor manufacturing by up to 10x. This helps engineers optimize equipment and processes, compare alternatives and decide which changes to test physically. Applied Materials and NVIDIA are collaborating to accelerate atomic-scale materials discovery and process development. By integrating NVIDIA cuDSS, Applied’s Ginestra simulation platform runs up to 10x faster than CPU-only approaches. And with NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo, Applied’s ACE+ multiphysics platform delivers topography simulations up to 35x faster. In some cases, acceleration doesn’t just shorten the calculation — it enables it altogether. Computational lithography — which defines how circuit patterns are printed onto silicon — involves calculations too intensive to complete on CPU at production scale. Siemens is integrating NVIDIA cuLitho into its Calibre lithography software, delivering up to 17x acceleration on key simulation workloads. That expands what engineers can verify before a wafer goes to print. As such, faster calculations can help researchers explore material behavior and reaction pathways that influence next-generation semiconductor processes. Predicting Process Behavior Without Running Every Simulation In addition to accelerating simulations, AI trained on physics can predict how materials and processes will behave — without running a full simulation each time. The payoff is most visible in complex calculations that are expensive even on accelerated hardware. Plasma — the electrically charged gas used in semiconductor etch processes — is one example. Modeling plasma behavior requires solving equations that capture how electrical, chemical and thermal processes interact, making repeated simulation costly. Lam Research demonstrated that the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework can predict plasma behavior in milliseconds, compared with days for a full simulation — giving engineers a faster way to explore process conditions without rerunning the full model each time. Agents Handle the Steps Between Decisions Engineers turn analyses into decisions — revising a design, investigating a test failure, adjusting a production process and more. AI agents can help carry out the steps between those decisions. Evaluating which AI model to apply to a given task is one example: a sequential, manual process that can consume hours on the test floor. Advantest is using NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard AI agents to automate that selection, reducing response times from hours to minutes. Testing Factory Changes Before They Reach the Line Digital twins let teams simulate equipment configurations, layouts and process changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. This reduces experimentation costs, especially as fabs become more complex and the stakes of a wrong change get higher. Applied Materials uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build physically accurate digital twins of entire fabs. Teams can simulate material movement, identify bottlenecks and evaluate layouts and operating strategies — extending virtual experimentation beyond individual processes to how the factory works as a whole. The future of semiconductor manufacturing lies in connecting these capabilities: using production data to inform models and models to evaluate changes, then bringing those findings back to the engineers making production decisions. That’s the promise of the AI-defined fab: where AI helps people learn from each production cycle and act on that knowledge sooner. events.title: 5 of the best and 3 of the worst looks at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards
events.summary: Pamela Anderson at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City. Taylor Hill/Getty Images Stars were out at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City on Monday. Many wore glamorous gowns covered in sequins and feathers. Others missed the mark in outfits that were too casual for such a high-profile event. Where there are celebrities, there's fashion . The 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, hosted at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City on Monday night, had both. Some walked the red carpet in iconic pieces of fashion history, while others showcased modern creations. Naturally, there were a few duds; some outfits were far too casual. These are the best and worst looks we saw throughout the night. Keke Palmer looked like a goddess in vintage Bob Mackie. Keke Palmer at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City. John Nacion/Getty Images The legendary fashion designer , who died in September, originally created the gold, halter-top gown in 1975 for Raquel Welch. She wore it on "The Cher Show." If you didn't know the gown's history, though, you might have thought it was designed for Palmer. It fit her like a glove and was the perfect color to complement her glowing skin and vibrant hair. Emily Ratajkowski should have picked a different outfit entirely. Emily Ratajkowski at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City. Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images She posed on the red carpet wearing a black long-sleeved sweater, a low-rise skirt in a bright orange shade, and pointed leather boots with skinny heels. The outfit looked more like something the model and writer would wear on a New York City outing in the fall than an outfit fit for an awards ceremony. Chloe Bailey could have been mistaken for a runway model. Chloe Bailey at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images The musician arrived at the CFDA Fashion Awards in a sheer black Christian Siriano design . The form-fitting piece had a high neckline, long sleeves, and tulle ruffles at the neck, wrists, and skirt hem. The latter three pieces were also embellished with tan feathers. Bailey's outfit was the epitome of high fashion and made for a memorable red-carpet moment. Ashley Graham wore a two-piece set that unfortunately wasn't memorable. Ashley Graham at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City. Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images Esque/By custom-made her black-and-white look. It comprised high-waisted black trousers and a deconstructed button-down shirt transformed into a strapless, bralette-style top. The pants were tailored perfectly to Graham, and her top was a unique idea. Still, there wasn't much else to the outfit, and it didn't stand out on the red carpet. Travis Scott showed how powerful a simple suit can be. Travis Scott at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City. Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images The musician looked sharp in a black satin suit perfectly tailored to his measurements. It included pleated trousers, a double-breasted jacket, and a leather top worn underneath. He also accessorized strongly with diamond earrings, dark sunglasses, and leather dress shoes. Shaboozey should have taken a bigger fashion risk. Shaboozey at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City. Taylor Hill/Getty Images The country star was dressed by Ralph Lauren for the night. He wore a white top, a matching vest, a cream-colored blazer, and distressed jeans. Shaboozey also wore leather flats with white socks, a belt with a massive brass-and-turquoise buckle, and a statement bolo tie. Because he wears outfits like this all the time, it didn't stand out on him — especially at a fashion-focused event. Allison Janney had a dramatic fashion moment, and it worked for her. Allison Janney at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City. Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images Christian Siriano designed the actor's hot-pink ensemble. It had a high neckline, long sleeves with shoulder pads, and cape-style detailing down each arm. On anyone else, this outfit might have been overwhelming. For Janney, though, it was the perfect color and design to bring fun to the red carpet. Pamela Anderson looked elegant in a little black dress. Pamela Anderson at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City. Taylor Hill/Getty Images The model and writer arrived wearing a black halter dress from Carolina Herrera. It had an ankle-length skirt, a fitted waist, and sparkling feather fringe along the neckline. The dress was celebratory, and Anderson styled it perfectly with embellished heels, a satin clutch, and red lipstick. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Do sports stars have the right to free speech?
events.summary: The Mbappe controversy demonstrates how market power in sport is being used to enforce conformity. Senior Editor for Inclusive Storytelling at The New Humanitarian. French football superstar Kylian Mbappe recently landed in trouble over a meme. Discussing an image that apparently superimposed his face on Mao Zedong’s, he referred to the late Chinese leader as someone he thought was a dictator, without naming Mao. The offhand remark became an international controversy. Chinese sponsors withdrew their support. State television suspended La Liga broadcasts. Apologies followed from Mbappe and his club, Real Madrid, while the league expressed regret over the offence caused. Mbappe was riffing on one of the running jokes about his outsized influence over his clubs and teammates. He was not delivering a considered assessment of Chinese history. Yet the response turned a passing remark into a test of respect for an entire nation. Mbappe is not the first athlete to discover how quickly political sensitivities become instruments of discipline. A decade ago, American football star Colin Kaepernick knelt during the United States national anthem to protest systemic racism and police killings of Black people, and was effectively frozen out of the National Football League. In May, after Spanish footballer Lamine Yamal waved a Palestinian flag during Barcelona’s title celebrations, Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, accused him of inciting hatred and demanded that the club distance itself from the gesture. Kaepernick and Yamal made deliberate statements. Mbappe made a joke. Yet the distinction offered the latter little protection. An athlete need not deliberately enter politics to discover how tightly his speech is policed. Mbappe’s extraordinary visibility gives him influence and makes him commercially valuable. But the commercial relationships that make him valuable also hand others the means to discipline him. The logic is an old one. In ancient Greece, victorious athletes could receive substantial rewards from their cities, including money, meals at public expense and civic honours. Sporting success could open a path to political influence, and their achievements brought prestige to the communities that claimed them. But the claim could become possessive. According to the ancient Greek geographer and writer Pausanias, the runner Astylus, originally associated with Croton, later proclaimed himself a Syracusan when competing at the Olympic Games. His former compatriots responded by pulling down his statue and converting his house into a prison. Today, sporting institutions make similar claims on the people whose achievements they celebrate. The athlete represents the nation, embodies the club, carries the sponsor’s values. Each relationship becomes a reason to keep an inconvenient thought to oneself. As Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho put it, “Often the best thing you can do is keep your mouth shut, because there’s danger in so many things you say or comment on.” When a single remark threatens access to a market, the club and the league acquire a financial interest in treating it as misconduct, and the pressure to recant can be extreme. When a state broadcaster suspends an entire league, it punishes thousands of players, staff and viewers who had nothing to do with the remark, effectively holding them hostage to one man’s apology. That is market power being used to enforce conformity. This is where the contradictions of celebrity become especially apparent. Sporting businesses sell courage, authenticity and individual character. They encourage audiences to identify with the person behind the performance. But the expression of that character becomes a problem when it threatens another part of the business. The athlete is invited to be themselves, subject to approval. Further, audiences add their own pressure. We increasingly expect sports stars to address moral and political questions, and we judge their silence as well as their speech. Fame does carry obligations. But athletic excellence does not confer political wisdom, and prominence is not a qualification. If we want courage from athletes, we must also confront the institutions that make courage professionally dangerous. Mbappe’s case is revealing precisely because he was not taking a heroic stand. The freedom to speak cannot depend on an athlete being historically knowledgeable, perfectly articulate or deliberately brave. It must leave room for an uncertain remark and a foolish joke, as well as a carefully planned protest. However, it is clear that freedom does not confer immunity from critique. Fans can disagree loudly, and athletes should answer for objectionable speech. But the test should be whether a remark harms people, not whether it embarrasses a state or threatens a balance sheet. The supposed neutrality of sport helps to hide these demands for conformity.

events.title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?
events.summary: Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise UK interest rates for the first time in more than three years at their next meeting. Most analysts believe the Bank rate will go up from 3.75% to 4%, following holds at the previous six meetings. Before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, rates had been expected to fall this year, but the economic fallout from the conflict has pushed up inflation across the globe. Interest rates affect mortgage, credit card and savings rates for millions of people. What are interest rates and why do they change? An interest rate tells you how much it costs to borrow money, or the reward for saving it. The Bank of England's base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings. The Bank moves its base rate up and down in order to keep UK inflation — the rate at which prices are increasing — at or near 2%. When inflation is above that target, the Bank typically puts rates up. The idea is to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises. What is happening to UK interest rates and inflation? The Bank of England's base rate rose to 5.25% in August 2023. It remained at that level until August 2024, when the Bank started cutting. Five cuts brought rates down to 4%, before the Bank held rates at its meetings in September and November 2025. It then cut in December 2025 before holding rates steady in January, March, April, June, July and September 2026. Meanwhile, the main UK inflation measure, CPI, has fallen significantly since the October 2022 high of 11.1%, which was caused by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. However, the rate has been heading back up and is expected to go higher. It was 3.5% in the year to September 2026 , up from 3.1% the previous month and well above the central bank's 2% target. The Office for National Statistics (ONS), which tracks UK inflation, blamed the acceleration on sharp rises in petrol and diesel prices. The US-Israel war with Iran has put up energy and fuel costs around the world, which has increased the pace of price rises more generally. What is happening to UK prices? Published 21 October What is expected to happen to UK interest rates? At the start of the year, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates twice in 2026, with the first drop predicted to come in March or April. However, the increase in fuel prices and inflation after the outbreak of the conflict has upended all of this. Oil prices initially rose sharply as a result of disruption to supplies in the region, but dropped back when various ceasefires were agreed. Oil prices rose again when the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July. UK household energy bills rose after the increases in the price cap in July and October, while global oil prices have risen again recently. Given the uncertainty, many analysts think UK interest rates will rise at the November meeting and again early next year. What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Published 28 September Why are UK fuel prices rising again? Published 2 October How do interest rate changes affect mortgages, loans and savings rates? Just under a third of households have a mortgage, according to the government's English Housing Survey , external . About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate. Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost would go up by about £31 a month if the Bank raises the base rate by 0.25 percentage points, but it depends on the size of people's loans. An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) would wait to see if their lender chose to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise. But the vast majority of mortgage customers - some 87% - have fixed-rate deals. While their monthly payments aren't immediately affected by a rate change, their future deals are. Most lenders have already priced in a rise in the Bank rate in November, so this is already reflected in the rates being offered. As of 3 November, the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate was at 5.97%, while the average five-year rate stood at 5.99%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts. The average two-year tracker rate was 4.67%. About 800,000 fixed-rate mortgages with an interest rate of 3% or below are expected to expire every year, on average, until the end of 2027. Borrowing costs for customers coming off those deals are likely to rise sharply. You can see how your mortgage may be affected by future interest rate changes by using our calculator: How much could my mortgage payments change?

events.title: Syria says it foiled Hezbollah plot to target Homs oil refinery
events.summary: Live: A year since fall of al-Assad Hezbollah denies the Syrian accusations, reiterating that it does not have any presence on Syrian territory. Syrian security forces have said they foiled a plot to target the Homs oil refinery in central Syria, arresting a cell affiliated with Lebanon’s Hezbollah armed group. Syria’s General Intelligence Service (GIS) said on X that “the preemptive security operation” was carried out in cooperation with the country’s Internal Security Forces. list 1 of 3 ‘People don’t have money’: Syrian fuel hikes deepen economic pain list 2 of 3 Syria removed: Which countries are still on the US ‘terror’ list – and why? list 3 of 3 Syria fuel price hikes test public patience with economic recovery It identified two arrested individuals with their initials – M S and B Sh – but did not elaborate on the time or the location of the operation, “which resulted in the seizure of explosive devices in their possession that had been prepared to execute the plot”. Hezbollah denied the Syrian accusations in a statement, reiterating that it does not have any presence on Syrian territory and is not ⁠involved in “any activity that undermines the ⁠security and stability of Syria”. Hezbollah ⁠fought alongside former President Bashar al-Assad’s forces during Syria’s nearly 14-year civil war, but relations with Damascus have deteriorated sharply since his overthrow in 2024. Syrian authorities have accused ⁠Hezbollah of involvement in a series of alleged plots, including planned assassinations, ⁠rocket attacks and arms smuggling. The Homs refinery is one of Syria’s two oil refineries, along with the Baniyas refinery, and plays a key role in securing petroleum products. In a similar operation, the GIS said on Sunday that they arrested two members of a suspected ISIL (ISIS) cell in the governorate of Deir Az Zor. Sunday’s statement added that investigations “showed the detainees’ involvement in carrying out a series of assassinations in the province, the latest of which targeted defence ministry member Ibrahim al-Jassem with a gunshot near the al-Rashid mosque in the city of Mayadin”. The operation led to the seizure of weapons and ammunition found in the cell’s hideout, the security forces said, adding that authorities were continuing investigations of “the terrorists to uncover their links in preparation for bringing them to justice”. On September 27, the security forces said they had arrested four members of an ISIL cell involved in planning and carrying out several attacks in different parts of the country. On September 30, the Syrian Electricity Company said the Deir Ali, Nasiriya and Tishreen power stations had gone out of service after an explosion on a gas line at the Tishreen station in the Damascus countryside, which cut off the gas supply needed to run them. On October 15, the Syrian Petroleum Company said the pipeline carrying petroleum products from Baniyas to Homs was damaged near the village of Hadida in western Homs countryside, causing a fuel leak, state media reported, in the latest in a series of attacks on Syria’s energy infrastructure . Last month, Syria’s security forces foiled a plot to target a police patrol in Damascus countryside, saying that an ISIL cell was preparing to carry out the attack, Syrian state television reported. They said the group was responsible for explosions and assassinations in Raqqa, Aleppo, Idlib and Homs. Damascus joined the US-led international coalition against ISIL last November, which was formed in 2014 and has carried out operations against the group in Syria and Iraq.

events.title: How US midterms have cost a record $12bn as cost of living soars
events.summary: Candidates, donors and super PACs are spending more than ever on political campaigns. The US midterm elections are on track to be the most expensive for candidates and political donors in history. According to OpenSecrets, a research group that tracks money in US politics, close to a record $12bn has been spent by candidates and outside political groups on campaigning. The world’s richest man, Elon Musk alone has given $445 million to the Republicans, according to campaign finance records. list 1 of 3 Is money ruining US elections? list 2 of 3 Tracking the money: The biggest donors in the 2026 US midterm elections list 3 of 3 Hackers target US campaign finance system days before midterm elections Critics have questioned the huge sums of money being spent to sway voting during an election cycle in which the cost of living and affordability have been the key issues in most campaign agendas. They argue that campaign spending policy gives wealthy donors, corporations and special interest groups outsized influence over candidate and policy selection. Why has so much been spent on these elections? US elections are funded in two ways. Firstly, candidates can directly raise money for their campaigns. In the lead-up to these midterms, Democratic candidates are expected to have spent more than $2.2bn compared with $1.4bn by Republican candidates, according to OpenSecrets. Secondly, corporations, unions and other associations can spend money on election campaigns, independently of individual candidates’ campaigns, in a process known as “outside spending”. Previously, these organisations were barred from funding adverts close to elections in order to prevent corruption or the appearance of corruption. But in 2010, the US Supreme Court overturned that rule, treating election communications as protected political speech. In a related ruling, a lower court struck down limits on the size of contributions these groups could raise, provided they did not coordinate directly with candidates. Since then, Federal Election Commission disclosure data shows such spending on elections has increased hugely, nearly tripling in the past decade alone from $4.12bn in 2016 to an estimated $11.9bn for 2026’s midterm elections. This “outside spending” is largely driven by groups called independent expenditure-only political action committees – better known as super PACs – which organise the funding and then spend it on advertising or other initiatives in support of candidates or parties. There are no limits on the amount of money donors can give to outside spending groups such as super PACs. That has been the case since the Supreme Court ruled that unlimited contributions to groups which do not coordinate directly with candidates are protected under free speech laws. The majority of super PACs are politically aligned and organised in line with either the Democratic or Republican Party. Among the largest super PACs are the Senate Leadership Fund, which has spent $489 million, and MAGA Inc, with $353 million, both for Republican candidates. The Senate Majority PAC and the House Majority PAC have spent $248 million and $192 million respectively on Democratic candidates. Other super PACs are organised by individuals and special interest groups, such as the Republican-supporting America PAC founded and funded by Elon Musk and the Democracy PAC funded and organised by George Soros which backs Democratic candidates. Super PACs report on their direct contributors as well as financial activity to the Federal Election Commission (FEC) every month during election years, and every six months during non-election years. But contributors may include organisations whose own funding sources are not publicly disclosed. This means that funds can pass through multiple organisations – sometimes through other PACs, known as “shell PACs” – before they are spent on campaign-related activities or advertising, making it difficult to trace contributions back to their original source. When an original source of political spending cannot be identified, the funds are commonly described as “dark money”. According to OpenSecrets, “dark money” contributions will surpass a record $1.5bn in these midterm elections. That is up from the previous record of $1.35bn set in 2024 and has prompted concerns about the transparency of funding for political candidates. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accused the nonprofit lobbying group, American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), of spending “millions in dark money”, for example, on pro-Israel candidates. Public records reviewed by Al Jazeera found that AIPAC has channelled millions of dollars through shell PACs ahead of the US midterm elections. AIPAC is one of the best-known super PACs and has attracted criticism in recent years, particularly in light of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. The lobbying group decided to end endorsements and direct campaign contributions after a challenging year.

events.title: As a flight attendant, I wish passengers would leave the window shades open. I've got great reasons, but it's not up to me.
events.summary: Regardless of whether you feel the window shade should be open or shut during flight, I (not pictured) say the passenger in the window seat should get to control it. Dobrila Vignjevic/Getty Images As a flight attendant , I prefer open window shades — but the choice is up to those in window seats. I love watching the scenery and feel safer, as we all get more visibility into our surroundings. Unless we're stopped at a warm destination or the cabin is rowdy, I am team window shades up. When it comes to whether window shades should be open or shut during a flight, my answer is simple: Generally, it's up to the passenger in the window seat . The choice is theirs to make, unless there's an onboard issue or the crew has instructed otherwise. If I'm in the aisle, and the person in the window seat has the shade down during my flight, I'll be disappointed, but I'll respect their decision. When I'm on the job as a flight attendant, I typically prefer it when my passengers keep the window shades open, too. Generally, I feel safer leaving the shades open When the window shades are open, we can all have a better view of our surroundings. Leanna Coy; Ignatiev/Getty Images Since becoming a flight attendant four years ago, I appreciate having the window shades up even more, especially during takeoff and landing. It gives passengers and crew members more visibility and can improve their situational awareness, which is crucial in the unlikely event of an emergency or evacuation. A passenger might even be able to spot a potential issue before the crew does. If there were a fire on the aircraft's wing, for example, someone in the window seat might be the first person to notice. Many international airlines actually require window shades to remain open during takeoff and landing, and some US airlines encourage the practice, even though it is not mandated by the Federal Aviation Administration. It also gives all of us the chance to catch incredible views I've seen national parks from above and caught glimpses of the northern lights outside of plane windows. Leanna Coy On a less serious note, it makes me kind of sad when passengers don't care about seeing the view out of the window. Even just a few decades ago, being able to look at the world from the sky was a much rarer experience. Many people never get the opportunity to do so, either. I've been on more than 800 flights, but taking in the scenery and sights never gets old. I've gotten aerial views of Canyonlands, Capitol Reef, and Zion National Park on the way to Colorado, and the Grand Canyon en route to Las Vegas. Are you team window shades open or closed? Who do you think should be in charge of the shade's position during a flight? Let us know in the comments — but first, read one former flight attendant's argument for keeping them shut . When I land in New England in the fall , I love seeing the vibrant foliage from above. I've also spotted fireworks from the sky a few times when I've flown on holidays — and once, I even got to see the northern lights from the plane window. I would've missed all of these moments if the window shades were down. When I'm a passenger, my shade almost always stays up. I love catching a good view when I'm working, too. If there's a pretty sunrise or sunset, you might see me sneak over to an empty row of seats to snap a picture. Still, I can admit that — in some cases — it's best to leave the shades shut If I'm in the window seat, I'll be keeping the window shade open to enjoy the views. Leannna Coy To be fair, there are times as a working crew member when it can be nice for passengers to keep the shades lowered. On long flights, I've noticed that people seem calmer when the cabin is dark and are more likely to fall asleep. Selfishly, this makes my job a little easier as a flight attendant. I don't think keeping the window shade open when it's bright out is rude, though. Instead, I recommend that a passenger pack an eye mask if they aren't sitting in a window seat and know they'll have trouble sleeping in the daylight. Ultimately, there's really only one common scenario where I'll ask passengers to close their window shades, and it's when we've landed at a hot destination and are getting ready to deplane. Direct sunlight can heat up an aircraft while it's parked, so shutting the shades helps keep the cabin cooler for the next set of travelers. However, if we're cruising and the cabin's comfortably cool, I'd love for my passengers to keep those shades up. Read the original article on Business Insider

The Ivy League institution first confirmed the attack, later claimed by ShinyHunters, in November 2025, although HIBP gave the first indication about how many people may have been affected by the breach for the first time today. Run by venerable infoseccer Troy Hunt, HIBP ingested all the files and revealed that the types of data stolen from the university extended beyond the personal and donation information it referenced in its initial disclosure. According to HIBP, the 850,000+ figure pertains to unique email addresses found in the data dump. The following data points may not have been collected about each and every individual, but are included in the stolen files: Harvard did not immediately respond to our requests for more information. Its disclosure at the time described the attack as an instance of "phone-based phishing" that targeted its Alumni Affairs and Development department, leading to unauthorized access to its systems. It did not specify the attacker by name, although ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the intrusion on the same day it listed the University of Pennsylvania on its leak site. The group claimed to have stolen more than 1 million records from Harvard and 1.2 million from Penn. In Penn's case, HIBP pegged the total number of affected individuals at around 623,800, based on unique email addresses, although additional data types such as donations, personally identifiable information, religions, and more were affected. ShinyHunters' raid on Harvard systems came around a month after the university probed a separate attack by Cl0p , which at the time was on a tear exploiting a zero-day in Oracle’s E-Business Suite. The impact from that attack was limited to a small amount of data at a small administrative unit, however. Earlier this year, Harvard was also affected by ShinyHunters for the second time in the space of a few months after the cybercriminals attacked Instructure, the EdTech vendor behind learning platform Canvas. events.title: Apple restricts dating apps and AI companions to users 18 and up
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Apple is adjusting its App Store policies to make it more difficult for minors to use online dating apps or AI companions that engage in “sexual or romantic content,” the tech giant shared in an announcement to developers on Monday. The new rules follow other changes the company has made to better protect minors, which include the rollout of its age assurance technology globally and more parental controls and child safety features . While most major dating services typically restrict their platform to adults, Apple’s new policy will require all apps offering dating or romantic relationship features to carry an 18+ rating. Starting November 16, developers will be required to include new content descriptors to ensure their app’s age ratings reflect its features, the company said. It’s perhaps more interesting how this rule could impact AI companion apps, or those where such functionality is one of many features. Often targeted at younger people, Character.AI, Replika, and other AI apps let people create AI companions, including friends, lovers, boyfriends and girlfriends, and other fantasy characters. xAI last year also launched 3D animated AI companions that allowed users to unlock NSFW capabilities . As of last summer, top AI companion apps across the Apple App Store and Google Play had been downloaded 220 million times globally . In addition to “dating and relationships,” apps will also need to indicate if they are sharing the real-world locations of a user with another person or group as part of their functionality. Any app doing so raises obvious privacy concerns, especially if the user wasn’t aware that their location was being shared. The company noted that in Brazil, apps that provide location-sharing features for families can request an official rating from the government’s Ministry of Justice and Public Security (MJSP/Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública), instead of being required to list them with the A16 rating, as the local law requires. events.title: Prediction markets have a lot riding on the blue wave
events.summary: Prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket officially don't care which side of a bet wins. There is no "house." They get their cut either way. It's a business model that's attracted billions of VC dollars. Yes, but: Kalshi and Polymarket should be pulling hard for Democrats in today's midterm elections. Even if that feels counterintuitive. Catch up quick: Prediction markets burst into the public consciousness two years ago, when their users correctly "picked" Donald Trump to beat Kamala Harris. It bestowed credibility at a time when public trust in traditional polling had cratered. Fast forward: More recently, however, they had electoral misses in Brazil and Israel. Three would be a trend. Both platforms currently have markets on Democrats sweeping Congress, with "yes" at around 75%. If that's how today plays out, it would further cement prediction market legitimacy. A Republican win in either chamber, however, would dump them into the same pot as pollsters — even if 75% probability includes a sizable improbability. Zoom in: Democrats are often more hostile to prediction markets than are Republicans, but companies like Kalshi and Polymarket don't have too much to fear from a Democrat-controlled Congress. Yes, there would probably be an uncomfortable hearing or two. But neither chamber would have veto-proof majorities, and the Trump administration has been very sympathetic to the industry. The real constraints, if any, are more likely to come via the Supreme Court. The bottom line: Political predictions generate much less revenue for Kalshi and Polymarket than do sports predictions, but they have a much longer tail.

events.title: Binance says fake job interviews and internal AI tool used in $6.3bn heist
events.summary: Cryptocurrency platform Binance has said fake job interviews and an internal artificial intelligence tool were used for the massive $6.3 billion breach it reported last week. The culprit leveraged the compromised computer of one of its engineers and used an AI tool to gain control of the wallets of two other engineers, Binance said in a post on Tuesday. That was “used as a springboard” on October 20, as “the attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise and an advanced transaction-authorisation method”, the company said. Preparations for the theft stretched as far back as June, traced to a supply chain attack in which an engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation to install a popular AI coding tool after finding it on a search engine, Binance said. Homebrew is software that allows users to easily install apps, particularly for Apple's macOS and Linux. Binance did not identify the AI coding tool and the search engine that were used. https://t.co/sU9dUqLQDH — Binance (@binance) November 3, 2026 By September, Binance had determined a social engineering attack – one in which someone is deceived into revealing sensitive information – hit one of its engineers through a legitimate job-hunting platform, with someone posing as a project director. It culminated in instructing the engineer to download an “assignment” that contained a malicious code, Binance said. Binance also said it has taken measures to protect its systems, including rebuilding the affected wallet system in a new environment and internal AI tools and access controls. It has also replaced affected devices and decommissioned credentials and tokens related to the affected engineers, and continues to work with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence companies and industry partners to trace and freeze the affected assets. Further action includes independent cybersecurity reviews with independent third-party experts to study the incident, expanded investment in AI security and prevention, and working on a security research fund and other industry initiatives to protect against such attacks. “We will continue to strengthen our measures as the investigation progresses,” Binance said. “There are a number of security measures we have implemented and are implementing that will remain private to prevent malicious actors from compromising our security.” Binance lost an estimated $6.3 billion to hackers last Friday, in what has been described as the single biggest theft of crypto on record, exceeding the $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit in February 2025 . The company, founded by Changpeng Zhao, previously said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than passing the losses on to customers. It resumed withdrawals on Sunday as investigations were under way. The FBI on Saturday attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit. Members of the group were observed by law enforcement converting the stolen assets into ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected further laundering through related technology.

events.title: Energy companies brace for new Iran tension as cost of resilience mounts
events.summary: Energy companies operating in the Middle East are preparing for another potential escalation in the Iran war, with executives warning that keeping businesses running through conflict comes at a growing financial cost. Speaking to The National at Adipec in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, industry leaders said they are now better prepared after months of adapting to disrupted supply chains. They have stockpiled critical supplies, shifted transportation routes and reduced workforces to withstand further disruption. Several executives said that resilience comes at a cost. Their comments came after the US struck Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday night, targeting a missile launcher after an American drone was brought down near the Strait of Hormuz. The attack raised new concerns about renewed regional fighting , as Americans headed to the polls for midterm elections that could influence Washington's next moves in the conflict. For energy companies, the question is no longer simply whether another escalation will occur but how long they can sustain operations if it does. Sherif Foda, chief executive of energy services firm NESR, said his company had continued operating throughout the conflict by relying on domestic employees and maintaining sufficient supplies to withstand prolonged logistical disruption. “We will be able to continue to operate as long as our clients are operating,” he said. “We are not going to evacuate. We are staying.” Mr Foda said the company had adopted a 30, 60 and 90-day contingency strategy, stockpiling spare parts, chemicals and other essential materials inside countries where it operates. The strategy allowed NESR to maintain operations even when international supply routes became unreliable. “I am insisting on having a local workforce,” Mr Foda said. “You have to really look at the localisation as a must, not as a nice to have.” Cost of survival While some businesses have maintained operations, others have been forced to make difficult financial decisions. Youssou Jules Diop, executive director of Senegalese engineering and procurement company Helix SEN, said the conflict had already forced his company to cut 30 per cent of its management team. The company maintains its treasury, board and key decision-making functions in the UAE, which Mr Diop described as an important hub for African businesses. “The ABC of business is trust and confidence,” he said. The financial pressure extends across the energy industry, particularly for companies dependent on maritime transport through the Strait of Hormuz . Bruno Placha, a senior quality and regulatory professional, said the initial disruption had severely affected operations as vessels stopped entering the region. “If we don't have vessels, we don't have work,” he said. The threat to shipping remains acute. The International Maritime Organisation said on Monday that at least 125 vessels had been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, including 34 in October, the highest monthly figure so far. Companies have since adapted by using alternative ports and moving more materials by road than by sea, Mr Placha said. The adjustments have also involved workforce reductions and a greater focus on longer-term projects, allowing businesses to operate with less dependence on regular shipping movements. George Alexopoulos, deputy chief executive of Greece's HELLENiQ Energy Holdings, said maintaining alternative supply arrangements had become essential, even when they were expensive. After the conflict disrupted crude shipments from Basra in Iraq, the company turned to the North Sea, the US and West Africa for replacement supplies. “Optionality has a cost and especially at times of crisis,” Mr Alexopoulos said. He cited tanker charter rates on Gulf routes to China reaching $1 million a day as an example of the extraordinary expenses companies face. “What is the alternative? Shut down your operations, so you have to go on.” His comments echo concerns raised at Adipec on Monday , when Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and Adnoc managing director and group chief executive, Dr Sultan Al Jaber, called for stronger energy infrastructure and diversified supply routes as shipping costs surged. Prepared but vulnerable Despite the industry adjustments, executives warn that another prolonged escalation could expose vulnerabilities that cannot be resolved quickly. Robin Mills, chief executive of Qamar Energy, said companies had made significant progress in rerouting logistics, expanding port capacity, and using road and rail networks. But it is not enough for long-term resilience. “There's a limit to what can be done in the space of eight months,” he said. Major infrastructure projects can take years to complete, leaving energy facilities and shipping routes exposed to further attacks. Nevertheless, he said energy companies remained active, with growing demand for maintenance, repairs, security and infrastructure development. That resilience comes as the UAE continues to emphasise the importance of avoiding another round of conflict, while remaining prepared for further escalation . For Mr Alexopoulos, even an immediate end to hostilities would not bring an immediate return to normal business conditions. He warned that damaged infrastructure, refinery disruptions and shipping shortages could take several weeks to begin normalising, while a full recovery could take years. His biggest lesson for companies navigating an increasingly unpredictable energy market was straightforward. “Keep options. Develop and maintain options. Options have a cost, but in this environment you have to pay the 'option premium' in order to be able to handle this and the next and the next crisis,” he said. Salma Arafa contributed to this report.

events.title: Guaranteed pension income ‘resurrected’ for 17m private sector workers
events.summary: Ministers propose new guided retirement scheme to help give savers protection for life Millions of private sector workers will be offered a guaranteed pension income for life under new rules designed to help them get the most out of their retirement savings. Over the past 30 years, the majority of final salary pension schemes offering a set payout for life have closed. Workers have instead saved into a scheme and arrived at retirement with a pot of money they have to decide what to do with. George Osborne scrapped the obligation to buy an annuity – a product offering an income for life – leaving many savers wondering how to manage their money. Proposals outlined by the government on Tuesday will bring in a default option for retirees, designed to ensure that the money they have saved provides them with an income for life. Under the guided retirement regime, people will still be able to withdraw their money or invest it elsewhere, but they will also be offered a simple option, with payments often linked to inflation. The government said the changes would affect 17 million workers who are investing in a pension. Savings have been boosted by an auto-enrolment system – introduced in October 2012 – that means employers have to put every worker aged 22 and over into a pension scheme and make a company contribution. Workers can opt out, but nine in 10 eligible private sector workers are now making contributions into a retirement fund, up from four in 10 in 2012. However, some retirees have struggled to know what to do with their money. The government says nearly half the pension pots accessed for the first time in 2025-26 were emptied out. This has left people at risk of outliving their savings and reliant on their state pension. The pensions minister, Torsten Bell, said: “Private sector workers deserve a much better deal when it comes to pensions. They are doing the right thing and saving for retirement, but when they get there too many are left without a genuine pension. “We are resurrecting proper pensions for private sector workers, guaranteeing them the option of an income that lasts throughout retirement and in many cases protection against the rising cost of living – things public sector workers take for granted.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Pensions experts were supportive of the move but said retirees should still have the opportunity to choose how to use their funds. Yvonne Braun, director of long-term savings policy at the Association of British Insurers, said the proposed scheme had the potential to simplify decisions about accessing pensions but it was important “that people continue to have the freedom to make their own decisions”. Although annuities are no longer a compulsory part of retirement planning, sales have been buoyant thanks to rising returns for investors, and changes to inheritance tax rules that have encouraged wealthy people to move money out of their pensions.

events.title: Meet the highest-paid White House staffers in 2026 — and see how much they make
events.summary: Stephen Miller, Susie Wiles, and Tom Homan are among the highest-paid staffers at the White House. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images/Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images/Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images The White House salary report shows its top-paid staffers earn up to $197,200 annually. Senior advisors, legal counsel, and policy directors are among the highest earners listed. Government salaries can fall below private sector pay but far exceed the national average income. Working at the White House might be one of the most exclusive and prestigious jobs in the US, but you'd be surprised by how much some of the people around the president make each year. For starters, having the top job — that is, being the president of the US — brings in a salary of $400,000, which some independently wealthy presidents, such as John F. Kennedy, Herbert Hoover, and Donald Trump, have chosen to donate instead. While the figure is significantly higher than what the average American makes — $72,800 in 2025, according to the Social Security Administration — it's also less than you would need to be in the top 1% of earners across all US states. In 2025, the top 1% of earners in Maryland and Virginia, which border the District of Columbia, earn $677,543 and $701,792 annually, respectively. Government salaries often lag behind what professionals earn in the private sector, since serving the public isn't as lucrative as maximizing shareholder value. Still, to say that those working at the White House are underpaid would be an overstatement. On July 1, the White House shared with Congress the salaries of all employees inside the president's executive office, including aides, advisors, and staff leaders, as it is legally required to. Some of the highest-compensated workers around the president include policy advisors and legal counsel, while others are responsible for the president's communications and personnel management. Lower-paid roles include research assistants and press assistants. Other notable names, like Marco Rubio and David Sacks, declared a $0 salary from the office of the president, either forgoing their salary or receiving compensation from other branches of government. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. See the 34 people who get paid the most inside the White House, after the president himself. events.title: Nordic nations refuse to face Russia in ice hockey World Championship
events.summary: Denmark, Norway and Sweden join Finland in refusing to face Russia in 2027 World Championships in Germany next May. Denmark, Norway and Sweden say they would refuse to play against Russia in the ice hockey world championships next year because of its war in Ukraine, a day after neighbouring Finland said it would also refuse. “The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association has decided that, based on the current situation and available information, Norway will not compete against Russia during the World Championships in 2027,” the association said in a statement on Tuesday. list 1 of 4 Ice hockey coach admits to faking COVID certificate to enter China Olympics list 2 of 4 Olympic athletes to get cash grants from new $100m fund created by IOC list 3 of 4 NHL superstar Ovechkin ‘was asked’ to film Putin ad, team says list 4 of 4 Russia back in ice hockey world championships after sport court ruling “Our view that Russia should be banned from all international championships for the duration of the war in Ukraine remains firm.” It said Norway would play its other group matches as planned. The Nordic countries have been strong supporters of Ukraine since the start of the war. Russia has been banned from International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) competitions since President Vladimir Putin launched the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30 that Russia must be admitted to the world championships following an appeal from the Russian Ice Hockey Federation. The 2027 world championships are due to be held in Germany in May, but the draw and scheduling for the tournament have already taken place, without Russia included. The IIHF has voiced its opposition to the CAS decision and said it creates “significant practical implications”. The head of the Danish ice hockey federation, Henrik Bach Nielsen, echoed that stance in comments to news agency Ritzau. “For the sake of the integrity of ice hockey as a sport, we cannot see ourselves playing against Russia as things stand now,” he said. “It will end in chaos if we do.” Sweden’s governing body for the sport said the same. “The Swedish position is crystal clear,” it said in a statement. “It has been and still is inconceivable for Russia to take part in international ice hockey as long as the war in Ukraine continues. “Swedish national teams will not play matches against Russian national teams.” On Monday, Finland’s ice hockey federation said it would use “all possible means to prevent Russia from being reinstated at the world championships”. “We are currently trying to rally as many countries as possible into a common front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia in the current situation,” said the federation’s president, Heikki Hietanen. The Finnish city of Turku also said on Monday it would withdraw from hosting the junior ice hockey world championships in 2027-2028 if Russia were allowed to participate.

events.title: Asda hires ex-Morrisons boss in bid to grow firm
events.summary: Asda headquarters are based in Leeds city centre Asda has appointed a former Morrisons boss as chief executive to help lead revival efforts at the supermarket chain. Asda, which is based in Leeds, said David Potts would take on the role with immediate effect, while current boss Allan Leighton would become non-executive chairman, two years after returning to lead the supermarket chain. Potts led Morrisons from its Bradford headquarters for eight years until 2023, overseeing a turnaround during which the supermarket chain was bought by US private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice. Potts said Asda had "made good progress but significant opportunities remain" to reinvigorate sales, with a focus on keeping prices low for shoppers. "By making improvements to the shopping trip every week, which customers can experience and feel in their pockets, we will revitalise the business and bring benefits for all our stakeholders, including our 116,296 very hard-working colleagues," he said. Before joining Morrisons, Potts was chief executive of Tesco's Irish business, its UK arm and its Asian operation. David Potts led Morrisons for eight years until 2023 According to Asda, Leighton had planned to step aside from the day-to-day running of the group, after he returned in 2024, more than two decades after serving as chief executive. "Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth," said Leighton. "David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him." Last year, issues with an IT upgrade hit product availability at the supermarket and dented sales, impacting its bottom line. But in August, it reported sales had returned to growth for the current quarter for the first time in two years.
