events.title: Mining giant joins fight to stop killer toad march across Australia
events.summary: Rio Tinto is ploughing millions of dollars into stopping the poisonous cane toad reaching the Pilbara region of western Australia, where the mining giant has a vast iron ore operation. The firm, alongside Curtin University in Perth and others, will spend A$28m (£14.5m) building a "toad containment zone" to prevent the pest travelling south. While the cane toad is not a direct threat to Rio Tinto's business, it produces toxins lethal to native wildlife and poses a threat to Pilbara's ecosystem. Rio Tinto has previously faced criticism for destroying two sacred Aboriginal rock shelters in Pilbara which sat above tonnes of iron ore. The decision cost the former chief executive his job, provoked a widespread backlash and saw Rio Tinto commit to rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities. Commenting on the proposed containment zone, Roberta Hunter, a ranger in Australia's Nyangumarta Warrarn Indigenous Protected Area, said: "Cane toads destroy the water and animals. "When toads come close to our country, we want to be there to stop them because we don't want the country to be destroyed." The plan is to cut off the toad's water supply by building a barrier across 7,500 sq km (2,895 sq m) of land between the Great Sandy Desert and the Indian Ocean. In drier months, the cane toad needs water every few days to survive. If there are no natural water sources, the toad relies on artificial water points normally used for cattle and irrigation. The funding will be used to stop the toad accessing dams, storage tanks or other ground-level water sources. The five-year project will begin in 2027. A number of native species are at risk if the toad gets into Pilbara. These include the northern quoll, whose numbers have been decreasing, the goanna lizard and the ghost bat. The toads were introduced into Australia in 1935 to control beetles within the sugar cane industry. The northern quoll is at risk from the cane toad in Australia Since then, they have been on a slow march west across the country's northern landscape, according to the Australian government, travelling between 40 km and 60 km a year. There are no predators or diseases that control the toads, which defend themselves using poison. Ben Phillips, a professor at Curtin University, said the toads would reach Pilbara within two decades without action. He said: "The toad containment zone is a once in a lifetime opportunity to stop one of the world's worst invasive species in its tracks and protect the region's unique wildlife." events.title: Democrats run more anti-tech ads amid AI boom
events.summary: Democrats running in more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races aired anti-tech or anti-data center ads this cycle, an increase over just two Democratic ads mentioning those topics from 2020 to 2024, according to a new analysis from the Tech Oversight Project shared first with Semafor. Democrats used these messages four times as often as Republicans, the report says. The ads appeared in nearly every battleground state, as well as three toss-up governor races. Ads cited by the report blame AI for price-gouging, harm to children, and even healthcare denial, while data center-focused ads press Republicans on water use and threats to farmland. “Democrats have potentially found a winning message. Now is the time to step on the gas and reject a return to business as usual in Washington, Silicon Valley fundraisers, and light-touch approaches,” the group, which is mostly funded by eBay founder Pierre Omidyar’s philanthropic network, writes in the report. “It would be a betrayal of their campaign promises, and not only would it squander our victory –— it would create resentment in the base that will cost us in 2028,” it continues. Groups that are pushing for stricter rules on AI and social media, like the Tech Oversight Project and other anti-AI organizations, see a huge opportunity to push Democrats in Congress and 2028 presidential contenders further on AI safety and data centers. They argue conservatives have already lost credibility on it thanks to President Donald Trump’s cozy relationships with billionaire tech executives.

events.title: Pokémon bakeoff reveals best JavaScript frameworks for AI
events.summary: Most JavaScript programmers default to their ride-or-die frameworks, but such loyalties can hinder them when they task AI agents with doing their dirty work. Human-friendly tools aren't necessarily the most effective ones for the model-powered minions. "One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based,” wrote Seattle-based Nolan Lawson , currently a developer at AI security firm Socket . That’s an understatement; the JavaScript wars have been well underway for over a decade now, with each new framework promising to cure the woes of last year’s release. Not wanting these vibey biases to seep into the realm of AI, Lawson created a benchmark to compare how different JavaScript frameworks perform under the same agentic model. He subsequently ran the test on 12 JavaScript frameworks, publishing the results in a post that compared each framework in terms of build cost, maintainability, and end-user performance of their agent-built apps. The results are illuminating. In general, agents tend to work more efficiently with server-centric frameworks than with client-heavy “Single-Page App” (SPA) frameworks (which should tickle for React haters ). But the biggest take-away should be less controversial: agents best utilize those frameworks that favor convention, API stability, and concision. How to compare JavaScript frameworks For the experiment, Lawson wrote a set of instructions for a Claude Code agent to build a basic Pokémon web application using the PokéAPI . The model used the identical setup on 12 different frameworks and JavaScript stacks: Angular, Astro, Gracile with Lit, Hono with htmx, vanilla JavaScript with Vite, Next.js, Nuxt, Qwik, React Router, TanStack Start, SolidStart, and SvelteKit. Lawson evaluated each stack across five independent sandbox runs; the repeated iterations smoothed the variance in the model’s performance. To verify the resulting app met the specs, Lawson deployed a custom automated test suite that queried the browser's accessibility tree to ensure interactive elements like buttons and inputs weren’t faked – a shortcut LLMs occasionally take. Lawson also used Google Lighthouse to measure transfer size and runtime performance. If the frameworks specified official MCP servers, Claude plug-ins, and agent-skill files, Lawson provided them as resources to the agents (though they weren’t always consulted). Otherwise, he did not mandate any specific architecture for rendering the app. Comparing 12 JavaScript frameworks The differences between the most cost-effective builds and the most expensive ones are substantial, to say the least, with the best lapping the efforts of the stragglers. If you want to build a Pokéworld cost-effectively, the strongest bet is on Hono paired with htmx . This tag-team of technologies had the most economical run, with a median cost of $2.67 per Pokéapp. Perhaps this is not surprising, given that the duo runs entirely on the server, thereby eliminating a whole set of checks required to synchronize an architectural split between client and server. It also helped minimize the code, which resulted in fewer output tokens being consumed. Nearly as effective was Astro ($2.76). Like Hono/htmx, Astro does everything server-side. Server-side data crunching also helped Astro achieve the fastest median time to build and test the app, at 8.2 minutes. Nuxt ($2.82) was the most cost-effective option for an SPA-like approach. Nuxt renders code on the server that gets hydrated on the client. Nuxt is actually built on Vue.js , but is “opinionated,” eliminating a lot of boilerplate that the agent must write. Nuxt also handles data transfer and file routing internally, which is more code not to fuss over. It’s also worth noting Nuxt consumed the fewest tokens of the bunch (3.85 million), though that did not make it the cheapest, given how Claude charges different rates for input and output tokens. Nuxt produced the app in 1,415 lines of code, which is second only to Hono/htmx's 1,370 lines. Overall, these top three frameworks were within the margin of error of each other, which means any one of them could have gotten the top score depending on what kind of day the LLM was having. Some of the more traditional frameworks lumbered way behind, however. A SvelteKit -based app cost $4.28 to generate, with the agent repeatedly going back to the SvelteKit documentation to get a better handle on how the recently-updated Svelte works. Angular was the most expensive way for an agent to build an app, costing $4.97 while taking 17.2 minutes and chewing up 9.76 million tokens (with the agent failing to even finish a working app in two of its five attempts). All the resulting apps aced the Lighthouse accessibility and performance tests. It’s a pretty simple app to render, Lawson acknowledged. Astro’s app had the fastest loading time (called Largest Contentful Paint or LCP) of 810 ms, while the slowest frameworks in the cohort – Next.js (2,090 ms) and TanStack Start (2,028 ms) – took more than twice as long to deliver the goods, perhaps because of all the JavaScript they shipped to the client. Gold stars for all Lawson hopes this work will set the stage for applying a bit more rigor in selecting frameworks for AI jobs, now that developers won’t have to do the actual heavy lifting themselves. But a few developers on Hacker News pointed out AI efficiency isn’t the only factor to consider. There’s the human component of maintaining the framework as well. “After a decade of React, I'm not going to go learn htmx or any other marginally better same-shaped tool for a new project, especially when it'd degrade my ability to review and debug another actor's work product,” one wrote. After all, the frameworks themselves might evolve with the help of AI, minimizing their differences over time. “Besides a rewrite to another framework using AI, another option is to modernize the framework with AI instead,” someone else noted. ®

events.title: Belarus hosts trans-Atlantic security group's chief, part of efforts to improve ties with the West
events.summary: The chief of a top trans-Atlantic security grouping has visited Belarus for the first time in years TALLINN, Estonia -- The chief of a top trans-Atlantic security grouping visited Belarus on Tuesday for the first time in seven years as the country’s authoritarian President Alexander Lukashenko has sought to normalize ties with the West. Feridun Sinirlioglu, the secretary-general of the Vienna-based Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, visited Belarus to attend an international security conference and met with Lukashenko. Sinirlioglu’s visit to Belarus marks the first such trip by the OSCE’s chief since 2019. Belarus, a close ally of Russia , has faced Western isolation and sanctions for years. Speaking at the start of his meeting with Lukashenko, Sinirlioglu noted Belarus’ role in helping organize exchanges of prisoners of war between Russia and Ukraine. The Belarusian leader said that he “highly appreciates” Sinirlioglu's visit, but he also criticized the OSCE for what he described as its purported pro-Western stance and unfair criticism of elections in Belarus and Russia. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov attended the conference along with diplomats from ex-Soviet nations, China and other countries. Lukashenko has governed the nation of 9.5 million with an iron fist for more than three decades, and Belarus has been sanctioned repeatedly by Western countries — both for its crackdown on human rights and for allowing Moscow to use its territory in the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022. Belarusian opposition leader-in-exile Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said that “for Lukashenko, a meeting with the OSCE's secretary-general is already a significant and entirely undeserved political reward.” Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Parents and 2 young children among victims of Learjet crash in Florida, family says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say “High-level visits and meetings with Lukashenko — if they don't lead to concrete changes — only strengthen his regime and foster a sense of impunity,” Tsikhanouskaya told The Associated Press. “Engagement must yield real results — the release of political prisoners, an end to repression, and a withdrawal of support for the Russian aggression — rather than serving as a tool to grant the regime international legitimacy,” she said. Lukashenko’s rule was challenged after a 2020 presidential election that kept him in power, when tens of thousands of people poured into the streets to protest a vote widely seen as rigged. In an ensuing crackdown, tens of thousands of people were detained, with many beaten by police. Prominent opposition figures either fled the country or were imprisoned. Since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House for his second term, Lukashenko has released hundreds of political prisoners in a series of U.S.-mediated deals that also lifted some U.S. sanctions, part of his efforts to overcome isolation and normalize ties with the West. As part of a deal in March that Washington helped broker, Lukashenko ordered the release of 250 political prisoners, while the U.S. agreed to lift sanctions on two Belarusian state banks and the country’s Finance Ministry, and to remove the top Belarusian potash producers from a sanctions list. And in September, Belarusian authorities released 25 prisoners in exchange for the lifting of U.S. sanctions against two Belarusian companies. The Belarusian opposition has welcomed the prisoners’ release, but noted that many others remain in custody. Belarus still has 887 political prisoners, according to the Viasna human rights center. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Medact flags 29 disputed entries as ministers weigh £330M deal's future NHS quango warns of risk to GP patient data after website vendor collapse 4 days ago British intelligence agency misplaced 'thousands' of storage devices, years later still can't say how many 4 days ago Day 2 of canceled classes at University of New Mexico after Health Sciences Center cyberattack 7 days ago UK ministers had plenty of time for AI datacenter bosses, but none for environmental groups 7 days ago UK Biobank back online soon, months after someone tried to sell 500k people's data on Alibaba 8 days ago Twenty-nine NHS trusts listed as benefiting from Palantir's Federated Data Platform (FDP) said in Freedom of Information responses that they were not using it, according to health worker campaign group Medact. That represents about 21 percent of the 137 trusts NHS England lists as "realising benefits" as ministers weigh whether to continue the contract. The government must decide in December whether to continue the £330 million agreement with a Palantir-led consortium supplying the platform. Medact, which is campaigning against the deal, collected the responses to scrutinize the government's case for retaining Palantir. The relationship between the US tech biz and the NHS began during the pandemic with contracts worth £60 million awarded without competition. NHS England awarded the FDP contract in November 2023. It says the platform brings together operational data held in separate systems to help staff work more efficiently. NHS England's September figures list 142 trusts as live on the platform - 137 of which it claims are benefiting. Among the disputed entries, NHS England cites University Hospitals of North Midlands NHS Trust as receiving benefits from the platform, but in response to an FoI request in July, the trust said: "FDP is not live. We do not intend to roll it out in the future. A variety of factors prevent roll out, but primarily it does not appear to provide functionality over and above what we have already." Meanwhile, a response from Nottingham University Hospitals said "no implementation timeline has been agreed," according to The Guardian . The Register asked NHS England to explain the discrepancy. An NHS spokesperson said: "The NHS Federated Data Platform is universally available for all NHS trusts and integrated care boards across England, with local NHS organisations able to select individual tools depending on their needs. "137 NHS trusts have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform – helping staff join-up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently." Palantir maintains its software is playing an important role in improving patient care and helping to deliver 100,000 additional operations, a 12 percent reduction in discharge delays and the removal of 675,000 patients from waiting lists. In July, the UK's statistical regulator told NHS England to ensure greater accuracy in quoting figures following a row over data used to promote the purported benefits of the FDP. Dame Chi Onwurah, the chair of the House of Commons Science and Technology Committee, has given the government until today to clarify its response to questions over whether NHS England has any exit plans should it decide to end the Palantir contract in February. James Frith, a junior minister in the Department of Health and Social Care, wrote [PDF] to the Committee in October explaining that the contract has "measures built in to facilitate exit and transition including clear intellectual property rights in NHS build products or components." He continued: "Publishing more detailed information on the Exit Plan would, or would be likely to, prejudice commercial interests and NHS England's ability to secure best value for taxpayers in future commercial activity." Onwurah replied : "I understand that you will not publish the exit plan, but will you confirm if one has been prepared?" The Register asked Palantir to comment.

events.title: The TechCrunch Founder Summit agenda is only half the reason to be in Boston on Nov. 4
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. You can learn a lot from a great founder session. But sometimes the conversation that changes what you do next happens five minutes after it ends. And with the event happening tomorrow, there is another reason to make sure you are in the room: the format is designed to help founders learn in different ways throughout the day. On November 4, TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 brings founders and investors together at SoWa Power Station in Boston for one day of practical learning, candid conversations, live pitching, smaller roundtables, and networking. Register now to save up to $100 on your pass , plus get a second for free. Or save up to 30% on group bundles . Start with the Build Stage: practical lessons for building what comes next The Build Stage focuses on the decisions founders make while they are still shaping, testing, and growing the business. These sessions get into the mechanics behind building a company, from distribution and fundraising to team building and pitching. Hunter Worland of NEA opens the conversation on why distribution can become a startup’s next competitive advantage, especially when strong technology alone is not enough to win customers. Kristen Craft of Fidelity Private Shares brings a current view of fundraising trends, helping founders understand how the capital environment is shifting and what that means for the way they approach their next raise. The stage also gets tactical about building high-performing teams and sharpening the story you tell investors, customers, and potential hires. Dave Balter of True Ventures and Edisyl takes on a deceptively simple question: Does your pitch earn the next conversation? The value of the Build Stage is straightforward: these are lessons founders can take back to their companies immediately. Use the Impact Stage to think about what happens after something starts working If the Build Stage is about creating momentum, the Impact Stage is about what happens once that momentum becomes real. This is where founders can step back and think about bigger decisions around product-market fit, scaling, enterprise relationships, leadership, and long-term growth. Steve Fredette , president, co-founder, and director of Toast , brings the perspective of building and scaling one of Boston’s most recognizable startup success stories. Rudina Seseri , founder and managing partner of Glasswing Ventures , explores the tension every founder eventually faces: when to scale and when hitting the brakes may actually protect the business. Kent Bennett of Bessemer Venture Partners tackles product-market fit before scale, helping founders think more critically about whether the signals they are seeing truly justify the next phase of growth. Chase Garbarino , CEO and co-founder of HqO , brings the conversation home with the Boston Founder Playbook and a perspective on building ambitious companies outside the Bay Area. The Impact Stage is valuable because it creates space for founders to get out of the weeds for a moment and ask whether they are scaling the right things, in the right way, at the right time. Main-stage sessions can give you perspective. Roundtables give you room to get specific. Founder Summit’s smaller roundtables are built around highly focused problems that many founders are actively solving right now, from entering difficult verticals and building enterprise trust to creating lean teams and opening doors with major customers. Chirag Shah of Define Ventures digs into what happens when your first vertical is also one of the hardest to enter. A technical session with Shishir Tewari of Procore Technologies moves the AI conversation from broad hype to the practical challenge of reducing hallucinations with better enterprise context. Merve Kitapci of ADIN.AI gets highly specific about enterprise selling and what it takes to land major global customers before Series A. Andy Tang of Draper Associates opens a different kind of founder conversation: what if you are building something the market does not even have a name for yet? Linden Tibbets of IFTTT explores how AI may change the assumptions founders make about team size, productivity, and what a smaller company can realistically accomplish. The value here is participation. Instead of simply hearing how someone else approached a problem, founders can bring their own questions, compare experiences with the people around the table, and leave with ideas that are much closer to their actual business. Watch the startup pitch advice get tested live Founder Summit also gives attendees the chance to see what happens when founders put their stories in front of investors in real time. During So You Think You Can Pitch?, founders make their cases in front of investors, including Dave Balter , Chirag Shah , and Simran Suri of Maveron.

events.title: I made marinara sauces using 4 celebrity chefs' recipes, and the best came from Ina Garten
events.summary: I compared sauce recipes from four different celebrity chefs, including Tyler Florence, Giada De Laurentiis, and Ina Garten, to find a solid, go-to marinara that also tastes delicious. Paige Bennett I made marinara sauces using recipes from celebrity chefs like Alex Guarnaschelli and Ina Garten. Giada De Laurentiis' sauce had a celery aftertaste I didn't like and took the longest to make. I loved the sweet, rich flavor and inclusion of red wine in Garten's marinara recipe. I love a simple bowl of pasta with a classic marinara, especially when the sauce is homemade. Homemade marinara is easy enough to make on a busy weeknight and uses ingredients already in my pantry, like tomatoes (often canned), onions, garlic, olive oil, and herbs. In search of a sauce recipe I want to make and eat on repeat, I tried recipes from celebrity chefs Alex Guarnaschelli, Tyler Florence, Giada De Laurentiis , and Ina Garten. Here's how it went. Florence's simple marinara uses basic pantry staples. Paige Bennett Florence's marinara-sauce recipe , which I found on the Food Network website, takes only about 30 minutes to make and relies on dried herbs for flavor. His recipe called for canned crushed tomatoes, one onion, minced garlic, sugar, salt, pepper, dried basil, dried oregano, and a bay leaf. The recipe required very little prep. Paige Bennett I already had all of these things in my pantry, which meant I was off to a great start. Plus, this recipe didn't require much chopping, aside from about three cloves of garlic and one onion. Once those were chopped, I sautéed the onion and minced garlic in oil for about five minutes, then added the remaining ingredients. The sauce was done pretty quickly. Paige Bennett While the tomatoes and spices simmered together, I boiled some pasta. I made sure to occasionally stir my sauce so it wouldn't stick to the pan. In about 35 minutes, I had homemade marinara and pasta ready to go. The flavor was good, but I'd prefer fresh herbs over dried ones. Paige Bennett This marinara was chunkier thanks to the tomato and onion. I liked the slightly sweet and herby flavors, but if I made this again, I'd follow Guarnaschelli's lead and stir in some fresh basil at the end. Though it would increase the cooking time, I would also sauté the onions a little bit longer than five minutes since they were chewier than I wanted. Still, this pantry-staple marinara is a great option for an impressive weeknight dinner — especially if you haven't had time to pick up groceries. Guarnaschelli's sauce uses grated carrots for a touch of sweetness. Paige Bennett I found Guarnaschelli's sauce recipe on the Food Network website. It's a recipe the chef got from her mother, cookbook editor and publisher Maria Guarnaschelli. The ingredients are simple and include whole, peeled canned tomatoes, grated carrots, extra-virgin olive oil, sugar, red-pepper flakes, yellow onions, garlic, basil, and freshly grated Parmesan. This sauce contains a decent amount of produce. Paige Bennett I began by chopping two large onions, slicing the 10 cloves of peeled garlic into thin slices, and peeling and grating three carrots. I sautéed the onion, garlic, sugar, salt, and red-pepper flakes until the onion was translucent, and then added the grated carrots. By this point, the caramelized onions and carrots smelled amazing. The prep was minimal, and most of the recipe just required watching and stirring. Paige Bennett I was worried adding the whole, peeled tomatoes would create a weird texture (the other recipes used crushed tomatoes), but they broke down nicely as the sauce simmered. From there, making the sauce was mostly a game of watching the pot, stirring occasionally throughout 45 minutes. Per Guarnaschelli's instructions, I poured in a little water whenever the sauce started to look dry. I finished the sauce with a handful of fresh basil and freshly grated Parm. Guarnaschelli's marinara had a nice balance of flavors. Paige Bennett The flavor was well-balanced, with a kick from the red-pepper flakes, sweetness from the carrots and sugar, and savoriness from the onions and garlic. The basil also tasted fresh, and it all worked well with the sprinkling of salty Parmesan. This marinara is definitely worth making again, but next time, I'd mince the garlic instead of thinly slicing it since I didn't love that texture. De Laurentiis relies on several fresh ingredients for her marinara. Paige Bennett I also found De Laurentiis' recipe for marinara sauce on the Food Network website. I liked that it incorporates fresh ingredients like onion, garlic, carrot, and celery. Though I'm not a big fan of celery, I figured it would be delicious when sautéed with the other aromatics. The recipe also required crushed tomatoes, extra-virgin olive oil, salt, black pepper, and a dried bay leaf. My grocery store didn't carry any 32-ounce cans of crushed tomatoes, as requested in the recipe, so I picked up a 28-ounce can and supplemented it with extras from another can. I made sure to cook all the vegetables until they were soft. Paige Bennett I started by finely chopping all the fresh ingredients, then sautéed the diced onion with my single clove of garlic, minced. Then I added the finely chopped carrots and celery, along with salt and pepper, and cooked until all the vegetables had softened. De Laurentiis' recipe required the longest cooking time. Paige Bennett After a 20-minute sautéeing process, I added the canned tomatoes and dried bay leaf. Once everything was stirred, I let the marinara simmer for an hour to meld the flavors. I made sure to occasionally mix it so nothing would stick to my pot. Although it was an easy, mostly hands-off recipe , this marinara took me the longest to make. For me, the celery flavor overpowered this marinara. Paige Bennett This marinara was pretty chunky from the diced carrots and celery. At first, I loved the sauce's sweet flavor , but there was a strong celery aftertaste. I used only one celery stalk in the entire batch of marinara, so I was disappointed that I tasted this ingredient more than anything else. Because of the time commitment required to make this marinara and the lackluster end result, I probably wouldn't make it again. If I did, I'd grate the carrots for a better texture and omit the celery completely. Garten uses a red wine in her marinara. events.title: UK will face AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure by 2028, official says
events.summary: Britain’s cyberchief says the U.K. is likely to face artificial intelligence cyberattacks on its critical infrastructure by 2028 LONDON -- The United Kingdom will likely face artificial intelligence cyberattacks on its critical infrastructure by 2028 as criminals and states, including China and Russia , increasingly use AI in their cyberactivity, Britain's cyberchief said Tuesday. That could include AI-powered malware for ransomware attacks as the technology will allow “vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long” to be discovered and exploited “at a scale that was once unimaginable,” said Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Center. One such vulnerability was discovered in refrigeration units that were targeted by hackers who turned up the temperature, causing food to thaw. The U.K. has also been affected, Horne said. In a speech marking the publication of the annual cyber report by the National Cyber Security Center, or NCSC, Horne said that the leaders of businesses and organizations of all sizes who have “got away with tech on the cheap” will have to explain why “food isn't on the shelves, lights aren't on, businesses have gone under,” if they fail to invest in cybersecurity or update out-of-date technology. Chinese cyberactivity is the “most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the U.K.” while both Russia and China will routinely use AI to achieve their geopolitical goals, the report said. Russia is intentionally conducting cybercampaigns which fall below the threshold of armed conflict, while Iran is carrying out attacks against the U.K. and targeting individuals who are a threat to the Iranian government, Horne said. The use of AI by states and criminals is highly likely to increase the scale and efficiency of hostile operations, but AI is more likely to be used to enhance and scale existing tactics and techniques rather than find brand new vulnerabilities, the report said. Technology “underpins the automation of physical processes that are vital to modern life,” Horne said. That includes, he said, electricity switching, sluice gates in water facilities, dam operations, manufacturing lines, heating and refrigeration controls. The recent cyberattacks on refrigeration systems in French supermarkets showed how easily hostile actors could exploit civilian infrastructure, Horne said. Fridges across Europe have been affected, including in the U.K., where security experts from the NCSC worked “through the night” to contact organizations with the vulnerable technology, Horne told The Associated Press. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Parents and 2 young children among victims of Learjet crash in Florida, family says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Refrigeration systems in France were attacked because they were using old technology which was no longer being updated and that was connected directly to the internet with default passwords, Horne said. It was, he said, not an AI attack but one where bad actors exploited vulnerabilities that have existed for a long time and showed the need for businesses to address the security of operational technology. Last week, governments and corporations worked on urgent security updates after the AI-assisted discovery of vulnerabilities in a programming language vital to 70% of websites globally. The two critical flaws identified by AI could allow bad actors to get unauthenticated access to sites which, in theory, could allow them to control a web server remotely without needing a password. Russia has already attacked critical infrastructure in Europe, according to the U.K. and European Union member states that said Russia's FSB security service was behind an attack on Poland's energy grid in December 2025. If the attack had been successful, 500,000 people could have lost electricity during winter. In the U.K., malicious cyberactivity is costing organizations almost $20 billion every year, the NCSC said. In 2025, the carmaker Jaguar Land Rover suffered more than $260 million in direct losses following a cyberattack which also hit suppliers and dented the U.K. economy. “We need every organization in the U.K. to take action now. Not only to protect their customers, services and livelihoods, but because cybersecurity is now part of the front-line defense of our nation,” said Anne Keast-Butler, director of GCHQ, Britain’s signals intelligence agency, which the NCSC is part of. That includes implementing basic but effective cybersecurity measures such as making sure devices are up to date, limiting administrator access to systems and backing up important files and data, the NCSC said. events.title: Voyager CEO on space death, why Mars matters, and how to fix data centers 500 miles up
events.summary: The money crunch that has hit AI in recent weeks is coming for the space industry, which shares DNA, investors, and market vibes with artificial intelligence. “If you’re a high-quality, well-run company with a good balance sheet and a good business model, you are very well positioned because everyone’s paying attention,” Dylan Taylor, CEO of Voyager Technologies, said on this week’s episode of . Everyone else is “being cast aside.” Voyager builds space infrastructure for the Pentagon and defense contractors, and is working on a commercial space station, Starlab, to replace the International Space Station when it is retired in 2030. The company is publicly traded, which last month allowed it to raise $400 million on terms roughly in line with a hot convertible-debt market. “Low cost of capital [is] a secret weapon,” Taylor said, “because the first question is, ‘how do you compete with SpaceX?’” Even Elon Musk’s behemoth is feeling the squeeze: It throttled usage of its Grok AI bot this week because, as Musk said in an X post Sunday , it was getting too expensive. Taylor, like most space executives today, counts Musk as both a competitor (for contracts and capital) and collaborator (Voyager’s hardware hitches a ride on SpaceX’s rockets). The space and AI trades are increasingly twinned, tapping into similar pools of capital, riding similar national-security vibes, and carrying similar potential of catastrophic escalation. “It’s the same thing,” Taylor said of the two, but for a different reason: their potential to reshape every corner of the economy. “Everyone is in the space industry,” he said. “They just don’t know it yet.” We also talked to Taylor about building data centers in space, which would sidestep the energy needs and political backlash back on Earth. And if they break? Just “build more,” is Taylor’s quintessentially American answer. — Liz Hoffman and Rohan Goswami

events.title: Global refinery inputs fell sharply in the second quarter of 2026 before modest recovery
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: Kpler Note: 2Q2025=second quarter of 2025 Global crude oil refinery inputs fell by 4.8 million barrels per day (b/d) in the second quarter of 2026 (2Q26), or 6%, following the start of conflict in late February in the Middle East, according to data from Kpler. Throughput then increased by 1.8 million b/d in the third quarter, primarily as refiners in the region adjusted to new trade flows. Crude oil inputs to refineries typically increase in the second and third quarters of the year as refiners complete planned maintenance and gear up to meet peak seasonal demand for refined products, such as gasoline and jet fuel. Global crude oil inputs increased by 0.3 million b/d in the second quarter of 2025 and by another 2 million b/d in the third quarter. The countries with the largest refining capacity in the world are the United States, China, Russia, and India. Refining in countries most directly impacted by the loss of crude oil supply from conflict in the Strait of Hormuz saw the largest declines. Crude oil refinery inputs in China fell by 2.1 million b/d in 2Q26 and by an additional 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26, while crude oil inputs in India, South Korea, and Japan fell by more than 1.0 million b/d collectively in 2Q26 before rebounding by 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26. Crude oil inputs also fell in the Middle East as the closure of the strait significantly limited the export of refined products. Crude oil inputs fell by 0.7 million b/d in Kuwait, 0.7 million b/d in the United Arab Emirates, 0.3 million b/d in Saudi Arabia, and 0.2 million b/d in Iran in 2Q26. Total crude oil inputs in these four countries increased by 0.4 million b/d in 3Q26. Increased attacks on Russian oil infrastructure during the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine reduced refinery crude oil inputs in Russia by 0.6 million b/d in 2Q26 and an additional 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26. Russia is a major fuel exporter, especially of diesel fuel, so the decline in exports affected global diesel markets that were already tight from earlier geopolitical developments . This loss in refinery operations compounded reduced refining activity in Asia and the Middle East, contributing to diesel prices increasing to the highest nominal levels on record in September . Although crude oil inputs were falling in some countries in the second and third quarters of 2026, they increased in the United States and in some other regions that were able to find alternative sources of supply. Crude oil refinery inputs in the United States increased by 0.5 million b/d in 2Q26 and by an additional 0.5 million b/d in 3Q26, as the United States increasingly exported refined products around the world to make up for lost supply. Global refinery crude oil inputs recovered somewhat in 3Q26, increasing by 1.8 million b/d overall as increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz, alternative routes, and ship-to-ship transfers put more Middle Eastern crude oil on the global market. Despite the increase in oil flows and refinery inputs, crude oil inputs in 3Q26 still remained about 5% lower on average than during the same period of 2025. events.title: BP not eyeing return to renewables
events.summary: BP isn’t likely to reverse its pivot away from renewable power generation anytime soon, CEO Meg O’Neill told Semafor. Since she took the helm in April, O’Neill has been focused on salvaging the company’s finances. She got a big helping hand in the third quarter as its profits nearly quadrupled thanks to high oil and gas prices and a busy trading desk, which O’Neill channeled into cutting debt by nearly 40% . She is also carrying forward the spinoff of BP’s renewable energy businesses that started under her predecessor, although it hasn’t always been easy: Lightsource BP, the company’s utility-scale solar arm, has been on the market for months. Lightsource “is a very big and complex business, but we’re making headway on that,” she said on the sidelines of ADIPEC. “In terms of investing in low-carbon [energy], we need to do that only when we can generate shareholder returns,” she said, citing green hydrogen projects in Europe as an example. But renewable power isn’t a good match for BP’s skill set, she cautioned: “There are people who can do utility-scale solar and make money at it. We’re happy to let people who are experts in that do their thing, and we will stay focused on oil and gas.”

events.title: Gas on the ballot in US elections
events.summary: Tim’s view Today’s US election is a test of how much voters will want to punish the president for soaring gasoline and power prices. Energy costs are always an important factor in elections; gas prices are the only economic indicator displayed in big bold numbers at major intersections. But between the war in Iran and the data center power rush, there’s rarely been an election in which energy prices — and the policy decisions pushing them up, from the White House to local zoning boards — are so much in the headlines. The average gas price during US President Donald Trump’s two years back in office is the highest it’s ever been halfway through a presidency, according to a Financial Times analysis. Since the oil embargoes of the 1970s, US presidents have been keenly aware that Americans have a very limited willingness to tolerate pain at the pump in the service of foreign policy objectives. And in many of the key congressional battlegrounds, AI-linked increases in household power bills are a central point of tension , making the votes a kind of referendum on how hard to hit the brakes on data center development, too. If Democrats succeed in regaining a majority in one or both houses of Congress, the US energy story is in for big changes over the next two years. The party’s leaders will face an immediate challenge, needing to decide how much hardball they’re willing to play with Republicans and the White House over permitting reform. Federal budget fights will likely resurface arguments about tax incentives for EVs and other clean tech. Investigative committees will demand answers from the administration about everything from offshore wind lease pullbacks to the diesel deal with Moscow. Meanwhile, a new cohort of state and local leaders will grapple with what kind of pressure to apply on the power demands of Big Tech. These are the storylines I’ll be focused on here until 2028. Happy voting! Notable The US attacked Iran’s Qeshm Island , the latest in a series of targeted strikes that came even as President Donald Trump pushed for an off-ramp in his war with Tehran.

events.title: What we're watching on election night for energy
events.summary: There's a lot at stake for energy in the midterms, from the fate of the bipartisan permitting deal to the growing backlash against data centers and electricity prices. Why it matters: The results could spotlight which energy topics resonate with voters — and which have become political liabilities. Gasoline and diesel prices have been big on the campaign trail, offering a chance to see how much voter frustration over energy costs matters at the ballot box. Data center politics: There are sharp differences between the parties, even though data centers aren't especially popular with either party's slate of candidates. Why it matters: The pace of the AI buildout affects power demand and emissions. State of play: 32.4% of Democratic candidates support moratoriums at the federal, state, or local level, compared to just 3.4% of Republicans, per Data Center Watch, which tracked hundreds of races. Zoom in: Meanwhile, Ballotpedia is tracking dozens of ballot measures on data centers, many of which would impose new restrictions. Ohio is a hot spot. Control and permitting: The outcome will affect the politics of the lame-duck session — and that means the politics of the bipartisan permitting deal. What they're saying: If Democrats take both chambers, "leaders might opt to wait until they hold the gavels next year to renegotiate compromises," the research firm ClearView Energy Partners said in a note. Yes, but: A reminder that backers of the current bill think it's folly to expect political space to write a more liberal bill that President Trump would sign, or that could even pass the Senate. Threat level: What if the results are very close? ClearView notes that if Trump and allies contest the results, "weeks of post-election skirmishing could complicate passage of any bill." Political lessons: The results could offer clues about where energy and climate policy are headed. State of play: Exit polling is not famously precise, but it could provide a barometer of how much voters truly care — or not — about data centers. It's also worth watching how candidates who made high gas and diesel prices central to their campaigns fare tonight. My thought bubble: Keep an eye on the performance of progressive vs. centrist Democrats. If the latter overperform, it could be another sign that aggressive climate policies won't return to vogue with Dems. Zoom in: Let's say, for instance, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's (D) victory is even more of a blowout than expected. That could bolster more centrist, oil and gas-accepting candidates in the 2028 cycle (when he might run for president). The next Congress: Regardless of chamber control, don't look for many opportunities for big new energy laws if permitting goes kaput. Yes, but: There will be no shortage of messaging bills and positioning for the 2028 White House race. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) has pledged to bring back clean energy tax credits killed in the 2025 GOP budget law. What we're watching: Limited chances for common ground around nuclear power and geothermal. For instance, the wide-ranging Senate permitting bill contains several bipartisan geothermal bills that already cleared the House. Oversight power: If Democrats take control of either chamber, expect aggressive investigations of White House energy policies and investments, a topic we recently explored. State utility bosses: A number of states have elections for electricity regulators, who often exert powerful control over power prices and planning. Zoom in: One place to watch is Georgia, where two Democratic victories would flip party control of the state's Public Service Commission for the first time in decades. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution has more. Governors: The winners of governors' races will have a big say in everything from oil and gas development to electricity prices. Zoom out: S&P Global has a nice look at energy differences in several governors' races, though a number of the contests are not especially competitive. Friction point: One place to watch is Texas, where oil and gas interests favor incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) in his surprisingly tight race against Gina Hinojosa. events.title: Car finance: Barclays becomes first big lender to offer payouts for mis-selling of loans
events.summary: Bank to make ‘early settlement’ offers before outcome of legal battle, with those who accept likely to get money before Christmas Barclays will this month start offering compensation to tens of thousands of people who claim they were mis-sold car loans, with some of those who accept likely to see the money land in their account before Christmas. Amid an ongoing legal battle over an industry-wide compensation scheme for victims of the UK’s car finance scandal, Barclays has become the first big UK lender to break cover and begin offering payouts to some customers who have complained. Under the rules, “early settlement” offers of this kind must at least match what people would receive under the multibillion-pound scheme that is being challenged – which may help to address fears that banks might try to make “lowball” offers. But consumers face a tricky decision as, depending on the outcome of the legal battle, they could end up with more money, less money or nothing at all if they decide to decline the offer and wait. In March this year, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) announced a £9.1bn compensation scheme for the millions of victims of the scandal. But legal challenges forced the regulator to partly suspend the scheme , and a hearing to decide what happens is due to go ahead in February next year. The FCA had expected to start paying out £829 on average this year to those affected by the scandal, in which drivers were overcharged for loans as a result of commission payments between lenders and car dealers between 2007 and 2024. Millions of people were treated unfairly when they took out motor finance to buy a new or secondhand car, motorbike or van, and ended up paying more than they should have done. Until the legal challenge is concluded, lenders do not need to pay compensation to people owed money under the scheme. However, Barclays Partner Finance – part of the banking group – has decided to offer payments now to some of those who would be due compensation under the scheme. That has prompted speculation that other companies on the hook for payouts will follow suit. It is understood that over the next couple of weeks, tens of thousands of Barclays customers who have already complained will be contacted directly and offered “an early full and final settlement”. Barclays is using the FCA model to calculate the compensation offers. It said: “Acceptance is optional, and customers will receive clear information on how their offer has been calculated and what accepting it would mean.” They will have a month to accept or reject the offer, and if they say yes, the bank will pay the money into their designated account. It is thought the first payments for those who accept the offer will arrive before Christmas – which may feed into some people’s decision-making. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning But those who accept cannot then later seek additional compensation or pursue further complaints or legal claims relating to the commission on that agreement. Alternatively, people can reject the offer and wait to see what happens. The FCA said that if it saw off the legal challenge and its scheme was upheld, payments could begin in 2027, but if the judgment was appealed or the scheme was partially or wholly overturned, any compensation owed could be delayed until 2028 or later. Ultimately, depending on the outcome, those who decline the early offers could end up being entitled to “more, less, or no compensation”, the regulator said. It added that it supported lenders making settlement offers, “as long as customers are offered no less than they would receive through the scheme”. Barclays Partner Finance said it would not ask people who accept now to repay any of their compensation if the final outcome meant they would have been entitled to less cash. Barclays has set aside £430m in connection with alleged motor finance mis-selling, and it is not clear how many people could be affected in total, or what proportion will receive early settlement offers. Under the FCA scheme as it currently stands, compensation payments depend on the details of the case. By far the biggest category is deals that allowed the dealer or broker to increase the interest rate the customer would pay, to get a higher commission.

events.title: Investcorp readies for deluge of Gulf infrastructure deals
events.summary: Investcorp, one of the Gulf’s largest asset managers, is preparing for a spree of infrastructure deals in the region as governments look for new ways to finance massive investment plans to reduce their reliance on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Gulf states will be more open to partnering with investment funds to pay for new infrastructure projects in the future as they look to preserve cash, Investcorp chief investment officer Rishi Kapoor told Semafor. These funds have become more active in the Gulf in recent years as governments and state-owned companies seek to raise money by selling stakes in oil pipelines and other assets that for decades have been kept under state control. The scale of the buildout in new infrastructure needed in the wake of the Iran war is set to open up a bigger role for private investors. “One of the really attractive investment themes unfolding in the Gulf in coming years will be the renewed focus on building resiliency into essential infrastructure,” Kapoor said. Investcorp already has several deals to acquire Gulf infrastructure assets in the works and could look to raise a new infrastructure fund in the next year or two to help it boost dealmaking.

events.title: DOJ sending 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states
events.summary: The Justice Department said Tuesday it will deploy about 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states for the first time ever to watch the polls. Why it matters: The unprecedented effort comes after courts repeatedly rejected the DOJ's efforts to force states to restrict voting for alleged noncitizens. It comes amid a long-running Trump administration push to fight voter fraud , which studies say isn't nearly as prevalent as the administration suggests. Driving the news : The department, in a statement early Tuesday, said one of its most important goals was to protect election integrity. "Today, the DOJ will further this mission by engaging in its largest monitoring effort in history—with approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers deployed, and, for the first time, in all 50 states," the department said. The department said observers would come from the DOJ, U.S. Attorney's offices, and staff from the Office of Personnel Management. What they're saying: "I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner," assistant attorney general Harmeet K. Dhillon said in the statement. The intrigue: Some local election officials have already expressed concerns that such a massive wave of observers could intimidate or otherwise interfere with voters. What to watch: The DOJ is still pursuing legal efforts in multiple states to have ballots segregated or otherwise impact counting.

events.title: Drax wants to feed Britain's AI habit with £20B datacenter at biomass power station
events.summary: Britain's AI infrastructure boom could soon have an unlikely new home: Drax Power Station, where the operator of the country's largest biomass power plant has unveiled plans for a £20 billion datacenter development capable of consuming more than a gigawatt of power. Drax announced on Tuesday that it has teamed up with investment giant Brookfield and its UK-based AI infrastructure business Radiant to build the facility at its North Yorkshire site. The money would come through a joint venture between Brookfield and Qatar's Qai, although the £20 billion headline figure is more ambition than actual money on the table at this stage. The companies plan to start relatively small, at least by the standards of the AI industry's apparently bottomless appetite for electricity. The first phase would deliver up to 100MW of capacity by early 2028, backed by a proposed £2.5 billion investment. A second phase could add another 500MW between 2028 and 2031, with further expansion taking the site beyond 1GW after that. However, a few hurdles remain between today's announcement and a functioning AI megafactory. According to Drax's regulatory filing , the first phase still requires planning permission, regulatory and network approvals, commercial agreements, and final investment decisions. It also needs a tenant, which is a fairly important detail when you're proposing to spend billions on somewhere to house other people's computers. Drax reckons its existing infrastructure gives it an advantage over developers struggling to secure electricity connections. The 1,000-acre site already has access to 4GW of grid capacity, 2.6GW of active generation and cooling infrastructure, along with proximity to the UK's fiber network. The UK government estimated last week that all of Britain's existing data centers use around 2GW of electricity. Drax's proposed development alone could eventually need more than 1GW, although how much power it actually consumes will depend on how fully it's used. The first phase would draw electricity from the grid, but Drax wants to supply up to 500MW directly from its existing generating capacity under a long-term power purchase agreement, potentially allowing AI servers to run on electricity produced by burning imported wood pellets. That brings another complication. Drax signed a government-backed Contract for Difference agreement last year covering biomass generation between April 2027 and March 2031. The agreement allows the company to request permission to redirect up to 500MW of capacity towards a datacenter, but ministers and the Low Carbon Contracts Company would have to agree, taking into account consumer value, energy security, and sustainability. The announcement also arrives as enthusiasm for enormous AI server farms is proving rather less universal outside government and industry circles. Opposition to data center developments has been growing on both sides of the Atlantic, with communities raising concerns about electricity bills, water consumption, and the impact of industrial-scale facilities on their surroundings. A recent investigation found that businesses accounted for 84 percent of the stakeholders UK ministers met to discuss datacenters between July 2024 and June 2026, while environmental groups secured precisely zero meetings. Drax and its partners are promising a community benefits fund and say public consultation will begin this month. Whether that will reassure residents concerned about another enormous consumer of electricity is a moot point. Drax CEO Will Gardiner said the project could "help secure the long-term future of the site and protect hundreds of jobs," while supporting Britain's ambitions to become a major player in AI. The government, unsurprisingly, is enthusiastic. Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds welcomed the proposed investment as an opportunity to create jobs and support Britain's reindustrialization. “Investments like this will help pave the way to a new age of British reindustrialization, creating good jobs in Yorkshire and delivering growth right across the country,” she said. Ministers may be enthusiastic, but Drax still has to find a customer, secure planning permission, and convince regulators before anyone starts plugging in servers. ®

events.title: Saudi Aramco reports profit surge on higher oil prices
events.summary: Saudi Aramco reported a 9% rise in profit and increased dividend payments, most of which go to the Saudi state, as a jump in crude prices more than made up for lower production. Profit rose to $31.2 billion in the third quarter, driven by a 35% increase in the average selling price of its oil, even as the company tackled repeated attacks on its facilities from Yemen’s Houthis and Iranian strikes on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Despite Aramco’s ability to export oil at higher prices, its stock has lagged the global majors that mostly operate outside the Gulf. Although lower than prewar levels, Aramco reported higher oil production than the previous quarter as it embraced more risky ship-to-ship transfers to get crude out through Hormuz and boosted shipments through the Red Sea. Aramco is looking to maximize production through the end of the year, “utilizing all the routes that we have,” and sees buoyant demand lasting for several years, CEO Amin Nasser said on an earnings call. It could take two years to refill depleted global oil storage reserves even if the Iran war was resolved today, Nasser said. — Matthew Martin

events.title: At ADIPEC, war is the challenge and AI the opportunity
events.summary: Mohammed’s view Abu Dhabi’s annual energy exhibition is buzzing, tangible proof that the UAE has absorbed the blows of the Iran war and has its eye on the future. Most conversations I’ve had at ADIPEC, one of the biggest events on the global calendar, have focused on opportunities: oil above $100 a barrel, a new unconventional oil play being unlocked in the UAE, fusion, AI, and infrastructure upgrades. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman spoke at the opening ceremony, a symbol of the close relationship between energy and technology. There’s plenty to be excited about in the industry that remains the Gulf’s economic lifeblood. But this ADIPEC isn’t like its predecessors, and it’s not just because of the war. The UAE’s decision to leave OPEC has changed the gathering’s makeup. This event previously brought together the group’s energy ministers, with major decisions made on the sidelines. This year, Saudi Aramco doesn’t even have a booth, a sign of increasingly fractured Gulf business relations. While the biggest Saudi, Kuwaiti, Omani, and Qatari companies stayed away, the rest of the world is here, with participants from more than 170 countries. Yet the absence of top executives from ExxonMobil and Chevron, as well as US government representation, has been noticed. Amos Hochstein, a former senior energy and national security adviser to President Joe Biden, was forceful in his critique : “I think they should be here,” he said of US officials. “The United States and UAE are close allies, you have to be here when it counts.” The war is transforming everything in the region, from trade flows to alliances, but the conflict itself may, in hindsight, seem temporary. The bigger shift will arguably come from AI, determining the future winners and losers. Hochstein said the UAE is a “critical partner for the US when it comes to AI buildout,” and Sultan Al Jaber, UAE minister of industry and advanced technology and managing director and group chief executive of ADNOC, stressed the point by having Altman as the guest of honor. ADNOC agreed to become the first energy company to deploy OpenAI Frontier, part of a partnership with OpenAI and G42 to improve operations, strengthen resilience, and increase productivity. “From the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI,” Al Jaber said. “And now, together, we will find out what AI can do for energy.” Notable Energy executives in Abu Dhabi are saying disruption is now a permanent feature of their business, Bloomberg reported.

events.title: Reading the signs of war in the Gulf
events.summary: Separating signal from noise on whether the US-Iran war will escalate has been difficult for months, and now it’s a cacophony. Oil prices plunged on Monday on hopes of a deal with Tehran before jumping almost 2% Tuesday after the US struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, reportedly in response to Iranian fire at an American plane . Yemen’s Houthis are still attacking Saudi Arabia and have advanced toward Aden, threatening to outflank Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces and potentially extend Iran’s influence to Bab el-Mandeb, the Gulf’s other maritime chokepoint. Then there’s diplomacy. US President Donald Trump told Axios he’s in “ no rush ” to resume strikes and repeated that Tehran wants a deal. US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks are also returning to Abu Dhabi next week, with Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner expected to attend, making an escalation during their visit seem less likely. The US midterm elections Tuesday are perhaps the noisiest indicator. Democratic control of either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in his last two years, potentially accelerating military plans before the new Congress takes office in January. But the president will still have considerable foreign policy powers. The final signal probably matters most: Where are the bombs and planes? Three US aircraft carrier strike groups are expected to arrive near Iran within two weeks , with the USS Theodore Roosevelt the last one to make its way from Japan. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: OpenAI hires Republican adviser, bucking trend among tech companies
events.summary: In recent weeks, we’ve chronicled a rush of companies staffing up with Democrats in anticipation of a blue wave on Tuesday. But on Monday, OpenAI bucked the trend, hiring former US Army secretary Dan Driscoll for a new national security role just two months after he resigned after clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. While tapping a top Republican operative close to the vice president defies conventional wisdom, it’s a good reminder that Trump remains president for another two years — an eternity in AI time — and that OpenAI sees value in advancing its priorities while it still holds executive favor. Regardless of what happens in Tuesday’s midterm elections, OpenAI knows that Trump’s national security apparatus remains a powerful force in deciding which new models get approved for use and who can access them. — Ashley Gold

events.title: Virgin Media O2 outlines plans to lay off thousands as revenue falls
events.summary: Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) wants to chop a third of its labor costs and is expected to lay off thousands of workers, giving staff more to think about than Christmas presents during the run up to year-end. Shrinking the workforce is one of a number of cost reduction measures designed to save the UK's second largest telecoms provider some £800 million by 2029. It currently employs 16,000 people and redundancies will "equate to roughly 30 percent of the company’s total people costs" over the next two years, VMO2 said on Tuesday. The majority of the redundancies will come from "non-customer facing roles," it claimed. The Register asked the telco to be more specific on the headcount cuts and the type of roles are at risk. A spokesperson refused to provide a number, saying those plans are being finalized and consultations are due to take place. Logically, if more senior head office positions are hit then fewer people will need to leave to meet the £300 million ($402 million) target figure. The Reg understands thousands of roles are at risk. Another lever management at VMO2 is pulling involves halting investment in any further fiber network upgrades beyond existing commitments. Instead, a low-cost upgrade will be deployed to its hybrid fiber-coaxial (HFC) network (i.e. cable customers) to bring 2 Gbps services to the majority of the network in 2027. Full fiber merger pledges VMO2 was formed in 2021 by the merger of broadband and TV biz Virgin Media and mobile operator O2. The pair pledged to spend £10 billion (c $13.4 billion) on beefing up 5G coverage and laying gigabit "full-fiber" fixed-line networks. Both Virgin Media and O2 talked up those connectivity commitments when justifying the case to combine their businesses, saying they needed greater economies of scale to compete with their rivals. However, business has not gone as planned, with revenue falling over several successive quarters. The latest figures for Q3 ended September 30 show total revenue down 5.7 percent year-on-year to £2.43 billion. The networks giant blamed consumer fixed market pressures, among other things. VM02 forecasts a revenue decline of 3 to 5 percent for the whole of 2026. In the consumer division, VMO2 talked of more clearly defining the role for each of its brands. O2 Business is planning to streamline the product portfolio. Tom Oughton, senior analyst at Megabuyte, said the changes were expected. "VMO2 has undergone a strategic review as it looks to address rising leverage, with today confirming a transformation program to ultimately bring c. £800 million ($1bn) in cost savings ahead of its first debt expiry in 2029. The routes to achieve this are the most obvious ones: reduce capex on full fiber and focus on HFC upgrade (lower cost, quick payback) and reduce operational costs by cutting headcount," Oughton said. "The obvious question is how a significant transformation will impact the business. VMO2 focuses on the benefits, but the business is declining 3-5 percent organically with 16-17k staff, so reducing headcount by 25 percent or more could stretch operations, worsen customer support, and cause broader disruption." Paolo Pescatore, founder and analyst at PP Foresight didn't mince his words either: "Virgin Media O2 is in serious trouble, with customer losses and declining service revenue and earnings exposing the scale of the challenge." "The business has lost its strategic direction, and continued customer departures suggest it is struggling to rebuild trust while rivals give people compelling reasons to switch. Cutting costs can buy time, but it cannot repair those relationships or compensate for weak execution," Pescatore added. "Management must show customers why they should join and stay; otherwise, it risks shrinking the business without fixing what is driving people away. Shareholders need to take a hard look at these businesses and make even tougher choices about their future." Noel McClean, deputy general secretary of Prospect union, said the job cuts " will be devastating for those directly affected and will of course have an impact on colleagues remaining in the business. "Industry conditions are tough but this level of cuts will drastically alter the way VMO2 works." ®

events.title: The US midterms decide who gets blamed for the economy that’s coming
events.summary: Liz’s view Today’s US midterm elections are a race to see who gets blamed for a host of economic problems coming down the pike. Democrats are favored to take the House, with control of the Senate still a toss-up. Whoever wins Congress inherits a stack of problems due to detonate over the next two years — just in time to crater 2028 ambitions — and few have obvious fixes. Inflation is running around 3.7%, rising in six of the past eight months, and the Fed has gone back to unpopular tightening. That a Trump-picked Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, is leaning hawkish into a midterm election underlines how stubborn the problem is. The labor market is no better. Employers added just 29,000 jobs in September; July was revised into negative territory. Companies too uncertain about what’s ahead — and unsure of exactly how AI is muddying the employment picture — are neither hiring nor firing, leaving things in what Jerome Powell earlier this year called “ an uncomfortable kind of balance. ” Then there are the outside shocks. Reports that the White House is planning post-midterm strikes on Iran may push political fallout from an unpopular war outside the election window, but the economic weight of high gas and diesel prices lands on whoever’s nominally in charge come January. Those are the known unknowns. AI brings another set of unknown unknowns: A financial squeeze waiting to happen, as investment shows no signs of slowing down even as the returns on that investment appear even further out than we thought. A leaking AI bubble is likely to burst on the next Congress’s watch (as always, look to the jittery credit market , not the booming stock market, for signs of what’s to come). The second problem is political, and Congress has punted on it. Lawmakers left town in September with no movement on AI guardrails. Dozens of data-center moratoriums and AI referendums appear on the ballot today, with more than 20 in Ohio alone . Even some of President Donald Trump’s media allies concede that he owns the narrative on the economy no matter what happens on Capitol Hill. But a Democratic Congress would give the White House a foil it hasn’t had since the back half of Trump’s first term, and every stalled bill, shutdown, and soft jobs report could be pinned on the people holding the legislative pen — and subpoena power (more on that below in today’s newsletter). Either way, the winners tomorrow aren’t claiming a prize so much as signing for a package. Notable Who controls Congress will make little difference to the economy, analysts argue. “A lot of voters head to the polls Tuesday hoping for a fix for affordability,” The Wall Street Journal’s chief economics commentator wrote. “ They are going to be disappointed .”

events.title: Air India seeks more wide-body jets, sees profitability ‘very soon’, CEO says
events.summary: Air India CEO Tewolde Gebremariam speaking at the Aviation India event in New Delhi, on Nov 3. Air India wants to increase an order for wide-body aircraft as it seeks to boost international passenger traffic, chief executive Tewolde Gebremariam said on Nov 3, adding that the Tata Group-owned carrier would return to profitability “very soon”. The comments come three months after the former head of Ethiopian Airlines took charge of Air India , which is driving a sweeping turnaround while grappling with higher operating costs, geopolitical disruptions and losses. “We want more wide-body aircraft,” Gebremariam said at the Aviation India event in New Delhi, signalling the airline’s ambition to further strengthen its long-haul fleet as it pursues overseas growth. Air India has held talks with both Boeing and Airbus as it weighs the cost of running its older wide-body jets, said an industry source who sought anonymity for lack of authorisation to speak to the media. “The cost of operating old wide-bodies is high, and they’re not very efficient,” the source said, adding that newer aircraft would help the airline connect more cities and navigate the impact of Pakistan’s ban on use of its airspace. “There are so many cities they don’t connect,” the source added. Airbus said it does not comment on any discussion with its customers on their fleet plans, while Boeing did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Gebremariam did not respond when asked how many wide-body jets Air India seeks to order. Since returning to the ownership of India’s sprawling Tata Group conglomerate in 2022, the airline has embarked on a multi-billion-dollar transformation programme covering fleet renewal, cabin upgrades and network expansion. Tata owns about 75% of Air India, with Singapore Airlines owning the rest. It has been adding new aircraft and refurbishing older jets to improve service standards and compete more aggressively on international routes. REUTERS

events.summary: The witness-prep business is about to take off for Washington law firms. As Democrats appear poised to take the gavel, at least in the hearing-happy House of Representatives, the task of helping corporate executives prepare for their turn in the chair — a DC practice known as “murder-boarding” — will be in high demand. Democrats have been plotting for months about how to go after corporations that have courted Trump’s approval, Semafor’s Nicholas Wu reported earlier this year, citing missives sent to companies over things like ballroom funds, antitrust suits, and business deals involving the Trump family and one-time “first buddy” Elon Musk. “Companies that made investments or commitments at the president’s urging should prepare for scrutiny,” said J. Peter Donald, a former spokesman for the FBI’s New York field office and assistant NYPD commissioner who now advises companies in tight spots. “Everything will be on the table. CEOs should be ready to explain their decisions under oath.” It’s a good time for companies to prepay any outstanding law firm bills and book some time on CEOs’ calendars for mock grilling. — Liz Hoffman

How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal. Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice. events.title: Tech companies rummage for cash to fund the AI buildout
events.summary: Tech companies are turning over the couch cushions in their hunt for money to fund the AI buildout. Meta is prepping a big bond offering that includes its first-ever euro borrowing for up to $15 billion, people familiar with the matter tell Semafor, while Alphabet closed its second euro deal of the year. The tech giants that have run through US markets are now turning to other pools of capital. Alphabet this year issued its first-ever British sterling bond — a rare “ century bond ” that comes due in 2126 — along with deals that tapped Swiss and Japanese debt markets. For most companies, broadening lender bases is a test-the-pipes exercise to ensure that diverse funding is available if it’s needed. For hyperscalers today, it’s a globe-trotting bush-beating that’s crucial to funding the AI buildout that’s propping up their stock prices. — Ellen DiMauro
