events.title: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is rolling out into beta testing on Tuesday, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes. The news was first announced via an emailed press release sent out by Apple’s communications team in India early on Tuesday. The update rolled out in the U.S. and other markets later in the day. The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist. However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps. Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them. With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the stand-alone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation. Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things. When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said. These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them. The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations. Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information. Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone. This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features. At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days. This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning. Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night. Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center.

events.title: Aged over 50, experienced and looking for work. Will employers bite?
events.summary: Even as older workers are encouraged to remain in the workforce for longer, the question is whether employers are willing to hire them. Singapore will raise retirement age to 65 and re-employment age to 70 from Jan 1, 2029, as the Government backs plans to help older workers stay in work. Older jobseekers like Raj Bharij, Gurmit Singh Kullar and Jason say they face instant rejections, overqualification fears and long job searches after retrenchment or resignation. Data shows weaker hiring for older workers: 42% in their 50s and 39% over 60 found jobs within six months, versus 61% in their 40s; employers may still value contract roles and transferable skills. SINGAPORE – Raj Bharij lost his job in 2026 when his employer, a global bank, restructured. “I’m 50 years old,” he recalls thinking, when told of the retrenchment in April. “Is anyone going to actually hire me now?” Six months on and more than 100 applications later, the former transformation director is still searching for his next job. He has received “instant” rejections, within seconds, from some firms’ automated systems and radio silence from others. An artificial intelligence chatbot tasked with helping to refine his resume suggested he take five years off his age. Bharij and other mature job seekers whom The Straits Times spoke to believe that being older and more experienced has somehow made their job search harder. Their experiences highlight a question facing Singapore: Even as older workers are encouraged to remain in the workforce for longer, will employers be willing to hire them? Singapore will raise its retirement age to 65 and re-employment age to 70 from Jan 1, 2029 – one year ahead of an earlier target. This was announced on Oct 26, 2026, when the Government accepted recommendations from the Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment aimed at helping older workers remain in meaningful employment for longer. The move comes as the Republic’s population ages . The share of workers aged 50 and above in the workforce grew from 34% in 2015 to 40% in 2025, and is expected to rise further, a report by the workgroup said. Gurmit Singh Kullar, 52, left his job as a marketing director in July 2024 after experiencing burnout. Re-entering the workforce after a six-month break has proven an uphill task. Many marketing roles these days, he found, merge what would previously have been three jobs into one, effectively denting the value of his past experience. He applied to more than 200 openings in less than two years. When he did not hear back from prospective employers, he widened his search to include more junior or mid-level roles that paid just half of what he had been earning. Still, they did not bite. Hiring managers sometimes commented he had too much experience. “Isn’t it better for you to have someone more qualified?” he wondered. He attended career counselling and a handful of courses to learn new skills, where he encountered other mature job seekers in a similar situation. “Have you heard this line from people, that you’re overqualified?” he was asked by a man who had been retrenched from the insurance industry. Older workers are taking longer than others to find new work after losing their jobs, data from the Ministry of Manpower shows. In the second quarter of 2026, 42% of people in their 50s and 39% of those over 60 found new jobs six months after a layoff, compared with 61% for those in their 40s. A study by researchers, including Lee Zeewan from the National University of Singapore, found that 47% of employers surveyed were likely to hire workers in their 50s, compared with 35% who were neutral and 18% who were unlikely to do so. That number fell to 33% for workers aged 60 and above, they said, in a paper published earlier in 2026. Kirsty Poltock, a country manager for Singapore at recruitment firm Robert Walters, notes that the difficulties which older job seekers describe come as the market grows tougher for candidates in general, and firms’ hiring slows. She surmises that the labour market has become “less forgiving about a mismatch” between job seekers’ existing experience and the skills which firms are looking for, but believes there are still opportunities for workers in their 50s, having regularly placed such candidates in new roles. Contract work is one area that could play to senior workers’ strengths, she said, as more companies hire for non-permanent roles on a one- or two-year horizon as the economic outlook weakens. People who can articulate how their experience can help firms transform their human resources or finance operations, for instance, are seen as valuable hires, Poltock added. As their search for new work continues, Bharij and Gurmit are also having to deal with the emotional toll that being unemployed later in life brings, after having grown accustomed to the rhythm of work over decades. “The loss of identity is massive,” said Bharij, who used to describe himself as someone who worked at a bank.

events.title: Cities Worldwide Build and Scale AI Services With NVIDIA Physical and Agentic AI
events.summary: Cities generate enormous amounts of data from cameras, sensors and operational systems, but turning it into useful action — for planning, maintenance and public services — remains a challenge. Physical and agentic AI offer new ways to close that gap, from digital twins for infrastructure planning to vision and service agents, while keeping local governments in control of how sensitive data is processed and used. Building on initiatives announced at GTC Berlin , NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own. From resident services to vision agents, cities are adopting NVIDIA agentic AI to deliver faster, more responsive public services. City teams don’t need a massive infrastructure investment to get started building these AI services: depending on the workload, NVIDIA RTX workstations or a small GPU system may be enough. In Spain, 1MillionBot combines open source ALIA models trained at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center with NVIDIA Nemotron and other models in resident-service agents for Madrid Digital (Comunidad de Madrid), Administració Oberta de Catalunya and 150+ deployments across Spain, handling municipal procedures, appointment requests, urban-planning incidents and service inquiries. In the San Francisco Bay Area , LiveX is bringing its AI City vision to life with NVIDIA Cosmos world models and Nemotron open models, and Omniverse and Metropolis libraries on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs. The interactive, conversational AI hosts understand people’s needs, provide answers and take action, and can be tailored to local languages and service needs in airports, hospitals, local events and other public spaces. Vision AI agents can turn existing city camera feeds into operational insights, helping teams identify mobility and safety issues and coordinate emergency responses across city services. In Wrocław, Poland , K2K is building shared AI infrastructure using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Cosmos world reasoning models, and NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) to transform existing camera streams into actionable intelligence for mobility, safety and event response — using the same infrastructure across several city functions. In Malaysia , ITMAX bundles infrastructure and agentic AI applications into long-term managed services for cities, including for traffic management. Built with reference to Cosmos, Nemotron and the Metropolis VSS blueprint, ITMAX’s SamurAI V2 vision agents are scaling on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs to support 17,000+ cameras by 2027. ITMAX integrates TeraSim, an open source traffic simulation platform from Laplace Intelligence , to test signal timing, reducing peak-hour corridor travel times by up to 26%. Plan and Operate Critical Infrastructure With Digital Twins Beyond public-facing services, digital twins can help cities expedite infrastructure planning, minimizing disruption to local communities. City digital twins can also serve as a real-time operational simulation to facilitate faster decision-making. At Dangote’s Lekki refinery in Nigeria, Honeywell Technologies’ Forge Plant Cognition uses Nemotron-powered AI agents to understand operational data. A digital twin of the plant and its processes, built using Omniverse libraries, is also planned to support simulation and training. The platform, built on Dell PowerEdge servers with NVIDIA RTX PRO accelerators, helps operators identify bottlenecks, anticipate equipment and process issues, and optimize plant performance. In Taiwan , Linker Vision and Dutch architecture firm MVRDV are using NVIDIA Omniverse and Nemotron to build environmental, social and governance agents that can assess the environmental impact of various urban planning scenarios, simulating 15-year outcomes of an urban forest canopy in 10 minutes — increasing design iteration speed from two weeks per iteration to less than an hour. Cities can extend AI to more services by building on infrastructure already in place and adding capacity. Shared resources and managed services can help extend those capabilities across departments and municipalities. At Morocco’s Tanger Med port, Cires Technologies is expanding a sovereign AI factory for planned applications in worker safety, congestion analysis, cargo routing and port operations. events.title: Chalmers promises to be 'helpful' on inflation but rejects blame for rate hike
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government will play 'helpful role' on inflation but not at fault, Jim Chalmers says Jim Chalmers pointed to evidence that public sector demand was easing. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Jim Chalmers says the government's budget is "not what's putting upward pressure on inflation" after a fifth rate hike this year. The Reserve Bank made the widely expected move on rates. The government has promised fresh savings in the mid-year budget update next month. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has again denied his budget is the cause of persistent inflation, after the Reserve Bank raised interest rates for the fifth time this year. Facing political pressure over the level of government spending, the treasurer seized on the bank's assessment that public sector demand was "weaker than expected" in early 2026, the period when inflation began its resurgence. "Public demand growth has eased quite substantially at a time when private demand has tripled," he said. "Our budgets are not what's putting upward pressure on inflation, but we can play a helpful role and that's what we intend to do." RBA lifts interest rates to try to dampen inflation The RBA lifts interest rates to the highest level in 18 years in a majority decision by its board. Mr Chalmers has promised fresh savings in next month's mid-year budget update, but could not say whether the savings would be enough to outweigh new spending, a feat the Albanese government has not managed in any of the five years it has overseen. "We take responsibility for our part of the fight against inflation," he said. "We're helping with the cost of living at the same time as we manage the budget responsibly." Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock maintained her longstanding practice of avoiding direct comment on the government's budget, saying overall demand, combining public and private, remained too high across the economy. "It's up to the government, the elected officials, to decide what they want to do with the budget," she said. "Independence is a two-way street. I don't tell them what to do with fiscal policy. They don't tell me what to do with interest rates." Public demand eases, but question marks over role of NDIS Ms Bullock said the decision on rates, which was not unanimous, was motivated by the ongoing consequences of the Middle East and domestic factors. The main domestic driver, though not the sole one, has been artificial intelligence investment. The bank's updated forecasts predict business investment will grow by 12 per cent this year and public demand by just 2.1 per cent. The "weaker" public result was partly due to "the ending of some temporary cost-of-living measures", a staff note explained. Also cited was a "moderation" in spending on defence, disability and aged care. The largest single category of savings by far under the Albanese government has been to the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS), with $36 billion saved over four years in the May budget alone. But fresh doubts have been raised over whether that saving can be achieved, after the publication of preliminary findings from the Australian Government Actuary that the $36 billion figure was subject to "considerable uncertainty". Though cautioning that he did not have "sufficient detail" to draw a firm conclusion about the costings, actuary Guy Thorburn noted several risks, including an assumption of the numbers of children with autism entering the scheme not yet borne out by reality. The government has not been specific about where further savings will be found in the budget. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said she was "looking across government" for ways to cut back, but that these would be "difficult decisions". "We have to respond to the economic circumstances we face … [But] we're also mindful of the fact we need to support people through this as well," she said. "I hear a lot of calls for cuts to government spending, I don't hear as many specifics about where." Could government spending cuts fight inflation? The Reserve Bank is tipped to increase interest rates tomorrow because of an ongoing concern that inflation is not under control. But is there an alternative? Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said the government had a "spending addiction" and was fuelling inflation. "[It] will never pull in its belt, but it keeps telling Australians to pull in theirs. It stokes inflation, taxes inflation and spends inflation," he said. While public demand is growing much slower than private demand in the Reserve Bank's forecasts, the bank does expect it to grow faster than the economy overall.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Models are commodities, harnesses are the valuable part A whopping 3% of boardroom execs spy productivity and costs savings from AI 7 days ago Alibaba's Qwen AI caught trying to contact server in China 7 days ago IBM CEO says open weight models are now irresistibly good and cheap on-prem 12 days ago Nvidia woos wary Europeans with more open weights models 13 days ago The AI math isn't mathing as infrastructure spending forecast to outstrip expected revenue 20 days ago For-profit model-makers, many of which are spending billions on AI infrastructure, will be chasing revenue from just ten percent of steps involved in agentic AI workflows, according to analyst firm Gartner. “Nine in 10 agent workflow steps are routine, and open-weight models handle them at parity for a quarter of the price of the cheapest closed model,” the firm’s senior director Mark Petty and group vice president Raymond Paquet wrote last week in new document titled “Open-Weight Models Will Run 90% of Enterprise Agentic Workflow Steps.” “Typical operational workflows involve hundreds of routine executions, such as classification, tool calling, passing, validating and reconciling data,” the pair observe, before suggesting open-weight models “can handle hundreds of these routine steps for every one that needs frontier reasoning.” “Against the cheapest closed model at the same score, the open model costs a quarter as much. Against a frontier model run on every step, it costs as little as a twentieth,” the pair add. Those are the best-case numbers, because the analysts admit “Current open models can be more verbose and retry more often, so the saving per task against a frontier model is closer to five or six times.” That’s still a lovely saving, but the analysts rate it as the welcome by-product of moving to open models rather than an end in itself. “Years of workflow history are a large part of what an acquirer pays for in a SaaS company and every routine step sent to a frontier API moves a slice of it outside your perimeter,” the pair wrote. “Open-weights preserve your control. The cost saving is a bonus.” The two analysts therefore offer the following strategic planning assumption: “By 2030, 90% of enterprise operational agent workflow steps will execute on open-weight models.” They argue that enterprises will mostly adopt domain-specific open-weight models, because they do well “in scenarios where a small number of highly stable steps run millions of times a month.” Most models, however, are already commodities. Harnesses, the tools that run agents and manage agents, are the source of value in AI products, because one of their roles is to route work to the most appropriate model for a job, without users noticing any impact. A good harness saves money, imposes strong guardrails, and manages agent fleets. Less powerful harnesses leave users with more to do. The paper suggests frontier models will continue to have a role as the engine of research and development and are effectively capital expense. events.title: Victorian farmers blindsided by approval of 155-turbine wind farm ahead of election
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Victorian farmers blindsided by wind farm approval on eve of election caretaker period A 155-turbine wind farm has been approved for Victoria's north. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding ) The Victorian government has approved the controversial Meering West Wind Farm, which could include up to 155 turbines, a day before entering caretaker mode. More than 100 objections had been lodged and neighbouring farmers say their concerns have been ignored. The project's future could hinge on the November 28 state election, with the Coalition pledging to scrap the VNI West transmission line the project intends to connect to. The Victorian government has signed off on a large wind and battery project for the state's north, on the eve of entering caretaker mode ahead of this month's state election. Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny signed off on a planning permit for the Meering West Wind Farm on Monday, just a day before the caretaker period came into effect. The facility to be built at Meering West, about 140km north-west of Bendigo, would be one of Australia's largest, incorporating up to 155 wind turbines. Construction on the project, which would deliver 1.3 gigawatts of generation capacity and 1,000 megawatt-hours of battery energy storage, is due to start in 2029. Like other similar facilities, it has been deeply controversial among local residents, with many farmers rallying against its approval. The timing of the approval is further complicated by the facility's intention to tap into the VNI West transmission line, which is yet to be built and would be scrapped if the Victorian Coalition came to government. Tyler Nelson is one of many neighbouring farmers who have objected to the project. He said he was not surprised the government had signed off on it at the last minute. "I'm very disappointed, but at the same time I can't say I'm shocked with the behaviour of the Labor government," he said. "It's well established that there are a lot of projects being rushed through at the 11th hour and there's been a pretty poor process involved for quite some time." Tyler Nelson is among the many farmers who oppose the Meering West wind farm. ( Supplied: Tyler Nelson ) Mr Nelson said he and other neighbours had been unaware of the project until it was well advanced. "Most neighbours and those affected found out pretty late in the piece, once there were contracts and caveats in place," he said. Mr Nelson said more than 100 people had objected to the project, with concerns including noise, shadow, flicker, land devaluation, fire risk and impacts on the natural environment. He said their objections and requests, including removing turbines from the project footprint close to objecting neighbours, had not been adopted. The wind farm at Meering West would have 1.3 gigawatts of generation capacity. ( Supplied: Pixabay / JACLOU-DL / License /File ) Mr Nelson was reluctant to comment on the community divisions the project had created. "I've tried not to let it affect me, but it's difficult not to," he said. "Communities that usually stand together and talk, when that's taken away, it seems a bit odd." Victoria's election is nearly here — it's time to have Your Say Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most. Given the Coalition has committed to scrap VNI West, Mr Nelson said he hoped there would be a change of government on November 28, but he was not convinced it would leave the Meering West project dead in the water. "It would be nice to think that is the case, but what we're learning is we never know what's happening with backroom deals," he said. "Yes, scrapping VNI West is a good move by the Coalition, but what does it mean for this project? "It's my understanding that [project proponent Virya] will continue to develop on somehow, but I don't know what that looks like." The Victorian government, Meering West Wind Farm representatives and developer Virya were contacted for comment.

events.title: Hope for house hunters amid slump as realtor warns optimism premature
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Perth property price slump provides glimmer of hope for homebuyers Vanessa Bray says a drop in Perth house prices has given her hope of finding a home for her family. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) Home buyers are hopeful a drop in Perth property prices will help them break into the market. New data shows the city's median dwelling value has fallen to $942,018, but that is still 68 per cent higher than it was five years ago. A Perth realtor warns the optimism of those trying to buy a home may be premature, saying the figures do not represent the true state of the housing market. After years of searching for a home as Perth property prices continued to rise at an unprecedented rate, Vanessa Bray finally feels like she has a fighting chance of securing one. The single mum has been buoyed by new figures showing Australia is tracking towards its biggest housing market downturn in 40 years, with Perth's house prices dropping 5.7 per cent over the last three months. Data from property research group Cotality shows Perth's median dwelling price has fallen to $942,018 — a drop of nearly $100,000 since peaking at more than $1 million in April. Meanwhile, economists at the Commonwealth Bank today released an updated forecast predicting Perth property prices would plummet 18 per cent from that April peak, before prices begin to stabilise in the second half of 2027. For Ms Bray, the easing market spells hope of finding a home for her and her sons. Vanessa Bray is feeling a lot more positive about buying a home in light of recent data. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) "I can't even begin to describe the relief that I feel for myself and my kids that we could maybe have a home of our own," she said. "It's close. I feel like it will happen instead of the despair that I had that it was never going to happen." National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, according to property research group Cotality. Ms Bray has been looking for a family home since she and her partner separated four years ago. She needs to find something in their school catchment while staying under the $850,000 cap needed to qualify for the federal government's Help to Buy Scheme. Ms Bray said her experience of trying to buy a home had been '"devastating" and like being on a "rollercoaster". "[I've gone from] thinking, 'right, this could finally be it. I'm going to make it. I'm going to have long-term security for me and my kids' to the devastation of 'I've missed out again'," she said. Perth's median dwelling price has fallen by almost $100,000 in six months. ( ABC News: Gian De Poloni ) While the recent slump in prices represents a glimmer of hope for those trying to break into the market, the softening represents a small dent in the meteoric rise in Perth's property prices, which have risen 93 per cent in a decade, including 68 per cent in the last five years. Perth realtor Kyle Peters warned the optimism of those trying to enter the market could be premature. Mr Peters said the recent figures were not a good representation of the true state of Australia's housing market. "It would be an interesting anomaly that a housing market would crash when we have a housing crisis and don't have enough houses for people to live in," Mr Peters said. "At the rate things were ramping up before, there needed to be some abatement, but certainly we [still] have a housing shortage." REIWA president Rob Mandanici said even if prices did not continue to fall on the same trajectory, the slowing market still provided benefits for those entering the market. REIWA President Rob Mandanici says the easing should give buyers some breathing space. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) "They can take a little bit more time to make that purchasing decision and not feel that immense pressure to rush into a decision," he said. "The buyers themselves haven't disappeared, they've become more selective." House prices are falling all around the country. ( ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes ) Mr Mandanici said there was no doubt Australia was experiencing "a little bit of a market slowdown", but said the dip in prices did not amount to a crash. "We are seeing some prices across multiple Perth suburbs pull back, but a lot of those suburbs are coming off highs," he said. "We've got a lot of buyers sitting on the sidelines and I think today's interest rate decision will just give buyers the certainty that they want moving forward." On Tuesday the Reserve Bank increased interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, lifting the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, the highest it has been since 2008.

events.title: Aramco posts 34% jump in third-quarter profit despite attacks on energy infrastructure
events.summary: Saudi Arabia's Aramco , the world's largest oil-producing company, has reported a 34 per cent annual increase in its third-quarter net income despite disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on energy infrastructure in the kingdom. Net profit for the three months to the end of September rose to 135.94 billion Saudi riyals ($36.25 billion), up from 101 billion riyals for the same period last year, Aramco said on Tuesday in a statement to the Tadawul stock exchange, where its shares are traded. “Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security,” Aramco president and chief executive Amin Nasser said. “Despite challenges, the flexibility of our system and the strength of a supply network built over decades enabled us to continue delivering reliably to our customers through this extraordinary period.” Aramco's board approved a third-quarter base dividend of $21.9 billion, a 3.5 per cent year-on-year increase, which will be paid in the fourth quarter of this year. Revenue boost The annual quarterly increase was driven by higher revenue despite volatile global energy markets, where prices shifted according to geopolitical headlines. Total revenue for the reporting period rose to $140.5 billion, up from $111.6 billion recorded for the third quarter of 2025. “The increase in revenue was predominantly driven by higher prices of refined and chemical products and crude oil, partially offset by lower volumes sold of crude oil and refined and chemical products,” Aramco said. The company's increased quarterly income provides a boost for Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s biggest economy, which still relies heavily on the sale of hydrocarbons for revenue. Aramco, Opec’s biggest oil producer and the main driver of Saudi Arabia's industrial sector, has faced waves of missile and drone attacks from Yemen’s Houthi militants that have put pressure on government revenue. In October, a Houthi missile attack damaged Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran. The attack caused a fire in an administrative building in the complex. Several crude refining facilities, including those in Jazan in the west and Riyadh, have also been attacked in recent weeks, raising fresh concerns about Saudi Arabia’s energy industry and Aramco’s ability to continue supplying crude oil to its global clientele. The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks on vessels rose in October to the highest level since the US Iran-war began on February 28, is adding to oil exporters’ woes. Overseas storage To avoid Hormuz, Saudi Arabia has ramped up crude shipments from its main export hub at Ras Tanura. The kingdom has relied on its East-West pipeline to pump crude to its Red Sea port. However, the pipeline was temporarily shut down after missiles launched from Iraqi territory damaged a pumping station. Saudi Arabia, which is also facing a Houthi-enforced maritime blockade, is exploring more routes to keep servicing its customers in Asia. “We continue to explore additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes to further strengthen our global supply network,” Mr Nasser said. While the East-West pipeline provides export flexibility, the company remains focused on operations and will continue to invest in projects, Aramco said. Production started at the company's Zuluf crude oil increment project in October. Major upstream projects, including Jafurah phase two, the Fadhili Gas Plant expansion, and the Dammam development project, remain on track, the company said. Aramco's capital expenditure of $10.5 billion in the third quarter is, however, lower than the $12.6 billion reported for the same period in 2025. “Backed by our strong balance sheet, we remain focused on the disciplined execution of priority projects … to unlock new opportunities,” Mr Nasser said. “This is how we will continue to meet the world’s evolving energy needs and deliver value for our shareholders and customers.”

events.title: Adnoc Gas to supply TotalEnergies with up to 1.6 million tonnes of LNG in five-year deal
events.summary: Adnoc Gas has signed a five-year agreement to supply up to 1.6 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas to France's TotalEnergies, as the Abu Dhabi company expands its share of the global LNG market. The deal builds on a long-standing partnership between the two companies and reflects growing demand for LNG and confidence in Adnoc’s ability to deliver reliable supplies, the company said on Tuesday. “ Global demand for LNG continues to grow, and Adnoc Gas is well-positioned to capture that opportunity,” said Fatema Al Nuaimi, chief executive of Adnoc Gas. “This agreement reflects the strength of our LNG business, the competitiveness of our supply offering and our ability to secure long-term partnerships that support growth, enhance resilience and create lasting value for shareholders.” Adnoc Gas has continued to execute its long-term growth strategy this year, despite operational constraints. The company awarded $8.2 billion in engineering, procurement and construction contracts, part of its largest capital investment, for the second and third phases of the Rich Gas Development project – $3.9 billion for Phase 2, and $4.3 billion for Phase 3, the company said in August. These contracts build on Phase 1, announced in June 2025. The Rich Gas Development is a multi-phase, $13.2 billion capital investment programme by Adnoc Gas to expand gas processing and liquid recovery infrastructure across the UAE. The latest move strengthens Adnoc Gas’s commercial position at a time when demand for LNG is rising across Europe and Asia. Asia remains the main destination for LNG, accounting for about 65 per cent of global imports in 2025, while Europe has become a major buyer as it replaces Russian pipeline gas and manages storage needs, according to the International Energy Agency’s latest gas market report. “Thanks to its perfect location between Europe and Asia, this new supply will enable TotalEnergies to confirm its position as one of the main LNG portfolio suppliers,” said Stephane Michel, president of gas, renewables and power at TotalEnergies. TotalEnergies is both a shareholder in Adnoc Gas and a partner in the Ruwais LNG project. Adnoc Gas said it expects the planned integration of the Ruwais LNG project to significantly increase its production capacity, supporting its ambition to become one of the world’s leading LNG suppliers. The agreement between Adnoc Gas and TotalEnergies comes as Adnoc scales up a new global LNG marketing and trading platform that combines the marketing activities of Adnoc Gas and investment arm XRG with the trading capabilities of Adnoc Trading . The platform is aiming to reach 47 million tonnes per annum of marketable LNG beyond 2030, a level intended to place it among the world’s leading LNG marketing and trading businesses, Adnoc Gas said on Tuesday. Adnoc Gas supplies about 60 per cent of the UAE’s sales gas needs and supplies end-customers in more than 20 countries.

( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Journalist Kate McClymont has given evidence in the Alan Jones trial where she was questioned about whether her reporting on Mr Jones was profit-driven. Ms McClymont spoke with three of the five complainants in the trial for stories published in late 2023 and early 2024. Mr Jones's team has also accused her of "introducing" the words "go the grope" in her interview with one complainant. The journalist whose work sparked a police investigation into broadcaster Alan Jones has been questioned about whether she had a "profit motive" to run a series of stories about the former 2GB radio host allegedly indecently assaulting young men. Kate McClymont gave evidence on day 55 of Mr Jones's criminal trial at the NSW Local Court, where he has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. The court has heard Ms McClymont, who is a multiple Walkley Award-winning journalist and the Sydney Morning Herald's chief investigative reporter, spoke to three of the five complainants in the trial for stories published in late 2023 and early 2024. The defence has sought to poke holes in Ms McClymont's original reporting of the allegations against Mr Jones, some of which have since been explored during days of evidence in his criminal trial. Mr Jones's team has also accused the journalist of "introducing" the words "go the grope" in her interview with one complainant, and has suggested her reporting influenced the allegations other complainants made later. Mr Jones's barrister started her cross-examination of the reporter on Tuesday. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC probed Ms McClymont about why she wrote the stories, suggesting to her that there was a "profit motive" in writing articles about a high-profile person. "The story has to sell papers, doesn't it?" Ms Bashir asked. "That's not my problem," Ms McClymont replied. "It is correct to say that higher readership numbers encourage advertisers to invest in advertising with the paper?" Ms Bashir asked. "As a general proposition, yes, but that is not my role." Ms McClymont agreed Mr Jones was viewed "by some people" as "conservative leaning". "Alan Jones is a very public figure in New South Wales? He's a divisive figure?" Ms Bashir proposed. "If you say so," Ms McClymont replied. The journalist was also asked whether any money or benefit was paid to any alleged victim of Mr Jones in exchange for their stories, which she denied. Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching relating to five men. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) Ms McClymont confirmed she spoke to and published the allegations of three of the complainants in this criminal trial. She said she had no contact with two other complainants, the high-profile athlete known as Complainant M and a former up-and-coming athlete known as Complainant J. Mr Jones's lawyers have argued throughout the trial that Ms McClymont is on one side of a media rivalry which was set on "destroying" Mr Jones. That phrase became part of the headline of Ms McClymont's first article about Mr Jones, which was published in December 2023. events.title: UK job satisfaction at record low amid rising frustration over pay and flexible working
events.summary: Resolution Foundation study finds workers are less willing to go ‘above and beyond for employers than a decade ago’ Job satisfaction among UK workers has dropped to a record low, according to a study that shows a growing frustration with employers over pay and flexible working. Analysis by the Resolution Foundation thinktank shows that a lack of flexible working, insecure jobs and a loss of independence have undermined how workers feel about their employment. Based on the 2025 British Social Attitudes survey, the study found a sharp fall in satisfaction at work that translated into British workers being less willing to go “above and beyond for their employers than they were a decade ago”. Job satisfaction fell from 81% in 2015 to 74%, the lowest figure recorded in the British Social Attitudes survey since 1989, when the question was first asked. Fewer workers said they had an interesting job or one that offered the chance of advancement. The proportion of workers who said they would work harder than required to help their employer succeed fell from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025. The Resolution Foundation said its analysis would give policymakers an insight into how they could reverse decades of slowing productivity growth, low levels of job mobility and high economic inactivity among some groups, most notably younger people . Only 4% of workers said there was “little intrinsic value” from working – a figure that has remained flat over time. What has declined, the thinktank said, was the number of people feeling positive about the jobs they do. The proportion saying they have an interesting job fell over the decade from 74% to 63%. Hannah Slaughter, an economist at the foundation and co-author of the report, said there was a rise in the number of workers who said they suffered from low pay and this concern spanned all the pay scales. She said decades of low pay-rises and the spiralling cost of living was affecting the outlook of all groups, though the demand for greater flexibility was equally pronounced. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Workers increasingly want jobs that provide flexibility, independence and financial security. But many feel those expectations are not being met,” said Slaughter. “The result is rising frustration among workers, who report lower job satisfaction, declining willingness to go above and beyond, and a reduced appetite for full-time work. This ‘dissatisfaction drain’ is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn’t bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead.” Separate polling by Ipsos dating back to the 1980s supported the foundation’s study, with workers reporting much lower satisfaction this year than when the same question was asked in 1976 and 1986. In 1976 it found 83% were very or fairly satisfied with their work compared with 69% in 2026. John Curtice, the Strathclyde professor and pollster who is co-editor of the British Social Attitudes report, said the findings showed young people had not become more work-shy, “nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs. But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financial rewarding and have flexible work hours.”

events.title: ‘It brings soul into this sterile world’: the Birmingham clubbers fighting to save their patch – and Britain’s nightlife
events.summary: Digbeth is the city’s most thriving party district, but railway upgrades could tear it apart. Here, clubbers explain why they are doing everything to stop that happening H ouse beats ring out through the open air while a heaving crowd of young partygoers dance. Suddenly, they begin to chant: “Richard Parker, Richard Parker!” You might think he is the next DJ on the set list, but in fact he is the mayor of the West Midlands and this block party has been assembled to send him a message: leave Digbeth alone. It’s Sunday night and I’m in Birmingham’s trendy party district. It’s filled with bars, warehouse clubs and storied music venues. The 1,800-strong crowd of mostly twentysomethings at the Parker event fits right in. But buzzy scenes like this may soon be a thing of the past. Under plans proposed by the Midlands Rail Hub Alliance – including Network Rail, which owns and manages railway infrastructure in Great Britain – seven nightclubs, including XOYO Birmingham, Mama Roux’s and Club Colette, could be demolished from 2030. The aim is to expand a nearby viaduct, allowing more trains to run through Moor Street station rather than the more congested New Street, but striking a blow to the city’s nightlife. Ravers want Parker, who leads the region’s strategic transport agenda, to use his power to lobby against these plans. The proposal comes at a testing time for the industry. More than 26% of all late-night venues across the UK closed for good between 2020 and 2025, according to the Night Time Industries Association . Birmingham has been hit harder than any other major city, experiencing a 28% drop in the number of bars, clubs and other establishments where you might grab a late-night drink. But Digbeth, a former industrial centre where metal sheets, Typhoo Tea and Bird’s Custard were once manufactured, has stood strong as the city’s cultural bright spot – far cooler than Broad Street, Birmingham’s main clubbing strip, which has the vibe of a street-long All Bar One. It’s where some of the names now headlining electronic music festivals around the world caught the raving bug. The Birmingham DJ Fleur Shore, 30, has been coming to Digbeth since she was 15. “Here is where it all started for me,” she says from behind her decks. “Without Digbeth, I wouldn’t be where I am now. I get to go all over the world and do my job.” Shore has played gigs in the Argentinian countryside, the historic Plaza de España in Seville, Spain, and the mountains of Gran Canaria. But the UK has not always made it easy. “The UK is so strict,” she says. “They don’t embrace this part of people.” The Parker party is a way for young ravers to revolt, she says: “This country doesn’t value younger people who want to go out, let loose and socialise. When everybody’s all together, dancing to the same thing, it’s powerful.” The mooted demolition of Digbeth’s bars and clubs is just one example of the threats to British nightlife. In central London, a bitter battle is playing out between venues and the Soho Society, a community group aimed at “preserving the character of Soho”, which routinely objects to new bar and restaurant licences, often backed by Westminster council. Venues say the restrictions could “destroy Soho’s reputation on the international stage”, while the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, has criticised the council’s “breathtaking arrogance” . In Manchester, meanwhile, the famed music venue Night & Day cafe was threatened with closure after noise complaints from neighbours in new flats. After a three-year row, it was told to limit noise in the small hours. There is no doubt that noise can be a nuisance, but it is hard to understand how anyone who moves next to a decades-old venue in an area known for nightlife can claim to be shocked by it. The value of a good night out is being forgotten, says Shore: “There’s so much pressure in life. People come to these places to breathe, dance and not think about their problems. I feel like, the way things are going, we’re going to be a soulless nation.” Lina and Johnny, who are part of the crowd making its way down the Digbeth strip, agree. “People from all walks of life come together here to move our bodies and exist in harmony,” says Johnny, 24. “If this street is demolished, that will be a lot harder to do.” Lina, who is also 24 and a musician, says she has met “so many other beautiful, talented people” in the area. “Where would all these creative people go? It brings soul into this sterile world,” she says. Among a group who met only hours earlier are Hood Ssengendo and Daniel Wright. “The fact they want to demolish this whole thing is pointless,” says Wright, a 24-year-old music producer. “There is still a club scene, ravers and people that want to have a good time.” Ssengendo, a 25-year-old welder, says: “For most young people, this is their hotspot for a night out and to make friends.” For many marginalised communities, the district remains a safe haven for a night out.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters OpenVDDK is reportedly already being used in production, at scale GhostBSD 26.2 takes the fright out of FreeBSD with a friendlier installer 4 hours ago Broadcom denied names of cloud providers backing VMware merger challenge 9 hours ago SUSE to cut one in ten employees because of... AI 1 day ago 'Mother of all editors' Emacs is 50 2 days ago AlpineBSD announced – an AI-free FOSS OS 4 days ago A cloud architect has created an open source alternative to VMware’s Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK), which the virtualization giant recently withdrew from public downloads. VMware describes VDDK as “a set of libraries and utilities that enable software developers to create applications that can access and manipulate virtual disks” and “a valuable tool for developers of storage and backup applications.” Users, along with VMware’s rivals, had another use for VDDK: migrating VMs to alternative virtualization platforms. In August, VMware restricted access to VDDK downloads to its partners, meaning VMware customers couldn’t access the tool and some of its rivals’ migration tools became less effective. Cloud architect Andrija Panić decided to do something about it. “Many tools that have nothing in common except VMware use the same small library to read a virtual machine’s disks: virt-v2v and nbdkit, the importers in Forklift/MTV, Proxmox VE and Apache CloudStack, and countless in-house scripts,” he told The Register by email. “When public VDDK downloads ended, all of them became harder to install and run.” “I didn’t think it was fair that people’s ability to move or protect their own data should depend on a download page.” He describes the project as “an independent drop-in for libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3, the disk library that VMware backup and migration tools load to read virtual disks. It was written from scratch, using only public documentation and black-box testing, and contains no VMware code.” Panić told The Register he wrote the tool in Go, with a thin C layer that exposes exactly the same C interface, library name and symbol versions as VMware’s code. The tool cannot write disks, just read them for backup and migration purposes. In his email to The Register , Panić said he has successfully tested OpenVDDK on vSphere versions 6.7 U3, 7.0.3, 8.0.3, 9.1.1. He said that tests in his lab with the latter version, accessing OpenVDDK through vCenter on a standalone ESXi host, saw every disk read match. “Independent testers have reported successful use with Forklift (VMware to KubeVirt, cold and warm), MTV on OpenShift (cold and warm), a Proxmox VE pipeline and custom nbdkit-based tools,” the architect told The Register . “I've received reports of production use, including a German cloud provider migrating a large file server with V2K Migrate and a US-based company migrating to Apache CloudStack/KVM.” Panić was at pains to point out that the reports of successful use are “not independently audited customer endorsements or a guarantee of suitability for every production environment.” As is often the case with FOSS tools. OpenVDDK is not the only option for migrating away from VMware without VDDK. KVM-based OpenNebula has a tool called OneSwap that it says has a 96 percent success rate. Nutanix recently tweaked its “Move” migration tool so it can do the job without VDDK. Red Hat is working on a fix but has provided details of a workaround . Panić made OpenVDDK available under an Apache license, so perhaps Red Hat and others will find it useful as they re-jig their VM migration tools.

events.title: China to raise FX reserve requirement to slow yuan’s rally
events.summary: The People’s Bank of China said it would raise the foreign exchange reserve requirement ratio to 6% from 4%, effective on Nov 15. China’s central bank will raise the FX reserve requirement ratio to 6% from 4% on Nov 15 to slow the yuan’s strong rally and absorb US dollar liquidity. The move may remove about US$24 billion from the system and sent the onshore yuan down 0.37% to 6.6728 per dollar, its sharpest daily fall in six months. Markets see the step as mainly symbolic. The yuan has still risen more than 5% in 2026, backed by exports, trade surpluses and corporate FX sales. BEIJING – China is raising the amount of foreign currency that financial institutions must hold as reserves, in one of the strongest moves to slow the pace of a long rally in the yuan, setting the currency on course for its sharpest one-day drop in six months. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) said in a statement on Nov 3 it would raise the foreign exchange (FX) reserve requirement ratio (RRR) by 2 percentage points to 6% from 4%, effective on Nov 15. The adjustment would result in an extra US$24 billion (S$30.7 billion) being withdrawn from the financial system, according to a Reuters calculation based on official FX deposit data. The decision to raise the ratio is “aimed at strengthening the management of foreign exchange liquidity in financial institutions”, the PBOC said. The onshore yuan weakened as much as 0.37% against the dollar to a low of 6.6728 per dollar, the weakest level since Oct 23, following the announcement. And it looked set for the biggest one-day drop since May 15. Its offshore counterpart also followed the weakening trend. “The PBOC is responding to strong market-driven yuan appreciation,” said Marco Sun, chief financial market analyst at MUFG (China). “By absorbing part of the available US dollar liquidity in the banking system, it is attempting to reduce the momentum behind yuan appreciation and prevent the market from developing excessive one-way expectations.” The yuan has gained more than 5% against the US dollar so far in 2026, reaching its strongest level since 2022 and becoming one of Asia’s best-performing currencies. Its strength has been underpinned by robust exports, big trade surpluses and heavy corporate FX conversion. The FX RRR hike on Nov 3 would be a policy reversal of the PBOC’s decision in September 2023 to lower the FX RRR, which was a move to stem the yuan’s rapid losses and capital outflows. However, market participants do not expect the move to reverse the yuan’s upward trend. Xing Zhaopeng, senior China strategist at ANZ, said the move was likely to “carry greater symbolic significance” for the market. Corporates’ heavier FX settlement into yuan had “resulted in the current imbalance conditions of excess supply over demand”, Xing said. He added that the increase in the FX RRR would not be enough to ease the oversupply. Separately, the PBOC lowered its midpoint rate for a second day in a row on Nov 3 to 6.7150 per dollar, 661 pips weaker than a Reuters estimate – its largest weak-side deviation since Sept 10. The central bank has been gradually strengthening its daily yuan official guidance in 2026, but at levels weaker than market expectations, suggesting it is seeking to manage the pace of appreciation, market watchers said. Meanwhile, PBOC deputy governor Zou Lan reiterated the central bank’s stance on the currency. “China has promoted high-level opening-up and insisted that the market play a decisive role in the formation of the exchange rate,” he told a financial forum in Hong Kong on Nov 3. events.title: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
events.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.  Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).  The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.  It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).  But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.  So one month in, who’s on board? Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period. There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.  The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents). As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.  But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too. In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.  But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.   Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia. But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.  In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.  Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too . One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order , leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month. But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.  People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change. If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. events.title: SATS redeploys staff to baggage handling amid MOM probe into contracted firms
events.summary: Some SATS employees have taken on extra responsibilities or been temporarily redeployed to help the ground handler keep its baggage-handling operations running. SINGAPORE – Ground handler SATS has temporarily redeployed some employees and assigned others additional responsibilities to keep its Changi Airport operations running smoothly, amid investigations into possible work pass violations involving workers employed by its contractors and sub-contractors . In an e-mail sent to all staff and seen by The Straits Times on Nov 3, SATS thanked its employees for helping out and supporting the company through the “operational adjustments required in recent weeks”. “Some employees have taken on additional responsibilities or been temporarily redeployed to help ensure our operations continue to run safely and smoothly. Your dedication, flexibility and professionalism have been instrumental in maintaining service to our customers, and we thank you for your support.” The e-mail addressed to SATS employees also outlined a broader context on actions the firm has taken to “enhance verification process controls” to make sure contractor workers are deployed according to their work passes. “We are rectifying compliance deficiencies in accordance with MOM’s (Ministry of Manpower) guidelines,” said the company spokesperson in the e-mail, urging employees to reach out to team leaders if they have any questions or want to clarify facts after reading media reports on the investigation. A SATS employee, who did not want to be named, said employees, including those from non-operations departments, were encouraged to step up on a voluntary basis to help with baggage-handling services, especially to fill slots for the upcoming Deepavali long weekend. ST understands that employees who volunteer for additional 2½-hour block duties will receive $15 in NTUC vouchers, time off in lieu and transport allowance. SATS said on Nov 3 that it is regular practice for the company to invite employees across the organisation to volunteer their support during peak travel periods, and that the request for volunteers did not come as a result of the probe. The request for volunteers can include customer service and premier services ambassadors, as well as support for baggage services, added the SATS spokesperson. Vouchers or time off in lieu will typically be provided as a gesture of appreciation. “This provides colleagues from non-operational functions with opportunities to gain first-hand experience of front-line operations, while supporting operational teams and enabling front-line employees to take well-deserved breaks.” Responding to queries from ST, a spokesperson for Changi Airport Group (CAG) said it is working closely with SATS’ management team to “minimise the impact of the manpower situation on airport operations”. “CAG expects SATS and other operators at Changi Airport to strengthen the oversight of companies they contract with and to ensure that these companies comply with applicable manpower laws and regulations.” MOM said in a media statement on Nov 2 that it has identified around 270 workers, employed by SATS’ contractors and sub-contractors, whose deployment may not have been in compliance with work pass regulations. The ministry said it found Employment Pass holders deployed to perform baggage-handling services during a recent inspection. SATS’ share price fell 3.01% after the market opened on Nov 3, with about four million shares worth about $14.2 million changing hands as at 10.40am. Sharon Salim is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, with a focus on jobs, workplace culture and trends.

events.title: Interest rates highest since 2008 as inflation forecast to stay high
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts RBA lifts interest rates to highest level in 18 years to try to dampen inflation The RBA's monetary policy board has increased interest rates for the fifth time in 2026. ( Reuters: Jason Reed ) The Reserve Bank's monetary policy board has lifted interest rates by 0.25 percentage points. The decision lifts the cash rate target to 4.85 per cent, up from 4.60 per cent. It is the highest cash rate since late 2008. It is the fifth interest rate increase in 2026, and the RBA has left the door open for more rate hikes. The Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates to their highest level in 18 years, while acknowledging it will take much longer to drag inflation down than it was expecting a few months ago. It has increased rates by 0.25 percentage points, which lifts the cash rate target to 4.85 per cent, up from 4.60 per cent. The cash rate has not been this high in Australia since late 2008. It is the fifth time the bank has lifted rates in 2026. The brutal redistribution at the heart of the RBA's interest rate policy RBA officials argue the hit to borrowers' income isn't the main way rate rises lower inflation. But they often omit a key fact. The RBA board's decision to lift rates was not unanimous. Six members voted to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent, while three members voted to leave the cash rate target unchanged at 4.60 per cent. The majority decision will be another blow to households with mortgages. But individuals who have high-interest savings accounts will see their savings accruing more interest after today's decision, if their bank applies higher rates to their accounts. In a statement , the RBA board said inflation was now forecast to remain high throughout much of 2027 and was not expected to fall below 3 per cent until late 2027, which is "around three quarters later than previously forecast". "This presents upside risks to inflation expectations," it said. In recent weeks, RBA officials have been signalling their intention to lift rates at today's meeting, arguing that they can not afford to see peoples' inflation expectations drift higher. The RBA wants annual inflation in consumer prices to be around 2.5 per cent on average over the cycle. "There is an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that maybe 3 to 3.5 per cent is the new normal [for inflation]," RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser warned last month . It takes between 12 and 18 months for a change in interest rates to flow completely through the economy, so we will not know what total impact this rate hike will have on economic activity until 2028. Economy slowing, house prices falling, unemployment rising The RBA Monetary Policy Board said the cumulative rate hikes this year have tightened financial conditions in Australia. It says the economy is slowing, housing prices have fallen significantly this year, and the unemployment rate has risen. Why housing's the great Australian talking point Why are Australians obsessed with property? Because we have to be. And there are big reasons why it's always on our minds. Its new economic forecasts see growth in output slowing even further over the coming year, which is expected to reduce capacity pressures and help return inflation to target. It says employment is expected to keep growing, but the unemployment rate is projected to rise by more than expected. In August, it was forecasting the unemployment rate to average 4.8 per cent in the December quarter of 2028, but now it was forecasting it to average 5.1 per cent in that period. The unemployment rate is currently 4.7 per cent . But the RBA board has also acknowledged that there continue to be "heightened uncertainties" about the outlook for inflation and the economy. "The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is higher and activity lower than forecast," it warned. "Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation. "A period of prolonged uncertainty may also cause growth to be lower overseas and in Australia. "To date, however, growth in Australia's major trading partners has been stronger than expected, as the boost from AI-related investment has outweighed the adverse effects of the Middle East conflict," it said. Is the RBA pushing the economy into recession? In her post-meeting press conference, RBA governor Michele Bullock left the door open for more rate increases. She was then asked if the RBA was risking pushing Australia's economy into recession with more rate hikes.

events.title: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Google has launched its experimental AI app Dreambeans in India, its first market outside the U.S., as the company looks to tap the world’s second-largest internet market to bring personalized visual stories drawn from users’ digital activity to a broader audience. On Monday, Google expanded Dreambeans, available on Android and iOS, to India with support for 13 local languages, including Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali, alongside English. The launch comes less than two months after Google made the app available to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. Introduced in June, Google’s Dreambeans uses information from connected Google services, including Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube, to proactively generate personalized, illustrated stories about users’ interests and everyday lives, without requiring them to enter a prompt. The app initially featured static, AI-generated illustrations, but Google recently added a feature that uses its Veo video-generation model to even animate images in select stories. Google said it chose India as Dreambeans’ first international market because of strong interest from Indian users seeking access to the app and the widespread use of its services in the country. India stood out for its high overlap of users across Gemini, Gmail, and Google Photos, Google product manager Gozde Oznur said during a press briefing. Dreambeans has recorded nearly 55,000 downloads in the U.S. since its June debut, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with TechCrunch. About 63% of those downloads came in September, when Google opened the app to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. However, downloads dropped 84% month over month to about 5,500 in October. In the first 30 days after Google opened Dreambeans to all eligible U.S. users, the app recorded an estimated 29,000 downloads, compared with 7.4 million for Meta’s Muse, 2.8 million for ChatGPT, 362,000 for Grok Bot, and 155,000 for Claude during their respective first 30 days after launch, Sensor Tower estimates show. However, unlike those general-purpose AI apps, Dreambeans focuses on generating personalized stories instead of responding to a broad range of user queries. Even though Dreambeans supports many widely spoken Indian languages, users can select only one language at a time for their generated stories. The app can draw on information across Google services in multiple languages, but it cannot currently generate stories that mix languages, Oznur said during the briefing. That could limit Dreambeans’ appeal in India, where many people regularly switch between languages, including Hindi and English, often mixing the two in what is commonly known as Hinglish. Dreambeans’ dependence on information from users’ Google accounts also raises questions about privacy and data access. The app uses Google’s Personal Intelligence technology to draw on connected services and personalize its AI-generated stories. Those services can contain sensitive personal information that some users may not want to share with an AI app just to receive personalized content. Users can choose which Google services to connect to Dreambeans and disconnect them at any time, Oznur said. They can also delete their Dreambeans data from within the app. Moreover, Oznur asserted that information deleted from the underlying connected services is also removed from Dreambeans’ personalization system. Users, Oznur said, can tell Dreambeans to avoid certain subjects, including business-related information, and the app will try to adjust its stories accordingly. She added that Dreambeans is available only to personal Gmail account holders, not enterprise users, and that generated stories are visible only to the account holder. Dreambeans’ proactive approach also carries the risk of surfacing memories that users may find upsetting. Oznur acknowledged that Dreambeans could generate stories involving people who have died, for instance. She said users can tell the app to stop showing certain subjects, comparing the feature to controls in Google Photos that let users limit which memories appear. Oznur told reporters that Google is exploring ways to make Dreambeans more actionable, moving beyond personalized stories and recommendations to help users act on the app’s suggestions.
